October 4, 2009 – September 26, 2010

ii

Kenneth G. Nagel

Grand Master – 2009-2010
Brother Kenneth George Nagel, was Raised in 1972 in Liberty Lodge
No. 299 in Santa Clara. After serving as its Master in 1995, he assumed the office
of Secretary, a position he held for 12 years. An outstanding ritualist, Bro. Nagel
served as Officer’s Coach for Liberty Lodge and won the state jurisdictional
competition for the Staircase Lecture in the Fellow Craft Degree in 2005.
A native Californian, Bro. Nagel began his association in Masonry
through the Order of DeMolay. He was Master Councilor of Santa Clara Chapter
in 1969, holds the Degree of Chevalier and the Active DeMolay Legion of Honor.
He served as Chapter Dad for both Santa Clara and San Jose chapters, as well as
a member and Vice President of the Northern California DeMolay Foundation.
Brother Nagel served as Senior Grand Deacon of the Grand Lodge of
California, having been appointed to that position by Most Worshipful Sorsabal
in October, 2005. In addition he served as a Trustee and Vice President of the
Masonic Homes of California for eight years, as well as a member of the California
Masonic Foundation, the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the Nob Hill
Masonic Center. He has served Grand Lodge as Chairman of both the Masonic
Homes Endowment Committee and Fraternal Support Services Committee. In
1988, Liberty Lodge presented Bro. Nagel the Hiram Award for his many years
of service to the Craft.
Both an active Scottish Rite and York Rite Mason, Bro. Nagel served the
San Jose Scottish Rite Bodies both as Venerable Master of the Lodge of Perfection
and Wise Master of the Chapter of Rose Croix. In 2007, he received the 33rd
Degree, being coroneted an Inspector General Honorary in the San Jose Bodies.
His achievements in the York Rite have also been extensive. He has
presided over all three bodies of the York Rite, and his rank as a Knight of the
York Grand Cross of Honour recognizes his leadership to the organization. As
well, he has received the Meritorious Service award in his Royal Arch Chapter,
the Grand Master of Ish Sodi Award and Cryptic Mason of the Year in 2005 in
Cryptic Masonry, and Knight Commander of the Temple in his Commandery of
Knights Templar. Continuing his love of ritual, he served as the Grand Director
of Ritual for the Grand Council of Cryptic Masons of the State of California from
1998 until 2007.
His other Masonic memberships include the Sciots, the Royal Order of
Scotland, the Red Cross of Constantine, the Order of the Eastern Star, the National
Sojourners, and the Heroes of ‘76.

iii

Brother Nagel now lives in Santa Clara with his wife, Kathy. They met
while he was in DeMolay and she in Job’s Daughters. They have been married
for 39 years. Brother Nagel retired from the United States Navy as a Commander
in 1994 after 21 years of service and in 2006 retired as vice president of a small
software company in the Bay Area. He earned a Bachelor of Science Degree in
Administration of Justice from San Jose State University. Brother Ken was elected
Grand Master at the 160th Annual Communication in October 2009.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

One Hundred Sixty-First
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, September 24, 2010
The 161st Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master
Kenneth G. Nagel on Friday, September 24, 2010.
Worshipful Mark Litherland, Master of Liberty Lodge No. 299, raised
the opening session of Grand Lodge.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand Marshal
to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at the Altar.
The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, following which
the Grand Master, accompanied by the Deputy Grand Master, personally greeted
each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our Past
Grand Masters by the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters were
then escorted to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master then
directed the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the usual
letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional
number was present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following
were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

9

The Grand Master welcomed the visiting Grand Officers from other
jurisdictions and directed the Grand Marshal to afford the guests seats in the
auditorium.
The Grand Master then invited Most Worshipful Bud Banks, Grand
Master of Nevada to bring greetings on behalf of all the visiting dignitaries.
“Most Worshipful Grand Master Ken, Deputy Grand Master Bill,
Visiting Grand Masters, Past Grand Masters and all Brethren:
It is my honor and pleasure to bring greetings from across our great
nation to each of you here with a special greeting on behalf of a unique
group of Masons – some now Past Grand Masters and others of us soon
to be such – who shared an unforgettable year together as Grand Masters
in 2010.
Unique in that we all are Masons from Lodges in the Jurisdiction of
Washington, while serving as Grand Masters of Alaska, Oregon,
Washington, California and Nevada. It is not strange that this could take
place, for the bonds of union and friendship that Freemasonry provides
is truly universal.
We in Nevada this year celebrate our 145th Anniversary. Nevada became
the 36th State on October 31, 1864 and we owe to California a great
deal for our Masonic heritage. On January 17, 1865 the Committee on
Constitution was discharged and Nevada’s first Grand Master Joseph
DeBell was installed, Nevada joined the nation’s jurisdictions. Our
original Lodges were chartered under the California Grand Lodge
including Carson City No. 154 in Carson City, Washoe No. 157 in
Washoe City, Virginia No. 162 in Virginia City, Silver City (now Amity)
No. 163 in Silver City, Silver Star No. 165 in Gold Hill, Esmeralda No.
170 in Aurora, Escurial No. 171 also in Virginia City and Lander No. 172
in Austin. These eventually became numbers one through eight under
our Charter and four of them remain active today.
Last year in this beautiful Auditorium, each witnessed an unforgettable
experience, a very moving experience, about the early years of your
Grand Master and First Lady, as well as a tribute to the men and women
of World War II in which your Grand Master’s father served proudly in
the U.S. Navy as your Grand Master did in the years to follow. From
this experience your Grand Master introduced his project for the year
“Operation Greatest Gift.” In addition Ken’s theme for his year has been
“Coming Home.”
This highly successful theme has apparently carried over to the Navy
League of Nevada where on October 8th in Reno, Ken’s theme has been

10

Proceedings of the
adopted “Coming Home” to be used to recognize those remaining crew
members of the USS Nevada, who will be honored. The Battleship was
christened in 1914 by Most Worshipful Grand Master and Governor,
Tasker Odie, the only ship to get underway at Pearl Harbor in 1941.
Ever since the late 1950’s we all know that membership in Freemasonry
began a steady decline. Not until 2007, nearly 50 yers later, the growth
of Freemasonry has grown beyond our expectations. There are many
reasons for this, much not of our doing, other than keeping the light of
Freemasonry alive.
Most is the result of our information age, and a few books being written
and television programs that deal with the History of Freemasonry,
this has not fallen on deaf ears. As the men whose interest has been
heightened, are bringing with them, credentials to our doors not seen in
many years, and not seen in my 56 years as a Mason. This era is my era,
I am sure R.W. Senior Grand Warden Frank will agree, this was the era
of the Ying and Yang of Freemasonry. Science states, that nature truly
abhors a vacuum.
Men today have lived through the era of those who die with the most toys
wins. These men are looking for that which cannot be bought or sold,
they are looking for the priceless ingredient in their lives, my Brothers
we know that has to be Freemasonry.
Let us now return to where you are sitting today, in this Auditorium,
to last year at this time. Let’s now reflect on the events of this year, a
year that your Grand Master Ken has so well named “Coming Home.”
For those who have been honored by your Grand Master Ken, and for
your outstanding support of his Vision, his dream, his Mission. To give
thanks in the twilight years of those heroes of World War II, those who
protected our freedoms and our Great Country, by making available a
three day expense paid trip to the World War museums in Washington
D.C. Through your generous support of over $435,000 over 600
people made a trip to Washington D.C. as they were honored as our
Greatest Generation.
Most of these men and women have but few years remaining, through
this experience they were able to reflect on their nation and the memories
of their brothers and sisters with whom they served our nation, this will
remain forever with them.
There is another side to this great vision of Grand Master Ken. Each of
us know how busy our year as Grand Master is. Most Worshipful Ken’s
is no different. Except, he took that extra step for Freemasonry.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

11

This year Ken visited four jurisdictions and held eight meetings with
invited California Masons living in other jurisdictions. There he shared
his “Coming Home” story with all. A lot of tears were seen in the eyes
of both men and women. I had the privilege to attend one of Ken’s
presentations in Reno. His message “Coming Home” was to encourage
Masons to renew the gift of Freemasonry they received by attending
their lodge when in California. Also, to encourage them to attend a lodge
within their community where they now live, to revive that meaning
Freemasonry held in their hearts as they were brought to light, to share
that light with Brothers, so the light of Freemasonry will continue to
burn brightly wherever they travel.
Thank you, Grand Master Ken, on behalf of all of the Grand Masters
assembled here today and for Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth,
that your legacy leaves with each of us, we congratulate you on an
outstanding year.”

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

15

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Irwin M. Fershleiser,
Grand Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren.
“At this time we are assembled as Brothers in the family of fraternal
friendship and brotherly love, to pause and look back on the passing of many of
our brothers who have been called to the House not made with hands. They are
now gathered together in the glorious celestial lodge above where our fathers have
gone before us.
In this Masonic year, 2,300 of our brethren laid down their trowels to end
their earthly toils. They were my brothers but I knew them not. How often in our
lodges we stand in tribute to the name read of the passing of a brother, or read it in
an obituary, or are told of his passing by a brother. To some they are just a name,
to many they are someone we see from time to time, but do we get to know them?
Yes they were our brothers and at this time let us remember that without their
individual accomplishments and their many sacrifices, we might not have what
we have in Masonry today. So any time we stand in tribute, remember them not
only as brothers, but also as one whom we would have liked to have known as a
friend. Yes they are our brothers and we do know that what we have in Masonry
today we owe to them.
So in tribute: Oh glorious and everlasting God, in whose care and
keeping are the fortunes and affairs of men. We stand in tribute this hour to honor
our beloved brethren who have gone from our midst to take their places in your
celestial lodge where the Master of all workmen shall set us to work anew. Our
brethren lived well the tenets of Masonry, leaving the world, the richer and us
with fond memories to cherish until we are joined again in the House Eternal
– Heavenly Father, into thy hands we commit the souls of our good friends and
brothers.”
The Memorial Service concluded with a musical selection performed by
the Grand Organist.
At 12:00 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 1:15 p.m.

The Grand Master then asked the Grand Secretary to explain the balloting
procedure for the election of officers. No ballot would be necessary if the office
was not contested. If more than one nomination was received for an office, ballot
cards would be distributed for the purpose of balloting for that office.

Presentation of the Membership Development Award
The Grand Lodge of California saw another record breaking year in
membership this year. Our lodges conferred nearly 5,000 degrees which is more
per lodge than any year since 1977. Lodges also raised more Master Masons than
any year since 1994.
The Grand Master announced that two lodges will share the Membership
Development Award this year. Each lodge raised a total of 19 Master Masons.
The lodges that will share the perpetual membership award this next year are
Southwest Lodge No. 283 and Home Lodge No. 721.
Presentation of the Leadership Training Awards
The Lodge Management Certification Program consists of five courses
that are conducted simultaneously at a particular location or online. The
courses include: Hall Association Management, Lodge Finance, Membership
Development, Program Planning, and Lodge Administration. Each course is a full
day in length. At the end of each course, participants must pass an examination
before they are given a certification in that course.

Proceedings of the
Mason of the Year

“Since its inception, the Mason of the Year Award has honored those
Masons whose actions are forever engraved in the hearts of their brethren. Their
lives of service are an example of loyal dedication to the high ideals of Freemasonry
and to the improvement of mankind. Their achievements surpass the boundaries
of lodge duty and go beyond any local activity deserving recognition.
The recipient of the Mason of the Year Award is selected by the Grand
Master, and that selection is made only when the outstanding record of service
of an individual member cries out for special recognition. Therefore, the name,
Mason of the Year, implying an annual award for service during a specific year,
is probably a misnomer. Only ten such awards have been given by this Grand
Lodge.
The man recognized tonight truly embodies the spirit and mission of
the Mason of the Year Award. His service to mankind has made a remarkable
difference in the lives of thousands. His devotion to his work is unwavering and
continues to this very day. He was recently featured on the CBS news program,
60 Minutes. Here is a portion of the program they featured on our Mason of the
Year, Brother Forrest Morton Bird.
Brother Bird was initiated into Palm Spring Lodge No. 693 on March 11,
1957. He was passed on October 21, 1957 and raised to the Sublime Degree of
Master Mason on December 30, 1957. In April, 2008, his lodge recognized him
with the Golden Veteran’s Award for fifty years of membership in our fraternity.
He is here tonight with his wife, Pamela.
Brethren, ladies, and friends, please welcome to the podium this esteemed
inventor, historic aviator, and our Mason of the Year, Brother Forrest Bird.
Brother Bird, your great work has saved and improved the lives of
thousands. Words cannot express the appreciation of all those who you have
served. Your brothers in Freemasonry are also proud beyond words that you are
a member of our great fraternity. Please accept this vase as a token of our esteem
for you, which will commemorate this day when you have been named our Mason
of the Year.”
The Grand Master then invited all to attend the Public Ceremonies and
the Installation of Officers on Sunday morning, September 26, 2010 beginning at
9:30 a.m.

Patrick A. Plunkett
Brother Patrick A. Plunkett is a Past Master of Eureka Lodge No. 16 and
a member of Penrhyn Gold Hill Lodge No. 32. He served four years
as an Inspector for Grand Lodge and one year as the Grand Pursuivant.
He has worked diligently for California Rainbow for many years. He
served as a member of the Public Relations Team since it started in 2001.
Pat has never hesitated to travel where ever any Public Relations training
was needed. He is willing to do anything to add interest to the training
and continues to promote Rainbow statewide.
Pat has served for many years on the New Hope Assembly Advisory
Board and has served many times as Rainbow Dad. He is the recipient
of the Grand Cross of Color, the highest honor given by Rainbow and an
honor which is only presented to a few people for giving service beyond
the call of duty over several years. Pat is always ready to lend his hand
in any way he can to serve Rainbow.
Bud Riebel
A Past Master of Garden Grove Lodge No. 351, Brother Bud Riebel has
worked with the youth of our state for over thirty years.
He began his career in Masonry as a DeMolay in New Jersey and hasn’t
stopped working yet. If there is a job to be done in either DeMolay or
Jobs Daughters, Bud is there, ready, willing and able to handle most
situations.
He has helped with a variety of fund raisers from making snow cones to
selling strawberries to being a participant in a DeMolay dunk tank. Jobs,
Rainbow or DeMolay. It doesn’t make a difference who needs help, Bud
is there to lend a hand.
He served as Grand Chaplain for Grand Guardian Council in 2000 and as
the Associate Grand Guardian in 2002. His service to the Grand Guardian
has been invaluable: he has served as Chairman of Arrangements for
Grand Bethel, Captain of the Guard and served on the Grand Council
Ways and Means Committee.
Bud is always there for anyone, with his calm demeanor and sound
advice. He is the reason many young people continue to remain with
their organizations and return to help as young adults. Bud would never
tell you this himself. He is too humble.

Mike Salazar
Over the course of the last 15 years, few men have done as much for
DeMolay as has Brother Mike Salazar. He has spent a generation serving
our Masonic youth, instilling in them great values, heaping praise upon
them, recognizing them for their accomplishments and applauding their
good deeds. Few men have dedicated their lives so completely with such
enthusiasm and humility as Mike Salazar.
Mike is a member of Pleasanton Lodge No. 321. He was always a strong
supporter of Pleasanton Chapter and after his son was no longer active
in the Chapter, Mike’s contributions to the Chapter grew and grew.
He quickly moved into leadership roles in the East Bay Division and
the Northern California Jurisdiction. Mike is currently the Executive
Officer of Northern California DeMolay and an active member of the
International Supreme Council. He received the Executive Officer of
the Year award in 2009.
Under Mike’s leadership, NorCal DeMolay has flourished. New chapters
are being formed, membership is growing, and the cardinal virtues of the
Order of DeMolay are well entrusted within a man of great integrity.
Mike is a shining example of service to our Craft and for every person he
has inspired to greater service in any avocation.

Grand Master’s Message
Good Afternoon Brethren of the Grand Lodge.
“It is a Grand and Glorious Day To Be A Mason”! I first uttered those
words at our Junior Warden’s Retreat, three years ago. I said them again at my
Installation last year. And this past year, I saw first hand how true they are.
Welcome to the 161st Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge. To
the delegates and members of our constituent lodges, I hope you will find this
weekend rewarding and enlightening. You are Grand Lodge! To our guests, we are
so pleased to host you. Please give our best wishes and warm fraternal greetings
to your home Jurisdiction. And have fun in San Francisco.
It was a year ago that I knelt before you at my Installation. Today, as
this journey comes to an end, I am in awe of how great this Jurisdiction is and
how committed most of our Brethren are to its well being. I thank each of you for
allowing me to just temporarily hold this time-honored position on your behalf. I
continue to tell those up and down our State, “No one person should be allowed
to have this much fun.”
To Most Worshipfuls, Fred Sorsabal, Mel Stein, Dick Hopper and Larry
Adamson, thank you for getting me ready to take the oriental chair. It was an
education to watch your great leadership. To the brethren here assembled, if you
think my stewardship was on the mark and the year was generally successful, I’m
humbled and honored. But if, on the other hand, you think I missed the mark, I
would direct your attention to the four previously mentioned individuals.
To satisfy the requirements of Section 404.130 of the California Masonic
Code, I stand before you today, to speak to the general condition of our Craft.
The Proceedings will record all of my official acts and recommendations, but this
afternoon I wish to give an overview of the past year and our condition today.
This afternoon and tomorrow morning, I will present four pieces of legislation
for you to consider. I hope you will listen closely to my arguments and not let
preconceived ideas cloud your decision on how to vote.
To the general condition of our Jurisdiction, I would characterize it as
remarkable and on the rise. My theme was, “Freemasonry, the Foundation of our
Country, the Blue Lodge, the Foundation of our Craft, Coming Home”. The goal
was to move our entire Craft and Jurisdiction forward, not just the Grand Lodge
progressive line. Our lodge leadership responded. You responded. Our lodges
initiated, passed and raised more men than in the past 20 plus years – surpassing
even last year, which was record-breaking, as well. Our 337 lodges conferred
nearly 4,900 degrees, the most since the mid 1980’s, a time when we had some 550
lodges. Affiliations were the highest in four years. Restorations were the highest
in more than 20 years. Our total gains were the highest since 1990. The men that

38

Proceedings of the

are coming to our doors are of the highest quality. They have studied more about
our Craft on the internet than ever in the past. They are looking for answers on
what our Craft has to offer. They want to be involved in their communities. They
want to make a difference, and we must ensure we are ready for the call.
Our losses are just slightly higher than last year. Through a program
begun by MW Larry Adamson, we have sought out “lost” members, those we
had lost contact with. Through a dedicated staff member and a software search
program, we located nearly 1,500 of these “lost” members. Many have become
active again in their lodges. Others were found to be deceased, which contributed
to this year’s increased losses. The search continues, and I urge all lodges to work
with Grand Lodge to find your lost members. The program works.
Even with this larger reported loss, we had the smallest drop in
membership since 1928. I am confident that we are only a few short years from
starting a positive growth. Our current Master Mason membership totals sit at
approx 59,000 with another 7,000 Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts working
their way through the degree process.
Our Craft’s health is not simply about numbers, though. Behind each
of those numbers is an individual. This year I challenged lodge leadership to
make contact with every member of their lodge – not a letter or an e-mail or an
answering machine message, but a personal conversation. To find out how they
are, to remind them that they are valued members of the lodge. And finally, to
invite them to a special “Coming Home” event at their February Stated Meeting.
It worked. Over the previous twelve months, the jurisdiction’s overall attendance
at stated meetings had been, on average, about 6,400 Master Masons. At our
February “Coming Home” events, attendance was nearly 9,000. Some 2,500 more
of our Brethren came home, starting the process of becoming reacquainted with
their brothers and reengaged in our work.
I thank those lodges that rose to my challenge and are making a difference
with their members. Because of you, “Coming Home” was a huge success. In
some ways it exceeded my expectations. But in others, it was a reality check. First,
only about 1/3 of our lodges fully took on the project. They accounted for the large
spike in attendance. The other 2/3 of our lodges saw the direct results of their
efforts: essentially nothing. But most sobering was the number of members who
shared that, other than their monthly Trestleboard, the “Coming Home” phone
call was the first lodge communication they had received in 10 or more years. My
brethren, we have lost focus on what matters most to our lodges: caring about our
members. Here’s another example. One of the most rewarding things about being
Grand Master is the honor of presenting Diamond Jubilee pins to those of our
members that attain 75 years in our Craft. I was honored to present 6 of them this
year. But I was supposed to have a seventh. When I contacted the Brother’s family
to schedule the presentation, I was informed by his daughter that he had passed
away in 1989. He would have been 104 years old. The senior member of the lodge,

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

39

and they were unaware that he had died some 21 years earlier. That is a crime my
Brethren! And I know that it is the extreme, but I also fear that it is not an anomaly.
How many more of our Brethren are on our roles that have died some time ago?
And how many more truly need our support, but don’t even think to ask for help
because they have been lost to the lodge? We MUST reacquaint ourselves with
our members. I ask every lodge Master to work with their Secretary and Wardens
to make “Coming Home” an everyday thought. Divide your lodge roster into four,
one for each quarter. And every quarter, have those personal conversations. If
we do, then we touch the life of every member at least once a year. As I’ve said
before, we do not have a membership problem. We need only to find a reason for
our members that don’t attend lodge to “Come Home.”
As part of Coming Home, I wrote a letter to every California Mason and
his lady living in Washington, Oregon, Nevada and Arizona, inviting them to meet
with me and my wife in their home state. I was honored that nearly 500 took me
up on the invitation. I spoke to them about the state of our Craft in California, and
I was pleased to report that our Jurisdiction is strong and making great strides to
become even stronger. I spoke to them about their benefits as a California Mason.
Many thought they had lost their benefits once they left the borders of our state,
and I was able to correct that misconception. Finally, I spoke about “Coming
Home”. I said that I understood, for many, they would not be coming home to
California, but I urged them to come home to our Craft. I encouraged them to seek
out a lodge in their community and get reengaged. To find that fellowship that
they left behind. Masonry is Masonry no matter where it is practiced. I felt good
about rebuilding the fraternal bonds with these members, and I ask all our lodge
leaders to continue that process. Stay in touch. Remind them of their member
benefits, no matter what their zip code may be.
Within our jurisdiction, I am proud to say that for the first time in some
30 plus years, we are ending the year with more lodges than when we started.
After a positive vote at last year’s Communication we chartered and Constituted
Prometheus Lodge #851. Thanks to outstanding leadership in the Sacramento
area, we have since granted dispensation and Instituted two other lodges. First, we
Instituted General Douglas MacArthur Lodge, UD. Later in this Communication,
you will have the opportunity to vote on their receiving a Charter, as well as
Paideia Lodge, UD who were issued a dispensation by MW Larry Adamson and
then continued by me at the close of last year’s Communication. We also Instituted
Golden Compasses Research Lodge, UD. They will continue to work this coming
year with the prospect of requesting a Charter at our 2011 Communication. This
growth is balanced against only one Consolidation of two lodges earlier in the year.
This growth can be attributed to many factors. I think there’s one reason
that stands out. One of the best strategic moves our Grand Lodge has made over
the past few years was reforming and repopulating our Lodge Support Committee.
This committee was reestablished, a Tiger Team that we could place in front of

40

Proceedings of the

any fledgling lodge to show our support for their survival. The Brothers on this
committee are outstanding. They have spent countless hours working with the
leadership of the lodge determining strengths and weaknesses, and developing
a plan to keep the lodge open. I would like to mention one Brother in particular.
Wor. Bill O’Brien, PM of Glendora Lodge #404 who has chaired this committee
over the last couple of years. His leadership in training the members of the
committee and getting them into the field, together with his tenacious mentoring
and encouragement, has been phenomenal. His involvement has saved at least a
dozen lodges, and ensured that the loss of a lodge is the absolute last resort. Thank
you, Bill, for your caring for our Craft and for your Brothers.
I’m also proud to report on a trend that began last year: we have
reenergized member support for our youth groups. A resurgence is happening.
Our Craft has stepped up to fill holes, and to lend a hand when needed. New
DeMolay Chapters are being started in many of our communities. I had the honor
to be present at the Chartering of a new Bethel in Tracy, the first such Bethel to
open in 10 years. And our Rainbow continues to thrive and grow with our lodges’
participation. Thank you Brethren for continuing to make this a high priority.
Much credit must also go to MW David Decker and MW Fred Sorsabal, who
have co-chaired this committee to its many successes. Both are retiring from this
committee and their services will be sorely missed. Thanks to you both for giving
of your talents, your time, and your love for our youth.
My theme this year was anchored on the Blue Lodge being the Foundation
of our Craft. This year, we invited all of our members to talk about the future of our
Craft – where we need to expend our time, our efforts, and our dollars. More than
3,500 members spoke up, in Town Hall Meetings, in an online survey, in letters
and e-mails and discussion boards. Our Committee Chairmen and constitutional
Board Presidents are now working on a plan that fulfills your visions. The Masons
of California Strategic Plan for 2010-2015 is in the final phase of completion,
with priorities and objectives that come direct from you. You said that candidate
coaching needs improvement, and we will, starting with training. You said the
application and investigation process isn’t rigorous enough; we’re going to
refine it. Many of you pointed out a need for community involvement, including
a unified, statewide program for public education; we’re going to develop one.
We need everyone’s help implementing this plan, especially lodge masters and
wardens. Thanks to VW Allan Casalou, Terry Mendez, our Communications
Director, and her entire staff for seeking out our member’s thoughts, desires and
vision and putting them into a living document we can follow over the next five
years. But most of all, my thanks to the thousands of you who participated. You
are positioning our fraternity to grow and thrive.
This year, we saw much change at our Masonic Homes. You will hear
a detailed report from MW David Doan and Wor. Mike Neben regarding our
Homes and the Acacia Creek Retirement Center, but I would like to share just

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

41

a few thoughts on the impact of these changes. The Board has remained fiercely
committed to serving our children. The Masonic Center for Youth and Families
opens later this year, the result of two years of research and planning. We will
serve youth between the ages of 4-17 who struggle with behavioral, learning,
and emotional problems. The Center is devoted to understanding the whole child,
offering single point-of-service care from an industry-leading professional team.
It is one of a kind in this country, and will set a new standard for care. The Masonic
Home’s Board is working with national and international experts, including the
Yale Child Study Center and the Anna Freud Centre in London to make sure of it.
We’ll reach hundreds of kids throughout the state, fulfilling our pledge to make
a profound difference in the lives of our children and to the public debate about
children’s needs. This program will be offered to our Masonic children as well
as the community in the name of all Masons in California. As the program opens
later this year, please ensure all your members know that there is help for their
children if needed. They need only ask.
I also had the pleasure to officiate at the Grand Opening of our new
Acacia Creek Retirement Facility on our campus in Union City. This beautiful
retirement setting has already become home to many of our members and their
ladies. As you will hear from Wor. Neben, there are still challenges to face as
our new campus matures. But bottom line, we are now on-line and the care and
services for our Acacia residents will be second to none.
This was a remarkable year, and you’ll hear much more about our progress
in the proceedings for this Communication. But for now, I would like to spend
just a couple of minutes speaking about my Grand Master’s project. Two years
ago I had a vision to honor our WWII veterans. Being a third generation military
man, I have seen first hand the sacrifices made by the men and women of our great
country on our behalf. I wanted, in some small measure, to show all of them we
Masons have not forgotten their service. Not knowing exactly what venue that
thanks would take, I was introduced to the nonprofit organization Honor Flight.
The program was exactly what I was looking for. Through the efforts of Brother
Doug Ismail and his staff in the Grand Lodge office, we established a similar
program: Operation Greatest Gift. My goal was to send as many WWII veterans
as possible to visit their magnificent memorial, erected in 2004. Originally, I’d
hoped to raise $125,000. But we estimated that if we could raise some $400,000,
we could send 600-plus veterans on this beautiful venture. It was a demanding
goal for our lodges. First, lodges needed to seek out and refer the WWII veterans
within their roles. Second, they needed to get our veterans safely to and from the
airport – no small feat in a state as big as California. Third, and most importantly,
we needed Brothers to step up and act as Guardians for our Veterans while they
were away from home. Our brethren responded beyond my greatest hopes. We
had waiting lists of Brothers who volunteered to take time from their work and
families, pay most of their own way and care for our veterans during the journey.
I can not be more proud of our Craft and how they responded. When it comes to

42

Proceedings of the

doing the right thing, for being there to help another, for putting one self second
while caring for others, I needed only ask and they were there to fill the need. A
huge thank you goes to all those brethren who volunteered.
Lastly, I needed our lodges to fund our cause. I pressed hard for your
help, and am proud to say that nearly 1/3 of our lodges picked up the cause.
Through your generosity, we raised nearly $490,000 – the most money raised
directly from lodges for any Grand Lodge project. We sent 612 WWII Veterans
to see their memorial, nearly all of them brothers from our own lodges. And they
were accompanied by nearly 190 Guardians.
Many people have asked me why we took on such an ambitious cause.
The answer was simple. Because it was the right thing to do, and because we
are Masons.
Besides Bro. Doug Ismail, this project could not have succeeded if not
for the efforts of two extraordinary ladies who work in our Grand Lodge office.
Miss Joyce Hahn and Miss Denise Avila were the true Guardians of this project.
Doing Yeoman’s work, their passion, compassion and dedication to our veterans
is what brought my vision to fruition. I will never be able to repay or to state
my humble thanks for what they mean to me and the veterans whose lives they
touched. A special thanks also to Wor. Richard Wing, PM of Palo Alto Roller
Lodge who brought to me, two years ago, the concept of “Honor Flight,” who
trained our Guardians and contributed his invaluable experience to ensure we
were successful. And to Terry Mendez and the entire Communications team
who published the latest issue of the Freemason magazine which chronicled our
story. I might be prejudiced, but I feel it is finest issue we have ever produced. Its
poignant stories and beautiful pictures said it all in just a few pages.
I would like to conclude this message by giving a heartfelt thanks to
those who made this journey so rewarding and successful.
First and foremost, I have reiterated that our lodges are the foundation of
our Craft. It is our lodge leaders and brethren that move this Jurisdiction forward.
Thank you all for your dedication to our Craft and for ensuring each year is better
than the last.
To our Inspectors, thanks for your continued support of our lodges and
your support of me and my vision.
To all Committee and Board members, your unselfish efforts and
countless hours on behalf of our lodges are unparalleled. Thanks for a job
well done.

Special thanks must go to my Deputy, Bill Bray and his lady Linda. Your
support has been invaluable. Kathy and I will always be indebted for your caring

and our Craft will thrive under your leadership.
To our Grand Wardens, your counsel made decisions easier to make,

To our Grand Treasurer, your contributions to our financial health can

I can never express loudly enough what our Grand Secretary and his

I could not conclude without special recognition of my Grand Marshal,
John Fletcher and his wife Karen. You were always there to see to our every need.
This year would not have been as much fun if not for your sense of humor and
constant uplifting demeanor. I thank you for keeping me grounded and for just
being a friend. I can never repay you.
And to my Lady, Kathy, this journey would have been hollow without
you by my side. Your support and love made it easy to get going every day. Never
waivering from my side during good times and bad, any successes we had, are
yours to share. I love you dearly.

Brethren, all, thank you for your trust in me. I am so proud to have
represented you all wherever I traveled. I have been honored to be your Grand

Freemasonry has been my passion for 38 years, and this year will always hold a
special place in my heart.
God bless our gentle craft. God bless our great nation. Our Jurisdiction
is strong and we are only getting stronger. We have continued to be relevant in our
communities and you should all feel pride in what we are accomplishing.
As I started, I will finish, “It is a Grand and Glorious Day to be a Mason”!
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Kenneth G. Nagel, Grand Master

61

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2010/2011 Grand Lodge Budget
William J. Bray III, Deputy Grand Master

At the 2009 Annual Communication, the brethren approved the per capita
proposal that I submitted. I am very grateful for the support. Since that time, I
have been refining the budget while monitoring current income and expenses as
well as our membership activity. I have discussed the budget further with the
Senior and Junior Wardens at our retreats over the last two years. I have also
worked with the Grand Lodge Finance committee, our Grand Treasurer, Grand
Secretary and finance staff. All of this collaboration has resulted in the budget I
now place before you for consideration at the upcoming Annual Communication.
The revenue for the next fiscal year is estimated to be $2,534,189,
which is approximately $30,000 less than last year’s revenue. Of this revenue,
$1,855,029 is from per capita. The billable membership is projected to be 56,213.
The final audited membership numbers will not be available for several weeks,
but it appears the actual will be close to this projection. Application fees are
projected based on 1,800 applications. The distribution policy for withdrawals
from our investments is based on 4.5% of the Grand Lodge endowment. The
dividend from the Nob Hill Masonic Center will be $43,000 based on the profits
of the corporation for the fiscal year ending October 31, 2009. This dividend is
approximately $75,000 less than last year due this economy’s impact on parking
revenue in our garage. Other income includes revenue from a grant from the
California Masonic Foundation, and reimbursements from investments and
Masonic Service Bureau expenses. These revenues are explained further in the
enclosed materials.
With revenues lower than last year, we have worked to lower some of
the expenses. Reductions were made in fraternal expenses, appropriations, travel
and wages. As a result the expenses for the upcoming fiscal year are projected
to be $2,500,142. Fraternal expenses, which include expenses for the Annual
Communication, Ritual program, awards, travel, and lodge insurance, total
$794,221 and are approximately $30,000 less than last year. Appropriations for
Grand Lodge Committees and programs are $478,128, which is approximately
$23,000 less than last year. Administrative expenses are $1,127,792, which is
approximately 3% more than last year due mainly to a 2% increase in wages and
12% increase in health care premiums.
Reserving approximately $12,000 for depreciation, our projected net
revenue after expenses is $21,885.
Though our final membership report has yet to be audited and distributed,
it is clear that interest in Freemasonry continues to grow. Our lodges are busier
conferring degrees than anytime in the last 30 years. Our members are asking for

62

Proceedings of the

growth and improvement in the area of masonic education, the application and
investigation process, candidates coaching, and the entire membership experience.
We are looking for ways to expand our positive impact on our communities
throughout the state. Our strategy with this budget has been to reduce costs
without reducing services and programs. I am proud to say, that with the help and
input from a lot of our members and our professional staff, we have achieved that.
I thank you, again, for your previous support and ask for your support now as we
consider this budget for our coming fiscal year.

Fiscal Year 2010/2011
William J. Bray III, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue source has been per-capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge
Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates investment income. To better manage those monies, a four and a half-percent spending policy
has been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year valuation to ensure the preservation of the fund principle. The Grand Lodge may have other
income like interest on bank accounts and other financial instruments from time to time. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included in its
mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership training programs and now provides a grant for those purposes. In 2005, the delegates of
the 156th Annual Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by all applicants for degrees and out-of-state affiliations.
The Grand Lodge manages different service bureaus throughout the state and receives reimbursement for those expenses. The Grand Lodge also
manages the investments of its related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole
shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of the corporation.

Installation Address

William J. Bray III
Grand Master of Masons in California, 2010-2011
A wise man once said, “A journey of a thousand miles begins with but
one step.” Here I am, about to take that first step. It’s impossible to describe
how I feel.
It’s also hard to put into words how grateful I am, to so many people –
but I’ll try. First, I want to thank all of you for being here and sharing this moment
with my wife, Linda, with my officers, and with me. It is a thrill to see so many
friends, brothers, and families. You represent the goodwill, love, and spirit that
makes our fraternity so special.
Four years ago, our past grand masters had the confidence to recommend
me as junior grand warden, and our grand lodge had the confidence to elect me.
You made this journey possible. Thank you.
I have had the privilege of serving with many outstanding brothers on
boards and committees over the years. My brothers, you were some of the most
important teachers in my Masonic education. Thank you.
I need to give special thanks to my mother, Mercy, who suggested 38
years ago that I ask my grandfather about becoming a Mason. Mothers really do
know best. The rest is history. Thanks, Mom.
I have to thank Most Worshipful Ken Nagel, who has led this year with
such passion and vision. Ken and I are both military men. We speak the same
language. And he’s really showed me a thing or two about leadership. He also
managed to fill his year with sincerity and graciousness, and even fun. Most
Worshipful, it’s such a privilege to build on all the important work that you started.
You have set a powerful example, and I’ll do everything I can to follow it. Thank
you for showing all of us what real devotion to Masonry looks like. Thank you
for preparing me for this day. Most of all, thank you for your friendship. I cherish
it, and always will.
And Linda: my lovely wife, my best friend, my driver, my writer, my
lover, my golfing partner. Thanks honey, for all that you do to make me shine. I
love you from the bottom of my heart.
My brethren, we’ve got a great journey before us, and I can’t wait to
start. Let me share just a few highlights of the year ahead.
Our theme for the year will be: The past, the present, and the future.
Think about what those words mean to you: past, present, future.
Here’s what they mean to me. The past, to me, is our heritage. It’s carrying

72

Proceedings of the

on a legacy. It’s about who we are, our identity, shaped by older generations. It’s
about the great lessons of those who came before us. When I think of the past, of
all the respect and awe that I have for it, I think of this picture. This is me with my
grandfather, going to lodge together. He’s a great guy.
The present, to me, is represented by this picture. This is my son, Bill.
The present is living in this moment, and appreciating this moment, right now.
It’s knowing what’s important and behaving in a way that shows it. It’s every
action counting, no matter how small. I see this picture, and I think about our
responsibility – to our families, to our communities, and to our craft today.
The future, to me, is our obligation. When I think about the future, I think
about my grandsons, Billy and Petey. I think about all that I want to do for them.
The future is about seeing the big picture, the possibilities, and putting in the time
and energy to reach for it. It’s about moving forward, and building a great future
for our grandkids, and also for the future of California Masonry.
Here’s how I like to sum it up – and pay attention, because you’ll
hear it thousands of times this year: The past is our heritage. The present is our
responsibility. The future is our obligation.
Ladies and gentlemen of our craft, this year I want to focus on all of
those things: honoring our past, working hard in the present, and moving forward
to a better future. Masons are builders. Whether it’s the castles and cathedrals of
the Middle Ages, or the programs and fraternal bonds that lodges build today, we
are builders. And we know it takes a lot of hands to build something great.
We also know that it takes a lot of time. So I want to point out a few
initiatives that I’ll continue building this year.
A year ago, Past Grand Master Nagel stood right where I am and
announced his plan for Coming Home. He asked us to reach out to brothers who
were no longer active in their blue lodges, and remind them how important they
are. Remind them why they joined in the first place. Remind them that their lodge
needs them.
The plan was based on a simple act of fellowship: a conversation.
Lodges called every single member, and had a conversation about why they’d lost
touch. Brothers who had lost contact with their lodge, or worse, with that special
spark of Masonry, suddenly were reconnected. At a special Coming Home event
in February, some 2,500 brothers came back to lodge – many, for the first time in
years, even decades.
Those conversations reaffirmed what Masonry is really about. This is
such a wonderful project, and I know that if we continue reaching out to our
brothers, we will get them all back home in their blue lodges.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

73

I need all of your support and involvement to do it. Work with your
lodges to create a regular outreach program. Drop by a widow’s house to say hi.
Bring a brother who hasn’t been to lodge in awhile to stated meeting. Do it every
month, and encourage others to do the same. As Masons, it’s our responsibility to
each other. Let’s keep bringing our brothers home.
Two years ago, Most Worshipful Larry Adamson made it a priority to
rebuild our youth orders, starting with more fraternal leadership. Most Worshipful
Ken Nagel continued on this quest. It’s working. Our members are stepping up
to help, and for the first time in many years, the ranks of our youth orders are
growing and benefiting our support. The youth orders are where many of us began
our Masonic journey – they’re our roots. The extraordinary young people who are
in them today are, literally, our future. To all of the Masonic youth here today, I
want you to know something. You make us so proud. We want to make you proud,
too. We will continue to make you a priority and champion your cause; I’ll make
sure of it. We’re honored to help you build the future.
We Masons are building a future, too – the future of our fraternity. To do
that, we need a roadmap. And we’re drawing one, together – our Strategic Plan
for 2010 to 2015.
We started last spring under Most Worshipful Ken Nagel, when we asked
all of you to share your visions for the fraternity. What are your priorities for
California Masonry? How do you want the fraternity to look in five years? What
needs to change? What are we doing right, what needs improvement? More than
3,500 California Masons and others in our fraternal family spoke up – at open
forums, in phone calls and e-mails, and with responses to an online survey.
WE are California Masonry, all of us together, and so it only makes
sense that we all have a hand in this roadmap to the future. Based on everything
you said, the strategic plan is being shaped, and it’ll be completed by the end
of the year. You asked for more Masonic education. We’re going to offer more,
and use technology to do it. You told us that the membership experience could
be improved at all levels, from Entered Apprentice to Master Masons. So we’re
going to focus on engaging new members and helping lodges develop meaningful
programs. Many of you pointed out a need for community involvement, including
a unified, statewide program for public education; we’re going to develop one.
Those are just a few of the goals and priorities to look for, and they’ll position us
to make a profound difference – in our lodges, in our communities, and within
ourselves. And yes, we have our work cut out for us. But as Masons, if we
appreciate one thing, it’s that the journey is as important as the destination.
There’s one more part of this journey that I want to share with you. I’ve
mentioned a few of the projects that we’ve already begun, that I want to continue
to build. Well, Linda and I would like to start something of our own to build on,
something that’ll really touch the hearts and souls of our members.

74

Proceedings of the

You see, we know how difficult cancer is, for the person diagnosed with
it but also for his or her loved ones. Linda has been battling cancer for more than
20 years. Then, a few years ago, I was diagnosed with it, too. I remember when
I got that phone call from my doctor, asking me to come in, with my wife, to
discuss some test results. I remember saying to Linda, “Do you know what this
means? I have cancer.” That moment changed everything.
Although my battle with cancer is over, Linda’s isn’t. We both know
what it feels like to spend a lifetime with this disease. Our families know it, too.
That’s why Linda and I are starting my Grand Master’s Project this year,
called By Your Side. It is dedicated to families in California who’ve also gotten
that phone call.
Together we will fund educational resources for hundreds of California
nurses to become certified nurse oncologists. Cancer is a fight for your life, and
these specialists are the absolute best people to have at your side. Their presence
and expertise provides encouragement and support. With more of them in every
hospital, clinic, and medical care center, we will help provide comfort and hope
to thousands of patients and their loved ones.
We have a special guest here to tell you more about the project, and I’ll
introduce her shortly. But to wrap up my portion of this presentation, I want to
go back to my theme: The past is our heritage. The present is our responsibility.
The future is our obligation. Past, present, future. Ladies and gentlemen, there’s
one person who is all of those things to me. In fact, she is my whole world. Linda,
that’s you.
You know, Linda’s a Taurus. A real bull. I’m a Pisces. A bull and a fish
– we’re an unlikely combination. But when you love someone as much as I love
Linda, it’s possible. Thank God.
Honey, to say you have always been there for me is an understatement.
You have ALWAYS been there for me. Always. You make me a better man. You
make this world a better place. And every day – literally, every single day – I think
about how blessed I am that you choose to live in MY world. It would be empty
without you. So I’ll rely on four simple words to say what could take me a lifetime
to truly express: I love you, honey.
And now, to all of you gathered here today, here’s to the first step of our
journey this year. Thanks for bringing me along. Together, we’re going to do great
things.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2011-2012
Frank Loui, Senior Grand Warden

As your Senior Grand Warden, I am responsible for preparing and
presenting to the Grand Lodge a proposal for the per capita assessment that will
be collected in 2011 to fund the Grand Lodge fiscal year for the period November
1, 2011 through October 31, 2012.
Beginning with my term as Junior Grand Warden, I have worked with
the Executive Committee, the Finance Committee and the Grand Lodge staff to
develop projections of the income and expenses necessary during the 2012 fiscal
year to operate the Grand Lodge, fund our strategic priorities and initiatives, and
to provide programs and services to our lodges and members. There is a new
strategic plan being developed for our fraternity as we speak. We have incorporated
in our planning the important priorities that our members have expressed and
endorsed in the strategic planning process. I have had the opportunity to share
this proposal with the hundreds of Junior and Senior Wardens who attended the
Wardens Retreats this year and their input has been very important in this process.
The proposal that I enclose for you seeks to maintain the programs and
services of our Grand Lodge while planning for certain efficiencies that will allow
us to overcome the economic challenges that face all organizations today.
In order to establish an appropriate per-capita assessment, I have
prepared the attached budget. You will notice that the total expenses are only
1.7% higher than the proposed 2010/2011 budget prepared by our Deputy Grand
Master. While we have managed to keep expenses flat, there are certain factors
that will increase the per capita.
•

•
•
•

Membership loss. We project a total loss of 2,030 members, which
represents a loss in revenue of $66,990. This factor taken alone, we
would need to increase per capita $1.19 to make up for the loss in
members.
Insurance. We estimate that premiums for our lodge insurance will
increase by 5% or just over $7,000.
Personnel costs. Wages will increase by only 2%. Together with the
health care expense, personnel expenses will increase by 3.5%.
Inflation. Costs for a number of non-labor items are expected to rise by
2%.

There are a few factors, however, that will help reduce per capita.
•
•

Nob Hill Dividend. We project that the dividend from the Nob Hill
Masonic Center will be $75,000, which is $32,000 more than the
previous year.
Cost savings. We have identified a number of expenses that can be held
to last year’s levels without any factor for inflation. You will notice
that the expenses in many categories are nearly the same as the budget
presented by the Deputy Grand Master.

As a result of this increased dividend and our work to contain costs, we
can balance the budget with a per capita of $34.00. While this may seem that the
per capita is increasing, lodges will actually pay less per capita than the previous
year. In the budget presented by the Deputy Grand Master for the 2010/11 Fiscal
Year, the total per capita collected is projected to be $1,855,029. This proposal for
the following year, projects that the total per capita collected will be $1,842,222,
which is nearly $13,000 less than the previous year.
We still live in difficult economic times. Our membership continues to
decline. But we can overcome these challenges with smart planning and creative
thinking. In adopting this per capita proposal, we will insure that the Grand Lodge
can continue to provide the level of programs and services that will be needed
during the period of growth in our organization. I appreciate all of the assistance
I have received in developing this proposal and I look forward to your support at
the upcoming Annual Communication.

Frank Loui, Senior Grand Warden
Revenue Assumptions
PER CAPITA
There are several factors that affect per capita, membership levels and inflation being the
major factors. The membership analysis for the 2011/2012 fiscal year projects a total loss in
membership of 2,030 members. While this is one of the lowest loss of members in decades,
the membership decline will result in lost revenue of $66,990 or $1.24 in additional per capita.
Overall inflation is projected to be approximately 2.0%. This will result in additional expenses
of approximately $43,000 or $0.79 in additional per capita. All other things being equal, the per
capita would have to be increased by $2.03 to $35.03 in order to make up for lost members
and inflation. Due to improvements in the Nob Hill Masonic Center operations, the Nob Hill
Masonic Center dividend will result in a revenue increase of $32,000 or $0.59 in per capita
reduction. Because of the dividend offset and expense reduction efforts in fraternal,
appropriations, travel and wages expenses, the proposed per capita will only increase by
$1.00 to $34.00.

Report of the Grand Treasurer
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The general assessment of the financial aspect of your Grand Lodge is
that we continue to deal successfully with a struggling economy, a challenging
employment market and very volatile investment markets.
Each of you is aware of the state of the general economy and the
investment markets over the last year. Wile those conditions affect the Grand
Lodge’s financial activities, just as they do everyone else, the Grand Lodge has
survived them well, through the hard work and diligent efforts of our efficient
staff, the Grand Lodge Officers, Board members, and committeemen. Budgets
have been tightened and closely monitored. Efforts to conserve and curtail
expenses have been effectively applied by everyone involved.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee has, yet once again, intensified
their customary diligence over the Grand Lodge’s investment portfolio. They have
given special effort and consideration to the continuation of current economic and
investment conditions. The result is some studied changes in the make-up and
allocation of the portfolio to better reflect the economic and investment conditions
going forward. They continue to recommend the reduction in the percentage of
distribution to be taken from the portfolio for current budgeting purposes from
the traditional 5% per year to a 4.5% level, a move that has been adopted by the
Grand Lodge and each of the other entities participating in that investment pool.
Your Grand Lodge Insurance Committee continues to apply their
considerable expertise to the risk management of the Grand Lodge to keep the
various entities well protected at favorable and competitive premium costs.
The Finance and the Audit Committees perform their respective duties
with business-like efficiency of which any organization would be proud.
The dedicated and efficient financial staff in the Grand Lodge office
continues to provide unexcelled service in the management and reporting on the
financial affairs of the organization.
The ability of the Grand Lodge and other entities to weather the financial
storm as they have is a testimony to the disciplined and conservative manner
in which they have conducted their financial affairs for many years, particularly
in the good times. It has allowed the various entities to continue providing
uninterrupted programs and services to their constituents, without any budgetinduced lay-offs of staff and with balanced budgets all the while.
You can be very proud of the work that has been done by all those
involved in the financial affairs of our Fraternity, as I am, and you should offer
them your thanks.

84

Proceedings of the

The detailed information I am going to give you today is for a ninemonth period from the start of this current fiscal year, November 1, 2009, through
July 31, 2010. I will compare that information to like data for the same period a
year earlier. This report is already posted on the Member Center website under
Forms/161st Annual Communication. It will continue to be available to you
there until the official proceedings of this Communication are published. Those
Proceedings will contain the customary audited financials for the entire fiscal year.
It should be noted that this partial-year information has been prepared
internally by our fine financial staff and has not been audited.
As of July 31, 2010, your Grand Lodge had assets of $6,471,818 and
liabilities of $2,772,450 for Total Net Assets of $3,699,369. Those assets were
some 15.3% higher than at the same date a year earlier. Keep in mind that most of
the assets you might attach to the California Grand Lodge are not actually owned
by the Grand Lodge itself and do not appear in these numbers. I am referring
to major assets such as this facility, which is owned by the California Masonic
Memorial Temple Corp., and our homes in Union City and Covina, which are
owned by the Masonic Homes of California, both separate corporations.
The last several years have been difficult ones in the investment markets.
The investment accounts of the Grand Lodge were up 10/7% for the 12-month
period ending July 31, 2010. The annualized return for the prior three year period
was -3.5%, and the return was +2.7% annualized for the prior five-year period.
Your Grand Lodge continues to operate in the black on a year-to-year
basis. For the nine-months ending July 31, 2010, the total income was $1,776,552,
while total expenses were $1,591,972. That income is some 10.2% lower than
the comparative period last year. Expenses for the nine-month period ending July
31, 2010 were slightly lower than the same period last year, a difference largely
due to the timing of various expenses. While the Net Excess as of July 31, 2010,
of income over expense is some $184,580, it should be noted that approximately
20% of the total year’s expenses occur in the last three months of the fiscal year.
The current projection is that the Grand Lodge will end the fiscal year on October
31, with a slight surplus.
The nine-month expenses were divided in the following manner: 22.4%
for Fraternal matters (such as this Annual Communication, travel expenses of
the Elected and Appointed Grand Lodge Officers and Ritual Committee, and the
insurance for the constituent lodges), 22.7% for Appropriations and Programs
(such as various lodge support Committees, the Freemason magazine, and
Committees such as Policy, Jurisprudence, Investment and Trial Review), and
54.4% for General and Administrative items (such as salaries and benefits,
accounting and auditing, investment management fees, legal fees and general
office operations).

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

85

I must again comment on the concern and diligence which your Executive
Committee and the financial staff bring to the monitoring of the actual income and
expenses versus the budget. The numbers are compiled and studied by all parties
in great detail on a monthly basis, as the year progresses. You should know that
any surplus at the end of the fiscal year is not carried over into the next year, but
rather it is permanently transferred to the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund. The
result is that each Grand Master starts his year with a zero balance, with only the
budget for that year to work with.
I must offer a word of caution about the future. Many of our budgeting
processes use projected investment withdrawal amounts that are the result of
averaging investment values for the prior five years. That policy has served us
very well in that it smooths the ups and downs of the investment markets from
quarter to quarter. However, if the investment returns in the next several years do
not equal the years we will be eliminating when calculating the moving average,
the recent declines will continue to have a dampening effect on our available
investment withdrawals. In other words, we are not out of the woods yet in
our outlook.
I again pay tribute to the many highly dedicated brothers who serve on
the various Boards and Committees of this Grand Lodge and its related entities for
the extraordinary amount of time, energy, dedication and hard work they devote
to the business and fraternal affairs of our California Masonic community. Each
of you should seek them out and give them a hearty “Thank You” for the work
they do.
The dedication, efficiency and hard work of the Grand Lodge staff
deserve special comment. Under the able leadership of our Grand Secretary,
Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, this group of talented men and women perform
exceptional service for your Grand Lodge, often with little, certainly not enough,
recognition and appreciation. Our Grand Lodge organization and administration
is the model among sister Grand Lodges and it is due largely to our Grand
Secretary and his staff. Please join me in thanking them.
And finally, my brethren, I thank each of you for having allowed me
to work with you and for you during this past year. I am extremely proud and
honored to be a part of the California Masonic Grand Lodge team.
Respectfully submitted,
Glenn D. Woody, Grand Treasurer

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to present this, my third report, to you as your
Grand Secretary.
Lodge and Membership Information
As of today there are 341 chartered lodges in our jurisdiction, including
three lodges Under Dispensation. Two new lodges were created this year and one
was lost to consolidation making this the first year since 1966 that our Grand
Lodge has had an overall increase in the number of lodges.
Our membership at the beginning of the fiscal year was 61,044 and we
had 2,319 gains and 4,159 losses. Our membership as of June 30 was 58,866. I am
delighted to report that we had a total of 2,529 applications, which has surpassed
all forecasts for the year. This year we raised 1,380 Master Masons – a level of
activity not seen in the last twenty-one years.
Shared Services
The Grand Secretary serves as the corporate secretary to the boards that
work together with the Grand Lodge to advance the strategic plan of the Masons of
California. With the trustees and management of the Masonic Homes, California
Masonic Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple and the directors of
Acacia Creek Union City and the Nob Hill Masonic Center, the Grand Secretary’s
office develops and implements programs and policies that educate and engage
our members and encourage excellence in our leadership and throughout the craft.
We provide high-quality business services to ensure efficient and effective use
of our resources as we strive to make a profound difference in the lives of our
members and in our communities.
Philanthropy
Though a climate of economic uncertainty persists, I am pleased to report
that, as of the writing of this report, over 5,000 brethren have contributed close
to $1 million to the annual fund. An additional $450,000 has been raised for the
Grand Master’s Project: Operation Greatest Gift – which brought 612 veterans and
184 guardians to Washington, D. C. to visit the national World War II memorial.
Masons4Mitts, a strategic partnership of the Masons of California and the Giants
Community Fund, raised over $37,000 and provided a new baseball glove to more

90

Proceedings of the

than 1,800 Junior Giants. These efforts, under the guidance of Brother Douglas
Ismail, the Chief Philanthropy Officer and Executive Vice President of the
California Masonic Foundation, are a tribute to the generosity of our fraternity.
In the year ahead, led by the California Masonic Foundation, our craft
will renew its historic support for public education, a goal echoed in the feedback
we received from hundreds of members in listening sessions held across California
this year as we developed our strategic plan. This vision demonstrates how our
fraternity seeks to remain a vital and relevant force engaging our philanthropic
resources to address the critical issues of our day.
In partnership with the Masonic Homes of California, our fraternity
will launch a new Masonic Center for Youth and Families in San Francisco’s
Presidio that will offer cutting edge, comprehensive assessment and treatment for
youth who struggle with behavioral, academic, emotional or social difficulties.
This will be the only center of its kind in North America offering a 360 degree,
comprehensive program to empower youth to realize their potential. Through
these services, the fraternity strives to find solutions to critical health issues facing
our own children and families as well as youth and families across California.
Program Services
The Grand Secretary’s office provides support to the many programs
of the Grand Lodge in the area of communications, membership development,
leadership development, and Masonic education and formation.
A lot was achieved this year in each of these areas, but for this oral report
today, I would like to mention in particular our accomplishments in the area of
communications. The Association of Media and Publishing in an organization
representing nearly 1,000 membership organizations in the US. Each year they
recognize these membership organizations for their print and online publishing
efforts. They issue awards in several different categories and, in the fashion of
the Olympics, the top three organizations are awarded a bronze, silver, or gold
award in each category. This year, our online newsletter, The Leader, was awarded
a silver medal as the second best electronic newsletter in the country. Our 2009
Annual Report also won the silver award, just ahead of Rotary International who
received the bronze award. The member center on our website won the gold
award for the best member’s only website in the country, and our public website
freemason.org won the gold award for design excellence. We are very proud that
the publishing industry has recognized our efforts in these areas.
Over the year, the Grand Lodge made a particular effort to capitalize on
social media and technology to increase the reach of Masonry in this State and
to provide greater access to resources for our members. The re-designed Member
Center allows all of our members to access information and conduct important

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

91

business more efficiently. All lodge Secretaries now have automatic access to
iMember, making it easier for them to complete their reporting and other duties.
The Masons of California Facebook page now has over 6,100 friends and our
iPhone lodge locator and newly launched Freemason Magazine phone application
help members connect and deepen their appreciation for one another and for
our craft.
Dispensations and Charters
In accordance with §801.065 of the California Masonic Code, Paideia
Lodge U.D. has petitioned this Grand Lodge for a Charter. A dispensation was
granted to Paideia Lodge on September 9, 2009 by Most Worshipful Larry L.
Adamson. Grand Master Nagel continued the dispensation after being installed
Grand Master. In reviewing the records of the Lodge and from the information
provided by the District Inspector, it has been determined that Paideia Lodge has
met the requirements of the petition. According, Most Worshipful, I move that a
Charter be issued to Paideia Lodge U.D. and that it be entered into the Registry of
this Grand Lodge as Paideia Lodge No. 852. Motion adopted.
In accordance with the same Code section, General Douglas MacArthur
Lodge U.D. has petitioned this Grand Lodge for a Charter. Grand Master Nagel
granted a dispensation to this Lodge on May 29, 2010. In reviewing the records of
the Lodge and from the information provided by the District Inspector, it has been
determined that General Douglas MacArthur Lodge has met the requirements
of the petition. Accordingly, Most Worshipful, I move that a Charter be issued
to General Douglas MacArthur Lodge U.D. and that it be entered into the
Registry of this Grand Lodge as General Douglas MacArthur Lodge No. 853.
Motion adopted.
Appreciation
As I conclude my report, I wish to convey my deepest appreciation
and regard for the 340 lodge Secretaries and 178 Assistant Secretaries in this
jurisdiction who are such vital partners in sustaining the health of our lodges and
our Grand Lodge.
I would also like to thank the District Inspectors and Assistant Grand
Lecturers who work so diligently with the Grand Secretary’s office to support our
lodges and membership. In particular, I want to acknowledge the contributions
of Brother Vernon M. Dandridge, Assistant Grand Lecturer for Division V, who
is retiring at the end of this Annual Communication. Brother Dandridge has
been a tireless supporter of our craft and his devotion to our shared vision is
an inspiration.

92

Proceedings of the

I also work closely with the many boards and committees of the Grand
Lodge and want to express my sincere gratitude to all of the trustees and directors
and committee members who give so generously of their time and talent to support
the strategic vision of the fraternity.
I would also like to acknowledge the contributions of our Grand
Treasurer, the Very Worshipful Glenn Woody. His exceptional leadership and
ability were no more evident than in his unceasing efforts to maintain the health
and security of our investments and finances through these very volatile economic
times. We have all benefited from his experience and wisdom as well as his
heartfelt devotion to Masonry.
It is a privilege for me to work with the remarkable staff at the Grand
Lodge Office, including those in Union City and Covina, for whom the service to
our membership is much more than a job. They strive to give their very best each
and every day and I appreciate the support they give to our members, residents
and communities.
And finally, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Kenneth
G. Nagel, for the opportunity to serve with him. In every aspect of the role as
Grand Master, he has provided this Grand Lodge with tremendous leadership.
His passionate sense of gratitude for the service of the Greatest Generation, which
gave rise to Operation Greatest Gift, is the same profound spirit of gratitude
expressed in the theme “Coming Home” which conveys his heartfelt appreciation
for this generation and the daily contributions of every Mason. He has made it
easy to be proud of him and proud to be a Mason. Thank you, Most Worshipful.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary
