Report of the Grand Lecturer
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Most Worshipful Grand Master and my Brothers of the Grand Lodge.
Our Grand Master has started each of his addresses this year by expressing
his thanks to you all for allowing him the privilege of serving as Grand Master. As
your Grand Lecturer, I need to echo his sentiments and thank you for granting me
the honor of serving in this office.
Time is short this year, so let me just touch upon some of the things
we have accomplished. We’ve held the usual assortment of ritual conferences,
AGL schools for Inspectors and Coaches, Master Mason seminars throughout the
state, and the Division and District schools you’ve come to love. As I’ve traveled
around and been able to witness your degrees, I’ve been very pleased with the
overall quality of your work.
This past year we increased the number of Divisions to nine. We liked
it so well, we are adding a tenth, adding Frank Lee as an AGL on the Ritual
Committee. Speaking of AGLs, I’m very sorry to announce that we are losing
Vernon Dandridge in Division V. He has been a dedicated, loyal and valuable
asset on our committee, but his term has expired. We are pleased to name Lynn
Wallingford as his replacement, although Vernon insists he can’t be replaced.
We held another successful Ritual Competition, consisting of the
three full-form proficiencies. We were happy to see eight of the nine divisions
represented. The scores were uniformly high, with Lodi No. 256 as the winner. To
answer your unasked question, it has been decided to NOT hold the competition
this year.
We are happy to announce the completion of the revised and reprinted
Officers’ Monitor. In addition to its being slightly reorganized, we’ve made some
changes (although we all know ritual never changes) which we are sure you
will appreciate. For example, the book is larger and easier to read, the election
procedure for candidates and officers has been expanded and clarified, and we’ve
indicated where the raps should occur in the perambulations.
Something has recently come to our attention which I find deeply
disturbing. Several lodges throughout the state are committing secret work
to English text and sharing it with their candidates. When confronted, they
take refuge behind the fact that our obligation does not specifically prohibit
dissemination and distribution of our secret ritual, as long as it was written by
nameless others. Despite their semantic quibbling, this is a flagrant violation of
our obligation. The intent of our law is clear. Brethren, we should seek ways to
observe both the letter and the spirit of our law, not connive ways to circumvent it.
To do otherwise is shameful, and anyone who does so needs to seriously examine

112

Proceedings of the

his Masonic integrity. We have been advised by our Jurisprudence Committee to
consider any such practice a Masonic offense and deal with it accordingly.
Once again, I have to thank my friends and colleagues, the AGLs and
Inspectors, for their impressive efforts to raise and maintain the level of our ritual
performance. We are truly the envy of jurisdictions throughout the Country. My
Brethren, you have accepted an awesome responsibility and we all owe you a
huge debt for your unceasing labors. We also continue to praise the IDA staff for
all it does to put qualified Inspectors into the field. All of their efforts, of course,
would be in vain without their hard-working and conscientious audience, you, the
officers and members of our lodges. You are the reason we are envied by the other
jurisdictions. Without you, our Fraternity could not survive.
I’d be remiss if I failed to extend our gratitude to the Very Worshipful
Allan Casalou and his entire staff for being always ready and willing to help and
respond so promptly to our every request.
Also, I need to thank Most Worshipful Ken and Kathy for their inspiring
leadership and for their gracious inclusion of June and me in their Family. Ken
is an outstanding ritualist and has raised the ritual bar to a level which may never
again be equaled. He has performed virtually every one of our ceremonies, and
ALL from memory. Another example, my Brethren, worthy of all imitation.
In conclusion, my Brothers, keep in mind everything we do is intended
to help you make true Masons. As you assume your Masonic duties, either in
the Lodge or in public, be guided by the simple axiom, “Everything you do will
change someone’s life forever.”
Respectfully submitted,
Paul D. Hennig, Grand Lecturer

Grand Chaplain’s Message

by The Very Reverend Irwin M. Fershleiser
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Past Grand Masters, Distinguised and Honored
Guets, my fellow Grand Lodge Officers and Brothers:
My talk today was inspired by the words of Carl H. Claudy, Past Grand
Master of the District of Columbia.
The Forgotten Word
“Never have I been so glad to get to lodge as tonight!” said the New
Brother to the Old Tiler in the anteroom. “Someone here owes you some money
or something?” asked the Old Tiler. “No indeed! But lying awake last night,
thinking about Masonry, I tried to recall the word of a Master Mason and I couldn’t!
I couldn’t sleep all night, trying to remember. I couldn’t even remember it today,
and it bothered me! I was glad to come to lodge tonight and get instructed!”
“You shouldn’t have worried over that,” answered the Old Tiler. “Our
memories play strange tricks. You didn’t need it, did you?” “No, but a Mason
shouldn’t forget it. It’s the most important thing in Masonry.” “So we are told,”
answered the Old Tiler. “But it’s the meaning, not the syllables you are taught to
pronounce that is important.”
“Why, Old Tiler! How can you say that?” “Because it is true,” answered
the Old Tiler. “Is it important what kind of cloth is put in an apron? Is it important
what particular piece of iron is used to make a pillar, or what particular copy of
a Bible is on the Altar, or what particular piece of wood is used in the gavel?
Isn’t it important that we wear an apron, and know why, that we have a pillar to
teach a lesson, that we revere the Great Light in Masonry, that we have a gavel
for keeping order? Are the syllables of the word important, or is the spirit, the
meaning and the symbolism that is important?”
“Masons must know the word, the modes of recognition, the signs and
tokens. But all these may slip from the memory and still a brother should have
Freemasonry in his heart.”
“We are taught that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was
with God. Do you read into that statement some particular word? Or is the Word
here used in the Old Jewish sense of the truth, the light of knowledge for which
man may strive?”
“Masonry’s search for the lost word is far more than a syllable, my brother.
The substitute word is more than an exclamation. It is an inward knowledge of
oneness with the Great Architect, for which all men of all ages have searched. Not
all search in vain; many find their Word, but others continue to search.”

116

Proceedings of the

“It is this which is important. Do not be troubled if your mind plays
a prank on you. Better men than you and I have forgotten their own names.
Now and then one forgets the name of Deity. All you need is conversation with
a brother who sat in lodge with you. If you desire, nothing prevents you from
giving and receiving the lessons as Masons are taught to do.”
“Your only cause for worry is that you forget that Masonry in men’s
hearts searches for that which no man has yet put into words. The tender lesson of
the Master Mason is that which makes a good man better. It is this lesson which
you must never forget.”
“You should be a travelling lecturer!” said the New Brother. “But I’d
rather sit here and tile.” “But you can’t get anywhere!” “Neither can a sign post
by the road,” smiled the Old Tiler. “Yet it points the way.”
Now you go out there and point the way.

Grand Oration
Most Worshipful Kenneth G. Nagel, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters,
All distinguished guests and my brethren:
Good morning! And it is a good morning! However my Brothers I do
have a problem! I don’t know that anyone can help me with my problem; but,
please permit me to share it with you.
You see, one year ago I was appointed and installed the Grand Orator of
the Grand Lodge of California. Little did I know what a hallmark year I would
experience. Little did I know how much I would come to appreciate, admire, and
hold in such high esteem this Grand Master who has guided us with wisdom,
understanding, and a consuming desire to serve his brethren in Freemasonry.
Little did I know that I would work as a team with my brother Grand
Officers who would display charm, eloquence, friendliness, and a sense of humor.
Throughout the year, they would also exhibit their over abundant energy and
inspiring personalities to all.
Little did I know that my wife and I would have the privilege of traveling
with and getting to know the Grand Officers, as well as their escorts, as we came
together into a wonderful Grand Family. Our special thanks to both Ken and
Kathy who together, led the Grand Family and allowed us to serve our Craft.
Little did I know how totally impressed I would be with the devotion
and dedication of hundreds . . . no make that thousands of Masons throughout
California who supported us this year. Each time we would open Grand Lodge and
perform a Cornerstone Laying, the Masons in the area came out in large numbers
in support of what we were doing. It was exciting to see the many students, faculty,
public officials, as well as, Masons and their families in attendance.
Little did I know that I personally would enjoy, beyond my wildest
dreams, the extreme privilege of representing our great Fraternity outside this
lodge room and be allowed to testify to the world about the precepts, principals,
teachings, and honored ideals we as Masons practice daily.
Little did I know that my heart and my very soul would be so touched
by our Grand Master’s vision and the incredible devotion and generosity of our
members to “Operation Greatest Gift.” Just the thought of over six hundred World
War II Veterans, who put their lives on hold to protect our freedom, being able
to visit the World War II Memorial. What a wonderful, wonderful gift for our
veterans to be able to say good-bye to their fallen comrades, to bring to a close the
horrors of war, and to experience final peace. This should move us all.

120

Proceedings of the

Little did I know that “Coming Home” would have such a far reaching
impact on me personally, on my lodge, and to every Mason and Lodge in
California. “Coming Home” speaks to the return of inactive Masons to their
Lodges. Tens of thousands of our craft pay dues yet do not darken the doors of
our lodges or participate in our activities. The truly sad part of this is that many
of these members went for decades without receiving so much as a phone call.
My brothers, in this tragedy we are all remiss. Every man who becomes
a Mason does so for a reason. I grew up in a small town near Fresno of about
5,000 people back in the 50’s and 60’s. The movers and shakers of the community
all belonged to the Masonic Lodge. The Little League coach, the Scout Master,
Sunday school teachers, club members, firemen, policemen, teachers, and business
owners all participated and enjoyed the benefits Masonry had to offer; yet, about
two decades later that lodge closed their doors.
What happened? Where did we go wrong? How does a vibrant, alive,
thriving community organization consisting of good men who were leaders in
that very community cease to exist? You and I both know this is not an isolated
incident. This downward turn of events repeats itself in our lodges and in our
communities again and again. Every mason, me included, must do their part to
reverse this trend and revive our craft. Operation “Coming Home”, though very
effective, should be just the beginning of renewed dedication and involvement on
all our parts.
My brothers, we must reconnect with each other. We must reconnect our
inactive brethren and get them back. We need to identify the reasons why they
sought membership and proceeded through the degrees. We need to unite them
with other masons giving them a purpose if we are to survive. This will take a lot
of work but the return on our investment will be worth it. We also need to be the
instrument of needed change. Not our basic core values and traditional ritual; but,
the way we operate and do business.
Identify the needs of your individual lodge and go to work on what it
will take to make your lodge better. Work with a core group in your lodge to begin
with small steps, one step at a time, bringing others on board with each step.
Never change “just for change”, but always be open and ready to make changes
when and wherever needed.
It’s like the historian who heard of a farm family in Illinois that
possessed the axe that Abraham Lincoln used when splitting logs as a young man.
The historian found the farm and found the farmer in the yard splitting wood
for his fireplace. He asked him about the axe and the farmer said, “It’s true. Abe
Lincoln lived around here and split wood for my great, great, great grandfather.
It happened that my great, great, great Grandpa bought a new axe from a peddler
the day before Abe Lincoln came to work. He loaned the axe to Lincoln to use.
We’ve kept it ever since.” “That is a real historical treasure,” said the historian.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

121

“It should be in a museum. Would you mind going into the house and bringing it
out so that I may see it?”
“Well,” said the farmer, “I don’t have to go into the house. I’ve got it
right here.” He handed the horrified historian the very axe he was using. “You
mean you still use it?” the historian asked. “Sure do,” said the farmer. “An axe
is meant to be used.” The historian looked it over carefully and said,”I must say,
you’ve certainly taken good care of it.” “Sure,” said the farmer, “I’m protecting
history. Why I’ve replaced the handle three times and the head twice!”
Brethren, our beloved fraternity is like Abe Lincoln’s axe. We tend
to assume that it has always been the way it is. But the truth of the matter is
we’ve done more than replace the handle three times and the head twice. We
need to realize our lodges and our Craft in particular have had frequent and even
sometimes dramatic changes. We need to reach out and become a part of what is
happening, be involved in changes that are being made, and make sure that they
are for the betterment of not only our lodges, but also our Craft.
We must always remember . . . and I believe the lodge in my hometown
forgot to remember . . . that in spite of the many changes which have already
happened in the past, changes are bound to occur in the future. Get on board!
Bring others with you. Be a part of what is happening or you just might find you
will be left behind. Masonry is like any other living thing . . . it must evolve and
grow or it will die.
We need to be willing to work to have more “Coming Home.” We need
to make contact with all our members and revitalize them too. Just like Abraham
Lincoln’s axe, Masonry is best when active and used by all its members and
not just allowed to “rust away” in some historical museum. The return of our
members and “use by all” will keep us bright and sharp no matter how often
we replace the handle or the head. Remember the active, growing fraternity of
Masonry has and will change the world.
We need to experience “Coming Home.” We’re like hot coals in a fire.
Together touching each other continually, we burn bright and hot. But when the
red hot coals don’t touch and are separated, we, like the coals, begin to dim, lose
our glow, and eventually the fire goes out. We turn from glowing red to flat black
and our world turns cold. Just like the burning coals, we need each other to keep
the glow strong and warm.
We need the relationships with each other, with all our brethren, to keep
our fraternity strong and warm. Should we see a member separating from the
warm glow of our fire, we need to bring them back. Brothers, we need to do all
we can to keep our fire alive, to keep each other bright and burning, and to bring
light and warmth to an otherwise cold and uncaring world.

122

Proceedings of the

Brothers, we need to share our warm glow with not only our members
but with our communities as well. Imagine all we can accomplish if we would
just “reach out” to those around us who are not a part of our fraternity, sharing our
principals and our teachings. Encourage members to go out into the community
and make a difference by doing. Masons don’t just give “lip service.” Masons get
involved! Make your world and your community aware that it is richer and better
because “Masons step up and get the job done!”
My Brothers, the problem I alluded to earlier should be obvious. The
Grand Family of 2010 is just not ready to give it up. But on second thought, after
a closer examination, there really is no problem. Masonry is the greatest fraternity
on earth and even though the 2010 Grand Officers must reluctantly give up our
positions we were so honored to have, isn’t it exciting to know that together,
working with all of you, we will continue to make a difference?
Brethren, greater things are yet to come! Greater things are still to be
done! May God bless America, our great country; may God bless the Masonic
Fraternity and the great works we do; and may God bless each of you and those
you hold dear. And yes it is a grand and glorious day to be a Mason! Thank you
for your kind attention and thank you Most Worshipful.
Respectfully submitted,
John W. Herring, Grand Orator

Grand Master’s Recommendations
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 1
Increases the Representation on the
Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee
Our California Masonic Code defines the membership of the Junior
Grand Warden Recommending Committee as the Grand Master, Deputy Grand
Master, Grand Wardens, Past Grand Masters, and three members of Grand Lodge
appointed annually by the Grand Master.
Since being elected Junior Grand Warden in 2006, I have been a member
of the recommending committee on four consecutive occasions, including this
year when I chaired the committee as Grand Master. This experience has bolstered
my confidence in our procedure for recommending a candidate for the office of
Junior Grand Warden. However, I believe there is room for improvement.
As Grand Master, it was my responsibility to appoint three members of
Grand Lodge as members of the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee.
As Grand Masters have done before me, I considered the many Masters, Wardens,
and Past Masters of this jurisdiction and tried to appoint three brothers who were
representative of the Craft as a whole. This is a very difficult task in a state as
large and diverse as California. The recommendation of a brother for election as
Junior Grand Warden is one of the most important decisions to be considered each
year, and in my view, there should be greater representation of the membership
on the committee.
Our jurisdiction is already divided into Divisions and Districts as a way
to insure proper representation of the Grand Master and the Grand Lodge around
the state. It seems to me that this existing structure can aid in an effort to increase
the representation on the recommending committee.
I recommend that the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee
be expanded from three members of Grand Lodge to one member of Grand
Lodge from each Division appointed by the Grand Master annually. To assist the
Grand Master in surveying the entire state for possible appointments, I further
recommend that the Assistant Grand Lecturer recommend three members of
Grand Lodge from his Division to be considered by the Grand Master.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 404.420 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:

126

Proceedings of the

§404.420. RECOMMENDEE FOR JUNIOR GRAND WARDEN.
The Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, the Grand Wardens, the Past Grand
Masters, and a three members of Grand Lodge appointed annually by the Grand
Master from each division described in Section 404.315 of this Code to serve
for a single term only concurrently with his term and who are not past or present
elected Grand Officers, shall constitute a committee to recommend to Grand
Lodge a member for election as Junior Grand Warden.
The members of Grand Lodge appointed annually by the Grand Master from each
division to this committee shall serve for a single term only concurrently with his
term and may not be past or present elected Grand Officers. Each Assistant Grand
Lecturer may recommend three members of Grand Lodge from Lodges in his
division to be considered by the Grand Master for appointment to this committee.
However, the Grand Master may appoint a member of Grand Lodge who was
not recommended by the Assistant Grand Lecturer of the division in which the
appointee’s Lodge is situated.
The Grand Master shall call and preside at meetings of the committee, but shall
not vote except in cases of tie votes. A majority of the whole committee shall
constitute a quorum. A majority vote of those present and eligible to vote shall be
necessary to select the recommendee.
The recommendee shall be a member of a Lodge in the North and of a Lodge
in the South, alternately. A Lodge in the North is one whose meeting place is
located north of the southern boundary line of Monterey, Kings, Tulare and Inyo
Counties. A Lodge in the South is one whose meeting place is located south of the
northern boundary line of San Luis Obispo, Kern and San Bernardino Counties.
Within 30 days following the selection by the Recommending Committee, but in
no case later than 60 days prior to the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge,
the name of the recommendee and his biographical sketch shall be sent to:
A.

Each Inspector, to be communicated promptly by the Inspectors to the
Masters and Wardens of each Inspectoral district and through them to
other members of Grand Lodge in their respective Lodges; and

B.

To such other members of Grand Lodge as the Grand Master determines.

All dissemination of this information thereafter shall be oral and not by any means
of reproduction.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

127

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution recommends that the Junior Grand Warden
Recommending Committee be expanded from three members of Grand Lodge to
one member of Grand Lodge from each Division appointed by the Grand Master
annually.
The Recommending Committee will then consist of the Deputy Grand
Master, the Grand Wardens, the Past Grand Masters and one member of Grand
Lodge from each Division. The Grand Master is chair of the committee and votes
only in case of a tie.
This resolution expands the recommendation process to provide a
broader representation of the overall Masonic geography of the State. It does
expand the knowledge base of the potential leadership available throughout our
Grand Lodge.
The balance of the number of members of the Committee from the North
and the South is an element of concern. If there is a change in the number of
Divisions, then the members of this Committee will be adjusted accordingly.
The alternating of North and South Lodge residency of the recommendee
does not change.
The practice of selecting the Grand Lodge Junior Grand Warden
Recommendee by the Recommending Committee has been a long standing
policy. It was amended in 1993 to include the Executive Line and this Resolution
expands the Committee even further.
This recommendation is consistent with the Policy and General Purposes
of this Grand Lodge.
Recommendation CARRIED-OVER.
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 2
Protects the Benefits of Membership for Senior Members
Our fraternity is blessed with very high member loyalty. Most Masons
will remain members of the Craft for their entire life. As a result we have members
on our rolls from age 18 to 101. For some of our members in their senior years,
though, keeping up their membership in the Craft can be challenging. Not only
do some of them live on fixed incomes, but some find themselves at a point in life
where someone else is handling their affairs. Far too often these members are lost
and forgotten. They lose touch with the lodge and the lodge finds it difficult to
keep in touch with them. They are suspended for non-payment of dues at a much
higher rate than they have their dues remitted. We have made progress in recent

128

Proceedings of the

years in our efforts to locate members with whom we have lost contact, but we are
still suspending far too many of our senior members.
Today, there are 23,323 members in our database who are 80 years or
older. It astonishes to me that nearly 35% of our members over 80 years old have
been suspended for non-payment of dues, while only 6% have had their dues
remitted. We are suspending our most vulnerable members at a time when they
might need us the most. I have heard first-hand from senior members, their wives,
and widows who feel lost or detached from the lodge. I have known widows
that find themselves in a desperate situation, but they do not technically qualify
for Masonic assistance because the husband’s dues lapsed or he was suspended.
We must not let this trend continue. We must be vigilant in our efforts to stay in
contact with all of our members, especially our senior members. I believe we can
build better safeguards in our laws to insure that our lost senior brothers are not
completely abandoned by the fraternity and their wives and widows cast outside
the circle of our protection.
I recommend that we change our laws so that members who have reached
the age of 80 years or who have an aggregate number of years in age and active
years of membership in the fraternity equaling 120 or more may not be suspended
for non-payment of dues without a report from the Member Retention Committee
evidencing when and where the committee interviewed the delinquent member,
why the delinquent member has not paid his dues and whether the delinquent
member has the ability to pay his dues.

If you adopt this recommendation, Section 809.370 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:
§809.370. SUSPENSION FOR NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
If a member has not paid his dues during a period of 12 months, the Secretary
shall notify him that he will be suspended for non-payment of dues unless at
the Lodge’s next Stated Meeting either his dues have been paid or sickness or
inability to pay is shown as the cause for the failure to pay. The notice shall be
given either by certified mail, with return receipt requested, addressed to his last
known address, or by actual service of notice, duly certified by the Tiler. If all
dues due and payable have not been paid by the time of the Lodge’s next Stated
Meeting, he shall be declared suspended by the Master, unless for special reasons
shown the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant him further time for payment. No
worthy brother who is unable to pay his dues shall be suspended for non-payment
of dues.
No member who has attained the age of 80 years or who has attained an aggregate
number of years in age and years as a Master Mason in good standing equaling
120 or more shall be suspended for non-payment of dues without a written report
to the Lodge from the Member Retention Committee evidencing when and where
the committee interviewed the delinquent member, why the delinquent member
has not paid his dues and whether the delinquent member has the ability to pay his
dues. A copy of this report shall be provided to the Grand Secretary at least thirty
days before the vote may be taken on the suspension.
A member shall not be expelled from Masonry for non-payment of dues.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
All Masons have an obligation to pay their dues. If they do not pay their
dues they can be suspended. Our current policy is not to suspend those who are
unable to pay.
This legislation creates a separate category of individuals based on age
and years of service who can only be suspended if the following steps are met by
the Member Retention Committee:
1.

The delinquent member must be interviewed,

2.

Identify why he has not paid his dues, and

3.

Establish whether the delinquent member has the ability to
pay his dues.

If this legislation is approved, a lodge may suspend the member no
earlier than thirty days after the report from the Member Retention Committee
has been submitted to the Grand Secretary.
This recommendation is consistent with the policy and general purposes
of this Grand Lodge.
Recommendation APPROVED.
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 3
Modifies Masonic Trial Procedures
We live in an increasingly litigious society. People take their disputes
to court, even if those problems could be resolved by sitting around a table and
reaching a good faith compromise. In recent years, we have seen this trend in
our lodges. Disputes between brothers which should be resolved in the spirit
of brotherly love and truth are instead addressed by the filing of charges of
unmasonic conduct. In 2008, Grand Master Hopper suggested a mediation
procedure to resolve these disputes but too few Masons are taking advantage of
this alternative. Of course, some actions should be resolved by a trial and, if a
guilty verdict is rendered, should result in a reprimand, suspension or expulsion
of the brother committing them. For those matters which should be taken to trial,
they are generally moved to another lodge because of the strife which the dispute
has already created in the lodge in which the dispute arose. This transfer puts a
heavy burden on the Master, Secretary and other members of the lodge to which
the trial is transferred.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

131

Because of these concerns, I appointed a committee composed of
Worshipful Ralph Dash (Chairman of Trial Review), experienced Trial Masters
and Worshipful Brothers Robert Scott and Robert Sills and Most Worshipful
R. Stephen Doan (Chairman of Jurisprudence) to review our current trial
procedures. I asked them to consider ways to streamline the trial process and
make the procedures easier on those lodges which have a member accused of
unmasonic conduct and those lodges to which the resulting trials are transferred.
The committee members spent a considerable period studying these problems.
As a result of their study, they have proposed revisions to our current Masonic
trial rules and procedures. In addition to addressing my concerns, they have also
included in their proposal those best practices used by some Trial Masters which
should be made available to all Trial Masters. I recommend that you adopt their
proposed revisions which are set forth in this recommendation.
In summary, if you adopt this recommendation, these new rules and
procedures would:
1.

Streamline and shorten the entire trial process while protecting
the rights of all parties.

2.

Provide specific notices to let the parties know what are their
rights and duties.

3.

Add a requirement that the Committee on Jurisprudence
review all charges before the proceedings begin to ensure that
they are in proper form.

4.

Require Trial Masters to conduct pre-trial conferences where
all issues can be discussed, including settlement, before trial.

5.

Relieve lodges from many of the administrative burdens and
costs associated with the current trial process.

I believe that these proposed revisions to our trial rules and procedures
are a vast improvement over our current law and recommend their adoption.
If you adopt this recommendation, certain changes will be made to
the California Masonic Code. This changes are available at [insert the internet
address for the material].

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Nagel, recognizing both the litigious nature of our society
and the complexity of our current trial procedure, is recommending that Grand
Lodge adopt a revised code regarding the trial process. The purpose of the revision
was to simplify and shorten the procedure while maintaining the due processes
that are owed to an accused person. The passage of this recommendation will
change a number of our current practices.

132

Proceedings of the

The proposed new method would keep the trial in the lodge from which
the charges emanated. In order to maintain neutrality, the Trial Master and, if
needed, the Commission would be appointed by the Grand Master. None of these
men will be members of the lodge in question. The Trial Master has always been
appointed by the Grand Master. However, the lodge preferring the charges would
no longer elect the commission from its own membership. It is already part of
our law that, in the case of the trial of an incumbent Master, the commission is
appointed by the Grand Master; the new law extends this practice to all trials. It
is expected that the Masons who are appointed by the Grand Master would be
more familiar with trial proceedings, which should facilitate a number of trial
processes, such as notification and servicing.
This revision also changes the entity that receives the charges. If this
recommendation passes, the charges will be filed directly with Grand Lodge
rather than with the Master of the particular lodge. Under our current practice, the
Master of the lodge receives the charges and decides if they are serious enough to
justify a finding of unmasonic conduct if they were to be proven. This Committee
understands that this change was introduced intentionally. It was believed that
Masters are not always able to separate the charges from the personalities of the
accuser and accused. There have been documented instances in which lodge
politics, rather than the charges per se, have led to decisions to pursue or dismiss
accusations. This decision would be left to the Jurisprudence Committee, who
would be able to properly word the charges in a more timely fashion.
The revised procedure more specifically defines and outlines the
processes of the trial. The various parties are more clearly infored about their rights
and duties. Forms and check-lists are completed as this process is conducted. A
mandated pre-trial conference has been introduced. This conference allows both
parties to view the evidence, including witness lists, clarify and understand what
is going to happen, and even consider possible settlements instead of formal trials.
This procedure has been modeled after the one that is used in administrative law,
such as instances when a professional is faced with potential loss of his or her
license. Procedural safeguards were built in to protect due process.
Our current practice, according to data from the Grand Secretary, results
in lengthy and inefficient trials. Since Masons are entitled to a speedy tiral with
due process, this legislation is consistent with our policy and general purposes.
Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
The proposed revisions to the Trials section of our Code have been in the
making for the past two years. These revisions significantly streamline and speed
up the entire trial process while insuring that the rights of all parties are protected.
For the first time, the Code will have explicit rules governing every aspect of our
disciplinary system, rules that are easily understood. In addition, a series of forms
and checklists has been prepared to aid the Trial Master in his duties.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

133

Adoption of these revisions is of critical importance. Our current system
is cumbersome, time consuming and, to most Masons, incomprehensible.
Accordingly, the Committee on Trial Review recommends that Grand
Master’s Recommendation 2010-03 be adopted.
Recommendation APPROVED.
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 4
Restores the Historic Role of Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons
When one considers the officers required in the Ritual for a Lodge
of Entered Apprentice Masons and those of the two higher degrees, one might
question why the Treasurer and Secretary are required for the first degree and
not for the two others. This question might lead one to examine the history of
the transaction of business in Masonic lodges on various degrees. It would not
take long to realize that most lodges in the world conduct business on the Entered
Apprentice Degree and that such was the case in the United States until the midnineteenth century.
Looking back to the year 1826, and the two decades that followed, it is
found that in 1826, one William Morgan of New York, who had purported to be
a Freemason, disappeared. Though it was never proven that he had received the
first three degrees of Masonry, he did receive degrees in a New York Royal Arch
Chapter. After he was denied affiliation with a second chapter, word spread that
Morgan was about to publish an exposé revealing all of the secrets and rituals of
Freemasonry. It was then that he disappeared and Freemasons were accused of
murdering him. Though most of the facts surrounding William Morgan and his
disappearance have never been proven, this event had serious ramifications for
Freemasonry.
The Morgan Affair fueled an anti-Masonic movement that had been
brewing for over a decade. A fierce bitterness grew against Freemasonry and
individual Masons. Lodge meetings were interrupted by protests of angry and
sometimes violent mobs. Men pretending to be Masons lied to gain entry into
the lodge only later to publish exposés of what they witnessed. Others went so
far as to petition to receive the degrees and, once they were initiated, sought to
make money by selling their stories. Membership declined all around the US.
The national membership fell from 100,000 to 40,000 by 1836. In the State of
New York, the numbers dropped from 20,000 to a mere 3,000. Many lodges did
not have enough members to meet and surrendered their charters. Some Grand
Lodges ceased to operate all together.

134

Proceedings of the

This was the state of affairs in the late 1830s. The Craft was barely
limping along. Because so many of the men who were employed as lecturers had
to find other work, knowledge of the ritual was poor. Because different states
used different rituals, it was difficult to investigate visitors who claimed to be
Masons from other parts of the country. In 1839, a resolution was adopted by the
Grand Lodge of Alabama, which requested all Grand Lodges to send a delegate
to Washington, D.C. on the first Monday in March, 1842, “for the purpose of
determining upon a uniform mode of work throughout all the Lodges of the
United States and to make other lawful regulations for the protection and security
of the Craft.”
The Convention was held on March 7, 1842. Only ten of 23 Grand
Lodges were represented. While it was determined that there was not enough
representation from Grand Lodges nor enough time to agree upon a uniform
ritual, a number of recommendations were considered to protect the Craft from
the journalists and opportunists that sought to destroy Freemasonry, or at least to
make money by exposing its work.
It was recommended that certificates of good standing furnished by a
Grand Lodge be required of all visiting brethren. It was recommended by the
Grand Lodge of Missouri that business meetings be held on the Master Mason
Degree and not the Entered Apprentice Degree as a way to protect the privacy of
the transactions of the lodge. Though this recommendation was never formally
adopted, some Grand Lodges adopted this new procedure of conducting business
on the Master Mason Degree and excluding Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
Masons from the proceedings. Grand Lodges formed thereafter, like the Grand
Lodge in California in 1850, adopted this practice also.
Perhaps it was necessary during the Anti-Masonic Movement to protect
the Craft by excluding Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons from the
business transactions of the lodge, or perhaps this move was an unnecessary
overreaction to a very difficult challenge for the fraternity. In either case, the
exclusion of Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons from the business of
a lodge is a hindrance to their association with the fraternity today. It sets false
expectations for the new Master Mason. While there are certainly other factors,
I believe this exclusion contributes to the growing number of Entered Apprentice
and Fellow Craft Masons who do not advance in our Craft.
It is time to restore the historic role of Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft Masons and include them in the business transactions of the lodge. Many
Grand Lodges have done so over the years, including the Grand Lodge of Missouri
that made the recommendation back in 1842 to exclude them. California is the
only one of the ten western United States that does not permit business meetings
on one or both of the first two degrees.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

135

I recommend that California reinstate the historic role of Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons by holding Stated Meetings in a Lodge
of Entered Apprentice Masons. I also recommend that Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft Masons have the right to vote on any matter coming before the
lodge when they are present, except the right to ballot upon an application for the
Degrees or Affiliation.
If you adopt this recommendation, Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft Masons would have essentially all of the rights of members other than
the right to ballot and hold office. Perhaps it is again time to consider whether
Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons should also pay dues. Although not
officially part of this legislation, I recommend that our incoming Grand Master
appoint a committee to study the pros and cons of having Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft Masons pay dues and report back their findings at the next Annual
Communication.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made
to the California Masonic Code. Section 804.860 of the Code would be amended
to read as marked:
§804.860.
ADDITIONAL RIGHTS OF AND PROHIBITIONS ON
ENTERED APPRENTICES AND FELLOW CRAFTS.
An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft may sit in the Lodge in which he has
received the degree or degrees when open in a degree taken by him, while he
conducts himself with due order and propriety. He may advance after satisfactorily
passing a strict examination in a tiled Lodge. He may visit another Lodge working
in a degree taken by him, with the consent of the Master of his Lodge and the
consent of the Master of the Lodge visited, if accompanied by a Master Mason
who has sat with him in a tiled Lodge and vouches for him.
He shall not pay dues and is not entitled to vote or speak on any matter before the
Lodge, except as otherwise provided in Section 807.020 of this Code.
He may be buried with Masonic honors upon the request of his family, unless he
was a demitted, withdrawn, suspended or expelled Mason at the time of his death.
Neither he nor his widows or orphans are entitled to relief from the Lodge.
He shall not exercise any control over Lodge funds for charity or for other
purposes, except as otherwise provided in Section 807.020 of this Code.
Section 807.020 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:

136

Proceedings of the

§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO MEETINGS.
No Stated or Special Meetings of a Lodge shall be held on Sunday except for the
annual Installation of Officers or funeral services. If the Stated Meeting of a lunar
Lodge falls on a Sunday, the Stated Meeting shall be held on the following day.
All business, except the examination of candidates in the Candidate’s Lecture of
the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees, the conferring
of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees, and the
consideration of relief of a worthy Mason, shall be done in a Lodge of Master
Entered Apprentice Masons. When present, Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
Masons may speak and vote on all matters coming before the Lodge, except that
Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons may not ballot upon an application
for the degrees or for affiliation.
A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done or business transacted,
except by, or in the presence of, and under the continual direction of the Master,
the ranking Warden, the Grand Master or the Grand Master’s designated
representative.
No meeting shall be conducted by a Lodge unless the Charter of the Lodge is
present. A photocopy of the Charter may be made under the direction of the
Grand Secretary at the request and expense of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary
shall attach thereto a certificate with the seal of Grand Lodge affixed that the copy
is a true copy of the Lodge’s Charter. The copy may be used by the Lodge instead
of the original Charter at any time.
The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all meetings of a Lodge. At the

the manner prescribed in the Ritual. The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated
with any flag.
No Lodge shall transact any business with fewer than five members of the Lodge
present except the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while he is at his
post in the Tiler’s room.
Smoking is forbidden in the Lodge room at all times when the Lodge is in session.
There shall be no adjourned meeting. Each meeting of a Lodge must be closed
when the business proposed for transaction has been concluded.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The policy of this Grand Lodge since its formation in 1850 has been
to hold stated meetings in the Master Mason degree. Any change in this is a
significant change in our established policy.
The adoption of this recommendation has implications which must be
considered. An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft Mason who fails to advance
for more than three years (as per section 804.690 of the California Masonic Code)
would forfeit his fees, but still be able to participate in stated meetings and vote
on Lodge business. An individual who has not yet paid dues would be able to
vote on dues increases and investments of Lodge funds. Second and Third degree
proficiency examinations could not be conducted at a stated meeting.
However, it is one of the general purposes of this Grand Lodge to
encourage the advancement of Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts. This
recommendation would provide these Masons with increased opportunities to
participate in their Lodge.
This recommendation is not consistent with the policy of this Grand
Lodge, but is consistent with its general purposes.

Grand Master Adamson’s Recommendation No. 1
Two Grand Organists and Two Grand Tilers
To cut back on travel expenses, our Grand Lodge several years ago
authorized the appointment of an Assistant Grand Organist and an Assistant
Grand Tiler. If the Grand Organist is from the northern portion of the state, the
Assistant Grand Organist must be from the southern portion of the state, and vice
versa. The same rule applies to the Grand Tiler and the Assistant Grand Tiler.
The officer from the north performs the duties of the office when Grand Lodge
opens in the north, and the southern officer performs the duties when Grand
Lodge opens in the south. Only the officer performing the duties can submit for
expense reimbursement related to the opening. At present, there is no difference
in the duties required of the Assistant Grand Organist from what is required of the
Grand Organist nor any difference in the duties required of the Assistant Grand
Tiler from what is required of the Grand Tiler.
It is sometimes difficult for the Grand Master to decide between two
equally qualified brothers as to who will be the Grand Tiler and who will be the
Assistant Grand Tiler. This problem would be resolved if we could call both
brothers the Grand Tiler. To recognize the reality of the job requirements and
to recognize properly the brothers who serve in these offices, I recommend that
Grand Lodge grant this authority. The same rules would apply as before about
expense reimbursement claims: only one Grand Tiler could claim reimbursement.
However, both men could be introduced as the Grand Tiler. There would be no
Assistant Grand Tiler when there are two Grand Tilers. The same rules would
apply with respect the Grand Organist and the Assistant Grand Organist.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made
to the California Masonic Code. Section 20.000 of the Code would be amended
to read as marked:
§20.000. MEMBERS.

Grand Lodge shall be composed of a Grand Master (whose manner of
address shall be Most Worshipful), a Deputy Grand Master, a Senior
Grand Warden, and a Junior Grand Warden (whose manner of address
shall be Right Worshipful), a Grand Treasurer, a Grand Secretary and a
Grand Lecturer (whose manner of address shall be Very Worshipful), a
Grand Chaplain (whose manner of address shall be Very Reverend), the
Assistant Grand Lecturers, a Grand Orator, an Assistant Grand Secretary,
a Grand Marshal, a Grand Standard Bearer, a Grand Sword Bearer, a
Grand Bible Bearer, a Senior Grand Deacon, a Junior Grand Deacon,

a Grand Organist, a Grand Tiler, and, at the discretion of the Grand
Master, an additional Grand Organist an Assistant Grand Organist and
an additional Grand Tiler and an Assistant Grand Tiler (whose manner of
address shall be Worshipful), together with all of the Past Grand Officers
and Past Masters of this Jurisdiction, and the Master and Wardens of the
several chartered and duly constituted Lodges (except Research Lodges
or the Grand Master’s Lodge) of this Jurisdiction or the representatives

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This recommendation would eliminate the title of “Assistant” and give
power to the Grand Master to simply appoint two Grand Organists and two Grand
Tilers. Their function will not change and they will assist the Grand Master in his
travels throughout the state as they do now.
The purposes for creating the Assistant Grand Organist and Assistant
Grand Tiler was to provide the Grand Master with access to a brother at each end
of the state as he traveled from one end to the other. When these positions were
created, it worked as planned and it proved to be cost effective.
As the Grand Master has noted in his recommendation, one man is not
the assistant to the other. They bear equal responsibilities to the Grand Master
when they perform their respective duties. One man is no less qualified than the
other with respect to those duties. They both must be qualified in the eyes of the
Grand Master to serve Grand Lodge as required.
This recommendation will maintain the same structure of reimbursement
for travel currently in palce for these officers. This recommendation adds fairness
and is equitable as presented by our Grand Master.
This recommendation is consistent with the policy and general purposes
of this Grand Lodge.

Grand Master Adamson’s Recommendation No. 2
Personal Service of Grand Master’s Edict

As a general rule under our California Masonic Code, any notice to a
particular person must be either delivered in person or sent in a sealed envelope by
certified United States mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid, addressed
to the recipient at his address of record. However, when the notice is a Grand
Master’s edict addressed to a particular person, it must be delivered in person.
I have issued a number of edicts this year, and it sometimes have been
very difficult administratively to get someone to hand deliver the edict, particularly
if the person to whom it is addressed knew it was coming and was not anxious
to receive it. Before I became Grand Master, one brother who was breaking
our law received by mail an edict to comply with our law and acknowledged
receipt of the edict to the then Grand Master. However, because the edict was not
hand delivered, we could not bring this brother up on Masonic charges when he
continued violating the law after his acknowledged receipt of the edict! We need
to change this rule. I recommend that Grand Master be allowed to issue their
edicts by certified mail as other notices may be given.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 404.130 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:
§404.130. DUTIES OF THE GRAND MASTER.

A.

Exercise a general and careful supervision over the Craft, and see that

and benefits of Masonry;

D.

Cause to be personally served on issued to any Masonic Organization or

If the organization fails to act as required by the Grand Master, the Grand

support of Masonry to or personally participating in such organization,

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Last year Grand Master Adamson recommended a change to Section
404.130 of the California Masonic Code dealing with the duties of the Grand
Master as it relates to the service of Grand Master’s Edicts. Presently, the
California Masonic Code requires that such Edicts be personally served on
any Mason whom the Grand Master believes may have acted or failed to act in
violation of the requirements of this Code, the General Regulations of Masonry,
or of our Ritual.
Grand Master Adamson correctly pointed out that as a general rule
any notice other than the Edict must be either delivered in person or sent in a
sealed envelope by Certified United States mail, return receipt requested, postage
prepaid, addressed to the recipient at his address of record.
Grand Master Adamson indicated that, in some instances, it has been
difficult to personally serve such Edicts on a Brother who knew it was coming

and would make himself unavailable. The California Masonic Code presently
requires that such notices be served personally and, if not, the notice would be
invalid.
Grand Master Adamson’s amendment to our California Masonic Code
would provide one procedure for all notices, Grand Master’s Edicts, etc. to be
served to the members of the Craft by Certified Mail which is more reasonable.
This recommendation is consistent with the policy and general purposes

Grand Master Adamson’s Recommendation No. 5
Procedure on Ballot Box Rejection
I have dealt with at least nine different lodges during my term of office as
Grand Master where one brother used the ballot box improperly, either to punish
the lodge or someone other than the applicant. Many Grand Masters before me
have had the same problem. As have other Grand Masters, I have struggled with
how to preserve the unanimity and secrecy of the ballot box while finding an
effective way to prevent one brother from using the ballot box to keep a deserving
man out of the craft for unmasonic reasons.
I think that I have found a solution. To protect the sanctity of the ballot
box but assure that one brother cannot abuse his right to consent to the admission
of a man to his lodge, I recommend that we adopt the procedure used by the Grand
Lodge of Wisconsin in these instances. If you adopt this recommendation, we
would use the following procedure when only one black cube appears in the ballot
box, both on the first ballot and on the second ballot taken to correct a possible
mistake.
On the second ballot with only one black cube appearing, the Master
would announce that the member who has cast the negative vote may within
48 hours identify himself privately to the Master, either orally or in writing, as
having cast the negative vote and state the cause for the objection. The objecting
member would have no obligation to come forward. However, if he does not
come forward and state the cause for his objection, the Master at the next Stated
Meeting of the Lodge would declare that the applicant has been elected despite
the presence of the one black cube in the ballot box at the prior Stated Meeting.
If the objecting member does come forward and state the cause for the objection,
the Master would refer the matter to the Grand Master in writing. The Grand
Master would determine the legality of the objection and respond to the Master
in writing of his decision. At the Stated Meeting of the Lodge next following the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

145

receipt of the Grand Master’s decision, the Master would announce the decision.
If the Grand Master determines that the objection was not legal, the Master would
declare that the applicant has been elected. If the Grand Master determines that
the objection was legal, the Master would declare that the applicant has been
rejected. Neither the identity of the member casting the negative vote nor the
cause of the objection would be disclosed to anyone other than to the Master or
by him to the Grand Master.
A similar procedure would be used for an objection before balloting and
for an objection after balloting but before the complete conferral of the Entered
Apprentice Degree. This recommended procedure would apply only if there
is one objection. As before, if there are two or more objections, the applicant
is rejected or the already elected applicant is not made an Entered Apprentice
Mason. This recommendation does not change the procedure followed when an
objection is made after initiation or when an objection is made by someone other
than by a member of the Lodge. Sufficient safeguards are already in place to
protect against abuse in these circumstances.
My Brothers. I know that a number of you have had to live through
the nightmare of this kind of unmasonic behavior and the frustration that it has
brought. You’ve expressed to me your utter sense of helplessness as you’ve
watched your lodge become paralyzed and your members outraged. Some of you
have resorted to holding applications for months while you hope the perpetrator
(whoever he is) fails to show, but all the time not positive who he may be. Using
the ballot box as an instrument to punish the lodge or a faction within it or to
seek revenge against the Master is one of the most flagrant violations of one’s
Masonic obligations.
I urge you to put an end to this kind of abuse that hurts not only the
innocent and deserving applicant, but also disrupts our lodges and tarnishes the
overall reputation of our fraternity. Our code fails us as written in this regard and
allows the cowardly acts of some to hide behind its flawed structure. I, therefore,
urge your adoption of this Grand Master’s recommendation.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made
to the California Masonic Code. Section 804.440 of the Code would be amended
to read as marked:
§804.440. BALLOTING PROCEDURE.
A.

The Master shall read the name of the applicant with the essential
information about him, as supplied by the application and/or as furnished
by the Investigating Committee, after which a ballot shall be taken in the
usual manner;

B.

A Lodge shall have but one ballot for the three degrees;

Proceedings of the

C.

There shall be no discussion in the Lodge during a ballot or between
ballots;

D.

Every member of a Lodge, when present, must vote upon a ballot using
a ball or a cube;

The Master should not permit anyone to enter or retire from the Lodge
room during a ballot except for sickness or other imperative reason. For
this purpose, the “Lodge room” does not include the Tiler’s room or the
preparation room. Members and visitors may enter or retire between
ballots if in the Master’s judgment such will not interfere with the taking
of the subsequent ballot;

F.

When balloting upon two or more applicants, the Master may at his
discretion determine whether a separate ballot shall be taken on each
applicant or whether the entire group shall be balloted upon collectively.
When a collective ballot is used, the Master shall read the names of all
of the applicants included in the collective ballot, with the essential
information about each, as supplied by the application and/or furnished
by the Investigating Committee. A ballot shall then be taken in the usual
manner on the applicants collectively. If no cube appears, each applicant
shall be declared elected. If one or more cubes appear, the Master may
either direct an individual ballot or divide the names of the applicants
into smaller groups. The Lodge shall then proceed to ballot in the usual
manner on each individual or on each group. The Master shall declare
each applicant in a group elected if no cube appears. This procedure shall
continue until an individual ballot has been taken in the usual manner, if
necessary, and all applicants have been balloted upon;

G.

It shall require a unanimous vote of the members present to elect an
applicant. If all members of the Lodge have voted and no negative vote
appears, the ballot is unanimous regardless of the fact that one or more
members failed to deposit a ball at the time he voted;

H.

When balloting upon a single applicant, if only one cube appears, the
Master, without declaring the result, shall at once order a second and
last ballot for the purpose of correcting a possible mistake. The second
ballot shall not be postponed to another meeting of the Lodge. If in the
second ballot one two or more cubes appear, the Master shall declare
the applicant rejected. If in the second ballot only one cube appears, the
Master shall declare that accountability for casting the negative vote is
required in order for the applicant to be rejected. The Master shall then
state that the member who has cast the negative vote may within 48
hours identify himself privately to the Master, either orally or in writing,
as having cast the negative vote and state the cause for the objection.
The objecting member shall be under no obligation to identify himself
to the Master or to disclose the cause for the objection. However, if the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

147

member does not so identify himself and state the cause for the objection,
the Master shall at the next Stated Meeting of the Lodge declare that the
applicant has been elected. If the member does so identify himself and
state the cause for the objection, the Master shall refer the matter to the
Grand Master in writing. The Grand Master shall determine the legality
of the objection and respond to the Master in writing of his decision. At
the Stated Meeting of the Lodge next following the receipt of the Grand
Master’s decision, the Master shall declare that the applicant has been
elected, if it is the Grand Master’s decision that the objection was not
legal, or rejected, if it is the Grand Master’s decision that the objection
was legal. Neither the identity of the member casting the negative vote
nor the cause of the objection shall be disclosed to anyone other than to
the Master or by him to the Grand Master; and
I.

When balloting upon a single applicant, if two or more cubes appear,
the Master shall declare the applicant rejected, and there shall be no
second ballot.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Adamson proposed this recommendation last year to help
combat misuse of the ballot box. If adopted this recommendation would require
the Master to announce to the Lodge that the member who cast the negative ballot
must within forty-eight hours identify himself to the Master and state his reason
for the rejection. It should be noted that this is in the event of a single negative
vote. If no one comes forward as the objecting member, the applicant will be
declared elected. If the objecting member identifies himself and states his reasons
for rejecting the applicant, the Master will convey the objection to the Grand
Master who will decide the legitimacy of the objection.
While it is true tha this recommendation would change the standard of
no explanation required to object to an applicant, it would also give applicants an
added level of protection against ballot box misuse. Oftentimes personal disputes
between members turn into a “tit for tat” war at the ballot box and an unsuspecting
applicant can find himself rejected for no Masonic reason.
This problem has been a prevalent issue throughout the last century in
California Lodges. In fact, in the early 1900’s a similar resolution was proposed
to combat this very issue.
This recommendation is not consistent with the policy of this Grand
Lodge, but is consistent with its general purpose, namely to ensure fairness in the
balloting procedure.

Grand Master Adamson’s Recommendation No. 6
Modification of Fund Raising Rules

Our California Masonic Code is the law of Masonry in this state, and it
regulates not just California Masons but also any organization in California which
requires a Masonic affiliation or relationship as a prerequisite for membership,
such as the Shrine, the Scottish and York Rites and Eastern Star. However, few
other Grand Lodges regulate these Masonic Organizations to the extent that we
do. Our restrictions on fund-raising activities by Masonic Organizations is one
such area.
Beginning in 1991 and made part of the Code in 1993, we expanded
the list of activities by which Masonic Organizations could raise money for their
fraternal and charitable activities. These expanded rules are now found in Section
1200.035.B of the Code. However, these rules have not kept pace with changes in
our society. Today, university alumni groups, non-Masonic fraternal groups and
other affinity organizations offer their members third party credit card, insurance
policy, travel and other such opportunities and receive financial support from
the third-party businesses for which these solicitations are issued. For those of
you who belong to the Scottish Rite in the Southern Jurisdiction or the Shrine,
you have received such solicitations in the Scottish Rite Journal and in Shriners
International Feztivities which is distributed by e-mail. These solicitations violate
our current law. Our current law makes it difficult for Masonic Organizations
to have these fund-raising programs in their national publications because strict
compliance with our California Masonic Code would require them to publish a
separate magazine or other publication just for California Masons without the
prohibited fund-raising.
I think that this result is onerous, and I do not believe that these
solicitations are contrary to the spirit of our law, even though in violation of
the current letter of our law. According, I used my power as Grand Master to
waive compliance with our normal fund-raising rules for these solicitations by
the Scottish Rite of the Southern Jurisdiction under the following circumstances:
1.

These solicitations may be made only to the Masonic
Organization’s members and families;

2.

These solicitations must be within the bounds of propriety and
the prices charged must be fair; and

3.

The entire activity must be conducted strictly in accordance
with all applicable federal, state and local laws.

I believe that these solicitations are appropriate for Masonic Organizations
with these limitations. I therefore ask that you make this program permanent
and expand it to all Masonic Organizations by including this waiver with the
limitations just described in the California Masonic Code.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

151

If you adopt this recommendation, Section 1200.035 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1200.035. ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL SUPPORT.
A Masonic Organization may solicit and receive financial support for its fraternal
operations and charitable activities from the following additional sources:
A.

A Masonic Organization may hold periodic activities to which tickets
are sold to its members and their families and friends. No tickets to such
an activity may be sold to the general public nor may there be any other
public solicitation of support for such an activity. The sponsor shall
disclose that any profits from the activity will be used for the sponsor’s
fraternal and not charitable purposes, if such is the case. In the event
that such disclosure is not given, through inadvertence or otherwise,
all proceeds from the activity shall be given to a recognized Masonic
charity;

B.

A Masonic Organization may solicit and receive financial support for its
fraternal operations and charitable activities from its members and their
families and friends, as well as from the general public, if the sponsor
observes the following guidelines:
1.

The square and compass, the words “Mason”, “Masonic”,
“Masonry,” “Freemasonry”, “Freemason” and any variation of
any such words may not be used in connection with the activity
or any publicity associated with it;

2.

The activity may not be unethical, fraudulent, misleading or
illegal under applicable state and federal laws;

3.

The sponsor shall disclose that any profits from the activity will
be used for the sponsor’s fraternal and not charitable purposes,
if such is the case. In the event that such disclosure is not
given, through inadvertence or otherwise, all proceeds from the
activity shall be given to a recognized Masonic charity;

4.

Solicitation of support shall not occur on the premises of any
Constituent Lodge.

		

Permitted fund-raising activities shall include the solicitation of
advertising from any individual or business;

C.

A Masonic Organization may participate in local community fairs,
celebrations and similar community events by sponsoring, occupying
and operating booths for selling food or non-alcoholic beverages to
persons attending or participating in such events; and

152

Proceedings of the

D.

A Masonic Organization may solicit its members and their families
to participate in third party credit card, insurance policy and other
commercial activities and receive financial support from the businesses
for which these solicitations are issued. This financial support may
be used for the fraternal operations and/or charitable activities of the
soliciting Masonic Organization. Among others, these solicitations may
be in the form of direct mailings sent to the Masonic Organization’s
members and families and in the form of advertisements in the Masonic
Organization’s print or electronic publications which are distributed
primarily to its members and their families. These solicitations must
be within the bounds of propriety and the prices charged must be fair.
The entire activity must be conducted strictly in accordance with all
applicable federal, state and local laws; and

ED.

A Masonic Organization may participate in any other activity which has
been approved by the Grand Master.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Last year, Grand Master Larry Adamson proposed amending Section
1200.035 of the California Masonic Code to expand the range of fundraising
activities permitted by a Masonic Organization to include participation in third
party credit card, insurance policy and similar commercial solicitations. Direct
mailings to members of the Masonic organizations and their families would
be permitted, as would advertisements in the Masonic organization’s print and
electronic publications. Currently these types of solicitations are not allowed;
however, in practice, they have been tacitly accepted and therefore are allowed.
It has been the policy of this Grand Lodge that fundraising by Masonic
organizations be restricted to activities which bring no discredit to Masonry. Most
Worshipful Adamson’s recommendation specifically requires that any third party
solicitations be within the bounds of propriety that the prices charged be fair, and
that they be conducted strictly in accordance with all applicable federal, state and
local laws. These safeguards will ensure that these types of commercial activities
will bring no discredit to Masonry and will provide additional funds for fraternal
operations and charitable activities.
This recommendation is consistent with the policy and general purposes
of this Grand Lodge.
Recommendation ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 09-01
Creates The Hiram’s Pillar Award
The proponents of this Resolution seek to create the designation of Hiram’s Pillar
for the loved one of a Hiram Award recipient.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Hiram Award is given to Brethren who have consistently
and selflessly given invaluable service and time to their Lodges and the Fraternity;
and
WHEREAS, Brethren who receive the Hiram Award in recognition
usually do so with the incredible support of a loved one; and
WHEREAS, that loved one rarely receives the recognition they richly
deserve for their equally selfless support of and sacrifice to the recipient and his
Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 408.020 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§408.020. HIRAM AWARDS.
The Grand Lodge, upon request of a Constituent Lodge under its jurisdiction,
shall furnish a certificate honoring the Master Mason designated by the Lodge as
a recipient of the Hiram Award. The certificate shall be delivered to the Lodge for
presentation to the recipient. The Grand Lodge shall make available for purchase
a medallion and lapel pin for recipients of the Hiram Award.
The Lodge may only designate for the Hiram Award a Master Mason who has
served the Lodge and the Masonic Fraternity with devotion over and above the
ordinary. Service as an officer or as Master of a Lodge shall not be in itself
sufficient qualification for the award nor shall it be a disqualification. The award
should be based on what the recipient has done, not what positions he has held.
The Hiram Award shall be considered the highest honor for service that can be
bestowed upon a member by a Constituent Lodge. The presentation should be
made with appropriate ceremony. When a selection has been made, it should be
announced so the recipient may invite family and friends to the award presentation.
To maintain the prestige and importance of the Hiram Award, a Lodge may
present only one Hiram Award in any one calendar year. Such limitation should
not suggest that this award should be presented every year.
The Grand Lodge, upon request of a Hiram Award recipient, shall furnish a
certificate honoring an individual designated by such recipient as a Hiram’s Pillar.
The certificate shall be delivered to such recipient’s Lodge for presentation to

154

Proceedings of the

the individual so designated as a Hiram’s Pillar. The Grand Lodge shall make
available for purchase a pin for those designated as Hiram’s Pillars.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The California Masonic Code, Section 408.020, establishes the Hiram
Award as the highest honor for service that can be bestowed upon a member by
a constituent Lodge. It was first presented in 1979 to honor those Brethren who
have given of their time, talent and treasure to support their Lodges. This carryover resolution seeks to create an auxiliary award known as the “Hiram’s Pillar”
for another individual to be designated by a Hiram Award recipient.
This resoluction does not specify who that recipient might be. It could
be a spouse, friend, child or anyone chosen by the Hiram Award recipient. It
also leaves that designation solely to the good judgment and discretion of the
Hiram Award recipient. The Lodge would have no role in the selection, which
creates the possibility that the Hiram’s Pillar might be presented to someone not
considered deserving by the Lodge.
This resolution would also allow the Hiram Award recipient to request
the Hiram’s Pillar award directly from Grand Lodge. Our Grand Lodge policy
on awards is to respond to requests only from constituent Lodges and not from
individual members.
A lodge may currently recognize any deserving individual by any
appropriate means without seeking an award from Grand Lodge to do so.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 09-05
Allows Return of Unused Dues Without Lodge Consent
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow the payment of unused dues,
without Lodge consent, of a deceased Mason or a Mason who has discontinued
his membership.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 809.350 of the California Masonic Code requires
the return of dues in the event of the member’s death, demit, or discontinuance of
his multiple membership; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

155

WHEREAS, Section 809.520 of the California Masonic Code does not
include the return of dues as an exception to the requirement of Lodge consent
before an expenditure may be made; and
WHEREAS, the requirement to obtain the consent of the Lodge causes
a delay of up to a month in returning the dues to the member or his heirs.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.520 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.520. EXPENDITURES.
Lodge funds are trust funds set apart for the payment of the necessary, discretionary
and social expenses of the Lodge and for the special calls for charity.
No Lodge funds shall be expended without the express consent of the Lodge, even
though included in a Lodge budget, except that funds may be expended without
Lodge consent when:
A.

Dispensed by the Charity Committee;

B.

Due Grand Lodge; or

C.

Required to pay the taxes or other charges of local, State or Federal
governmental agencies.; or

D.

Required under Section 809.350 of this Code as a return of dues.

Lodges may approve bills against the Lodge only when the bills are supported by
proper documentation, such as an invoice or receipt. No warrant shall be drawn
unless there are sufficient funds to honor it.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution seeks to add to Section 809.520 to the California Masonic
Code a broader definition of what funds may be disbursed by a lodge without
prior consent of a lodge vote. The proponents point out that Section 809.350
clearly states that a lodge shall return the unused portion of a member’s dues,
when a member in good standing is deceased, has an approved demit or has been
issued a certificate of discontinuance of multiple membership.
As the proponsents point out, Section 809.350 of the code states that the
lodge has a fiduciary responsibility to a member, or his estate, and as such would
be required to make a disbursement, regardless of a lodge vote. This resolution
will allow the lodge Master and Secretary to work in a more timely manner.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of the
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.
