Resolution No. 09-06
Acknowledges Former Masters During the Opening of Research Lodges

The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow the Master of a Research Lodge
to invite former Research Lodge Masters to seats in the East.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Research Lodges open all their meetings on the Third
Degree; and
WHEREAS, Masters of Research Lodges upon completion of their term
of office are not entitled to the benefits or title of a Past Master; and
WHEREAS, it is only fair and proper that their Research Lodge
acknowledge their service as former Masters; and
WHEREAS, regular Blue lodges as well as Research lodges properly
and ritually welcome all Masters and Past Masters to seats in the East; and
WHEREAS, no such recognition is presently made in Research Lodges
recognizing former Masters.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that when opening a
Research Lodge the wording of the invitation to seats in the East shall be changed
from, “All Masters and Past Masters are cordially invited to seats in the East” to
“All Masters, Past Masters and Former Masters, are cordially invited to seats in
the East.” This change shall only apply to the opening of Research Lodges.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow the Master of a Research
Lodge to invite former Research Masters to seats in the East. Research Lodges
perform a valuable function in the discussion and preservation of Masonic
information and conducting programs that are of general service to the Craft.
They are a special classification of constituent Lodges in this Grand Lodge.
This practice is required in our constituent Lodges and it honors former
Masters for their contributions and efforts.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Report of the Committee on Ritual:
Brethren of Grand Lodge, the proponents of this resolution seek to
modify our ritual during the opening of a Research Lodge to say, “All Masters,
Past Masters, and Former Masters, are cordially invited to seats in the East.” This

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

157

change is to apply only to the opening of Research Lodges and not to the opening
of a regulary constituted blue Lodge. We acknowledge that the Masters of
Research Lodges dedicate themselves to the running of that Lodge, but modifying
our existing ritual for this is unnecessary. They can be invited to the East by the
Master as soon as the ritual opening ends. The Ritual Committee does not support
this resolution
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 1200.050 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§1200.050. GAMBLING.
Neither a Masonic Organization nor any of its members shall, directly or indirectly,
give or attempt to give the aid or countenance of Masonry to, or participate in, the
conduct or preparation of any raffle, lottery or other form of gambling, conducted
in the name of, or directly or indirectly for the monetary benefit of, any Lodge or
of any Masonic Organization. A Masonic Organization shall not accept any of the
proceeds or profits of any raffle, lottery or other gambling enterprise. Prizes may
be awarded if not purchased from monies collected as admission fees and if no
separate charge is made for the chance to win.
The foregoing notwithstanding, Masonic Organizations and their members may
conduct raffles, lotteries and bingo games for the benefit of their charities and for
the financial support of their fraternal operations, if:
A.

cConducted strictly in accordance with all applicable federal, state and
local laws:

B.

and Conducted strictly in accordance with the provisions hereunder
related to financial support;

C.

Conducted within the bounds of propriety; and

D.

Fair prices are charged.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 1200.055 of the California
Masonic Code which now reads as follows be repealed:
§1200.055. BINGO.
A Masonic Organization may sponsor a bingo game, if the sponsor observes the
following rules:
A.

Attendance at the event is limited to the sponsor’s members, their
families and friends;

B.

There are no signs or other advertising visible to the general public
referring to the game;

C.

No donation, admission fee, meal purchase or other charge is accepted or
required for the opportunity to participate; and

D.

Prizes of minimal value may be awarded if purchased by the sponsor
or donated.

160

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
From at least 1936 until 1995, the policy of Grand Lodge was to prohibit
gambling in any form, without exception. This prohibition applied to both Craft
Lodges and Concordant and Appendant bodies. In 1996, the law was changed to
permit bingo for purely social purposes; any prizes that were awarded had to have
been donated by the sponsor and be of minimal value. The next modification
occurred in 2006, when Concordant and Appendant Masonic Organizations were
permitted to conduct raffles for the benefit of their charities and Masonic Youth
Orders became able to conduct raffles for their charities and certain specified
needs, provided such activities did not conflict with Federal, State, and Local
laws. No other type of gambling other than raffles has ever been permitted and
even these proceeds could not be used for operating expenses.
Resolution 2009-09 allows any Masonic Organization to conduct raffles,
lotteries, and bingo with the proceeds being used for operating expenses as well as
charities. It would permit such events to be offered to the general public.
The proponents make the argument that Masonic Youth Orders are
already permitted to conduct raffles to support some specified needs. However,
our Youth Orders have always been viewed as having fewer fund-raising options
and as being structurally different from other Masonic organizations.
As Section 1200.050 would be rewritten, there is virtually no guidance
for Masonic Organizations regarding fund raising. Even gambling would be
allowed as a source of fraternal income.
While the committee is not in a position to offer an opinion on the tax
and other legal consequences of this proposal, the risks of soliciting the public for
financial support for non-charitable fraternal activities should also be carefully
considered.
This resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

2010 Resolutions
Resolution No. 10-01
Allows Masonic Hall Associations to Subsidize Masonic Groups
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow Masonic Hall Associations to
subsidize the rents charged to any Masonic Lodge or Masonic Organization.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, many incorporated Masonic Hall Associations do not
derive any income from commercial rental space and must rely solely on renting
meeting hall space for income; and
WHEREAS, Masonic Lodges and concordant bodies have experienced
a decline in membership; and
WHEREAS, a decline in membership has caused a decrease in income
from dues and aging members finding it difficult to engage in fund raising events;
and
WHEREAS, they do not have funds to pay “Market Rental Rates” or
“Operating Cost Rates” and raising dues is not a viable option.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 900.020 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§900.020. OPERATIONS.
All Masonic Hall Associations shall operate as follows:
A.

A Masonic Hall Association shall operate in strict compliance with its
Articles of incorporation, its Bylaws and this Code;

B.

A Masonic Hall Association may not hold or administer funds for any
purpose not specifically set forth in this Code;

C.

Masonic Hall Association funds, not Lodge funds, must be used to
compensate Association employees;

D.

No Masonic Hall Association shall use any of its funds and property to
subsidize, directly or indirectly, any organization using or occupying its
property, except as follows Masonic Youth Orders:
1.

A Masonic Hall Association may set rental rates for any
Masonic Lodge and any Masonic Organization using its facility
based on the tenant’s ability to pay; and

162

Proceedings of the
2.

E.

A Masonic Hall Association may permit any of the Masonic
Youth Orders to use its facility without rental charge or for a
reduced rental charge; and

A Masonic Hall Association may permit use of its facility without rental
charge for community or public activities consistent with the provisions
of this Code, provided the user defrays any separate expense resulting
from such use.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution No. 2010-01 would eliminate the existing
prohibition on use of any of the funds and property of a Masonic Temple Association
to subsidize any Masonic organization using or occupying its property, except
Masonic Youth Orders, and replace such prohibition with a provision allowing
one Masonic organization to subsidize another. Further Resolution No. 2010-01,
if adopted, would permit Masonic Hall Associations to set rental rates for Masonic
Lodges and Concordant Masonic Bodies based on their ability to pay, and further
would authorize Masonic Bodies sponsoring Masonic Youth organizations or any
other Masonic Body, including Masonic Hall Associations, to subsidize the rent
of such Masonic Youth Orders.
The effect of this Resolution would be to allow Masonic Hall Associations
to charge rental rates to Masonic tenants based on their ability to pay rather than
rates based upon the cost of maintaining and operating the Masonic Hall. Thus
Masonic tenants with the ability to pay would be asked to subsidize those Masonic
tenants who do not have the ability to pay.
It has been the policy of this Grand Lodge to encourage Hall Associations
to equitably spread the cost of operating the Masonic Hall among its Masonic
tenants with the exception of Masonic Youth organizations, and the effect of this
Resolution would be to violate this principle.
Resolution 2010-01 is not consistent with the policy and general purposes
of this Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Masonic Properties:
Your Masonic Properties Committee, to which Resolution 10-01 has
been referred, offers the following for your consideration.
Section 900.020 entitled “Operations” addresses the manner in which
Hall Associations must govern themselves in order to achieve legal compliance
and follow sound fiscal management practices. This section of our law has been

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

163

wisely crafted and intentionally restricted so as to insure prudent and uniform
practices amongst our Hall Associations.
The proponents of Resolution No. 10-01 seek to amend this section of
our code to substantially broaden the exceptions to subsidize the use of Masonic
owned properties. They seek to allow Hall Associations to charge rental or usage
fees to “any Masonic Organization” based on “their ability to pay.”
They justify this change on the assertion that a number of our Hall
Associations lack commercial rental space and rely solely on the fees from
meeting rentals for income. They cite that declining membership has limited
these other Masonic organizations’ ability to raise funds easily and that they can’t
afford to pay their own operating cost. They go on to assert that “they do not
have funds to pay, not only ‘Market Rental Rates’ but minimal rates that cover the
‘Operating Costs’ and that raising dues is not viable.”
First, it should be pointed out that nowhere in this section of our code
or anywhere within our entire code, is a Hall Association mandated to charge
Masonic organizations “Market Rental Rates.” In fact, Market Rental Rates
does not appear anywhere in our code. What is in our code, is the prohibition
against subsidizing organizations except Masonic Youth Orders or for community
activities. Subsidizing occurs when a Hall Association charges less for the use
of the premises than it actually costs the Hall Association. Renting the space at
a rate which covers the cost for the time the building is in use by the tenant is the
minimum standard set forth in our code.
Setting a rental rate at a level lower than this standard is asking a
Masonic Lodge through the operation of its Hall Association, to bear the cost of
these other organizations. Asking Hall Associations to consider absorbing these
costs could, in the long run, cause Hall Associations to face financial instability or
even insolvency. Determining and dispensing charity is a practice that has always
been, and should always be, reserved for Lodges not Hall Associations.
Your Committee on Masonic Properties concurs with the Policy and
General Purposes Committee and would add that implementing this resolution is
bad fiscal policy.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 10-02
Establishes Effective Date for Lodge Dues Increases
The proponents of this Resolution seek to establish a uniform effective date for
Lodge dues increases.

164

Proceedings of the

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Lodge dues increases become effective when they are
approved by the Grand Master; and
WHEREAS, a dues increase which becomes effective during a fiscal
year of the Lodge requires the Lodge Secretary to collect a prorata portion of
the dues increase from all dues paying members of the Lodge, resulting in an
excessive administrative burden; and
WHEREAS, this administrative burden would be relieved by establishing
the first day of the following fiscal year as the effective date for dues increases.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.310 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.310. DUES.
A Lodge’s dues shall be established in its Bylaws. The minimum annual dues
shall be $12. The Lodge Secretary shall issue to each member paying his dues
a receipt using, without change, the uniform receipt for dues available from the
Grand Secretary.
Dues shall commence with the first day of the month next following the conferring
of the Master Mason Degree or as provided in Section 804.740 of this Code for
members joining the Lodge by affiliation.
If a Lodge increases its dues, the increase shall become effective upon the start of
fiscal year of the Lodge following the Grand Master’s approval of the increase.
Mmembers who have paid their dues in advance for such fiscal year must pay
the increase.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to establish a uniform effective
date for Lodge dues increases. Currently, a Lodge’s dues increase becomes
effective when the Grand Master approves it. This causes undue confusion with
some Lodges, and thus it is unclear to them whether the change is effective as
of the date the Grand Master gives his approval or if it was approved for the
following fiscal year. It is particularly confusing when dealing with members
raised after the approved date, but before the start of the fiscal year, as to which
rate they should be charged.
Currently there is no clear answer in the code. Ambiguity in the code
could be construed to require that the Secretary of a Lodge send out supplemental
dues notices to collect the pro rata portion of the dues increase, and there is

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

165

evidence to indicate that some Secretaries interpret the code to require this action.
If so, this mailing adds expense to the Lodge, and an undue amount of work
for Secretaries.
To correct this ambiguity, this resolution would make all dues increases
effective as of the start of the fiscal year following the approval by the Grand
Master, thus eliminating any uncertainty in the interpretation of the code.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 10-03
Provides Procedure to Change Lodge Location in Its Charter or Dispensation
The proponents of this Resolution seek to provide a procedure to change a Lodge’s
location in its Charter or Dispensation.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, a Lodge may permanently move its meeting place by
following the procedures set forth in Section 807.050 of the California Masonic
Code; and
WHEREAS, a Lodge may have more than one permanent meeting
place by following the procedures set forth in Section 807.060 of the California
Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS, Section 807.040 of the California Masonic Code requires
the Lodge’s permanent meeting place to be in the city, town or community fixed
by its Charter or Dispensation; and
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code does not include a procedure
by which a Lodge’s Charter or Dispensation may be amended in the event that
the Lodge selects a permanent meeting place which is not in the city, town or
community fixed by its Charter or Dispensation.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that a new Section 802.015
be added to the California Masonic Code as follows:
§802.015. CHANGE OF LODGE LOCATION.
A Lodge may change the designation in its charter of the city, town or community
where the Lodge is located by satisfying the following procedure:

166

Proceedings of the

A.

Giving notification at a Stated Meeting that a written resolution to change
the city, town or community where the Lodge is located will be offered at
a succeeding Stated Meeting;

B.

Giving written notice to each Lodge member setting forth the text of the
proposed location change resolution and the date of the Stated Meeting
at which the vote is to be taken;

C.

Adopting such resolution by the vote of at least two-thirds of the members
present at such succeeding Stated Meeting;

D.

The adoption of a Lodge resolution under either Section 807.050 or
807.060 of this Code; and

E.

Obtaining the approval of the Grand Master.

A charter change under this section shall be processed by the Lodge simultaneously
with a change of meeting place under Section 807.050 of this Code or with the
designation of multiple meeting places under Section 807.060 of this Code. The
adoption of a Lodge resolution under either Section 807.050 or Section 807.060
of this Code shall be conditioned on the adoption of a conforming resolution
under this Section 802.015, if required, and vice versa.
The Secretary of the Lodge shall note in the minutes of the Lodge the notice of the
proposed location change resolution when made. When transmitting a location
change resolution for approval by the Grand Master, the Lodge Secretary shall
forward a certificate, under seal, showing that the law has been complied with and
that the location change resolution has received the required vote.
Once the Grand Master has approved the location change, the Lodge shall receive
a new Charter without charge or may have an endorsement of the authorization of
the new location made upon its existing Charter.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 807.050 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.050. CHANGE OF MEETING PLACE.
A Lodge may permanently move its meeting place from the previously selected
place only after:
A.

Obtaining a determination by the Inspector of the district in which the
Lodge is situated that the proposed meeting place is a safe and suitable
room for a tiled Lodge meeting;

B.

Giving notification at a Stated Meeting that a written resolution for such
move will be offered at the next succeeding Stated Meeting;

167

C.

Adopting such resolution by the vote of at least two‑thirds of the members
present at such succeeding Stated Meeting; and

D.

Obtaining the approval of the Grand Master.

In the case of removal to a city, town or community other than that named in
the Lodge’s Charter or Dispensation, the Charter shall be amended using the
procedure set forth in Section 802.015 of this Code by proper proceedings. In the
case of removal to a city, town or community other than that named in the Lodge’s

§807.060. MULTIPLE MEETING PLACES.

C.

Adopting such resolution by the vote of at least two-thirds of the members

D.

Obtaining the approval of the Grand Master.

in the city, town or community fixed by the Lodge’s Charter or Dispensation.
So long as one of the approved Lodge meeting places is in the city, town or
community fixed by the Lodge’s Charter or Dispensation, no change to the
Charter or Dispensation shall be required. In the event that no proposed Lodge
meeting place is in a city, town or community named in the Lodge’s Charter, the
Charter shall be amended using the procedure set forth in Section 802.015 of

168

Proceedings of the

this Code. In the event that no proposed Lodge meeting place is in a city, town
or community named in the Lodge’s Dispensation, the Grand Master shall make
an appropriate endorsement to the Lodge’s Dispensation when he approves the
meeting place change.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to provide a procedure to
change the Lodge’s location in its Charter or Dispensation. At the present time
the California Masonic Code does not provide the mechanism for a Lodge to
amend its Charter or Dispensation to select a permanent meeting place which is
not in the town, City, or community that is fixed in its Charter or Dispensation.
This proposal would provide the necessary procedure by which a Charter or
Dispensation can be amended. This is strictly an administrative matter to simplify
the method by which another meeting place location may be selected. Another
Charter or Dispensation will not be required.
Our Grand Lodge has attempted to make such matters as simple as
possible and this Resolution provides that method.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 10-04
Establishes Mandatory Closing Time for Lodge Meetings
The proponents of this Resolution seek to include in the California Masonic Code
the prohibition on Lodge meetings lasting beyond Midnight.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 807.020 requires only
that a Constituent Lodge must be closed when the business for which it was
opened is completed; and
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 807.020 also prohibits
the adjournment of a Constituent Lodge; and
WHEREAS, these two sections might be considered in conflict and
confusing; and
WHEREAS, a meeting spreading over two days must result in conflicting
dates in the minutes; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

169

WHEREAS, those attending at the beginning of the meeting might
not be the same as those in attendance after the adjournment thus causing an
inaccurate Tiler’s Register; and
WHEREAS, we have long been governed by the traditional rule that a
Lodge must be closed by midnight.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.020 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO MEETINGS.
No Stated or Special Meetings of a Lodge shall be held on Sunday except for the
annual Installation of Officers or funeral services. If the Stated Meeting of a lunar
Lodge falls on a Sunday, the Stated Meeting shall be held on the following day.
All business, except the examination of candidates in the Candidate’s Lecture of
the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, the conferring of the Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, and the consideration of relief of a worthy
Mason, shall be done in a Lodge of Master Masons.
A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done or business transacted,
except by, or in the presence of, and under the continual direction of the Master,
the ranking Warden, the Grand Master or the Grand Master’s designated
representative.
No meeting shall be conducted by a Lodge unless the Charter of the Lodge is
present. A photocopy of the Charter may be made under the direction of the
Grand Secretary at the request and expense of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary
shall attach thereto a certificate with the seal of Grand Lodge affixed that the copy
is a true copy of the Lodge’s Charter. The copy may be used by the Lodge instead
of the original Charter at any time.
The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all meetings of a Lodge. At the
annual election of officers, and at such other meetings as may be deemed desirable
by the Master, the Flag shall be formally presented at the Altar and received in
the manner prescribed in the Ritual. The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated
with any flag.
No Lodge shall transact any business with fewer than five members of the Lodge
present except the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while he is at his
post in the Tiler’s room.
Smoking is forbidden in the Lodge room at all times when the Lodge is in session.
There shall be no adjourned meeting. Each meeting of a Lodge must be closed
when the business proposed for transaction has been concluded, but in no event
later than the close of the day on which it was opened.

170

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Currently the California Masonic Code Section 807.020 requires that
a Lodge must be closed when the business proposed for transaction has been
concluded. It also does not permit a Lodge to adjourn. This resolution would add
the requirement that a Lodge must be closed in no event later than low twelve or
twelve o’clock midnight of the date it was opened.
Adjournment is defined as “a suspension of proceedings to another time
or place”. Legislative bodies are usually opened at the start of a session, adjourned
from time to time, and then closed months or years later by adjourning sine die
until the next session is opened.
Unlike a legislative body, a Lodge meeting must be closed when it has
concluded the specific business for which it was opened. It may be temporarily
called from labor to refreshment, but ultimately must be closed in the same place
that it was opened. A Lodge may not remain perpetually open.
At present, nothing in the California Masonic Code prohibits a Lodge
from opening on one day, calling from labor to refreshment, and then resuming
business on a later date. Such an action is effectively an adjournment under a
different name. This resolution would codify the long-standing practice that any
suspension of business is temporary and for a duration measured at most in a few
hours, not days or weeks.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Report of the Committee on Ritual:
The proponents of this resolution seek to include in the California
Masonic Code the prohibition of Lodge meetings lasting beyond midnight.
While nothing could be found in previous editions of the CMC, an
informal survey indicated that many in the Fraternity believe that this provision
already exists. It is reasonable for a Brother attending a meeting to expect that he
will be able to participate in all business or Degree activity. It is also reasonable
for a Brother to know that there is a time, beyond which, no further business may
be conducted. This resolution provides that certainty.
This resolution is administrative and does not affect Ritual.
Committee on Ritual recommends its adoption.
Resolution CARRIED-OVER.

Authorizes Foreign Language Degree Teams
The proponents of this Resolution seek to authorize the use of foreign language

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, there are various degree teams conferring degrees under
the charter of an inviting lodge; and
WHEREAS, there is an authorized Grand Lodge Ritual in French,
German, Italian, Spanish and Armenian; and
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge has granted Lodges in its jurisdiction the
right to confer degrees in foreign languages (CMC Section 402.070); and
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge has granted Lodges from other jurisdictions
the ability to confer degrees by an inviting Lodge of this Jurisdiction (CMC
Section 804.680); and
WHEREAS, the Spanish speaking population of the state of California
is predicted to soon equal the English speaking population; and
WHEREAS, many good men within the Spanish speaking population
are desirous to become Freemasons.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that a new Section 402.075
be added to the California Masonic Code to read as follows:
§402.075. FOREIGN LANGUAGE DEGREE TEAMS.
Degree teams composed exclusively of Masons whose language skills include a
language other than English may with the approval of the Grand Master and the
Grand Lecturer perform the Ritual in such foreign language and confer a degree
or degrees in the approved foreign language upon those candidates of any Lodge
who speak, read and understand such foreign language.

172

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to add a new section to the
California Masonic Code, section 402.075, which would allow foreign language
degree teams. At present a lodge which has a candidate who speaks a foreign
language may invite a lodge that works in that language to confer one or more
degrees on that candidate. As the lodge may be in a different part of the state,
it is often difficult for this to occur because of distance between the two lodges.
This resolution would permit the creation of a degree team which could confer
the degree in a foreign language upon request from lodges with such candidates.
The degree team would be subject to the same conditions and supervision as other
degree teams in this jurisdiction. Such degree teams would make it easier for
a candidate to receive his degree in a foreign language without another lodge
having to travel great distances to confer it. This resolution is simply expanding
the present ability of a lodge to have a degree conferred in the lodge by those
conversant with the language of the candidate.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
The proponents of Resolution 10-05 seek to amend the California
Masonic Code by adding Section 402.075 authorizing foreign language degree
teams. In support of their position, the proponents have cited the following:
1.

There are currently various degree teams conferring degrees
under the charter of an inviting lodge;

2.

There are many approved and authorized foreign language
rituals; French, German, Italian, Spanish and Armenian;

3.

Under Section 402.070 foreign language lodges are authorized
to do the work in their language;

4.

Under Section 804.680 other jurisdictions may confer a degree
in the inviting lodge from this jurisdiction;

5.

The Spanish population is growing in California; and

6.

Many good men within the Spanish speaking population are
desirous to become Freemasons.

Your Ritual Committee is fully aware that there are many degree teams
conferring degrees within the jurisdiction at this time. However, the responsible
Inspector in each district has the duty to see that the ritual of a degree team is
consistent with this Grand Lodge ritual. If the Inspector is not fluent in the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

173

language of the team conferring the degree, he cannot exercise his duty as the
representative of the Grand Master and insure that the ritual presented conforms
to the approved Grand Lodge ritual.
The lodges that are authorized by the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer
to confer degrees and work in their foreign language have Inspectors that are
multilingual and capable of determining the competency of the brethren engaged
in the work and the conformity to the approved ritual of the Grand Lodge.
It has never been the intent of the Grand Master or the Grand Lecturer
of this jurisdiction to judge the competency, conformity or presentation of other
jurisdiction ritual while they are guests of this jurisdiction. Therefore, the intent
of Section 804.680 is to promote a spirit of fraternalism, brotherly love, and good
will among Masons.
Your Ritual Committee further acknowledges the growth of the
California population among many ethnic groups, not just Spanish speaking
residents. This was also acknowledged by our Grand Lodge, when Resolution 0603, Lodge Formation, was adopted and Section 801.015 amended to require only
15 Master Masons to begin the process of Lodge Formation. It was hoped and
is still the intent, of the Grand Lodge to reach out into these ethnic communities
to form Lodges that operate within their native tongue. To isolate a candidate in
a Lodge that works in a language foreign to him, by sojourning degree teams, is
inconsistent to the goals of this Grand Lodge.
Sometimes Resolutions are presented by well intended proponents that
do not take into consideration other sections of the California Masonic Code.
Your Ritual Committee believes that this is the case in Resolution 10-05.
Section 804.620 Advancement

Presumably, the candidate utilizes English as a second language and no

proficiency.
Section 804.860 Additional Rights of and Prohibitions on Entered

Proceedings of the

§809.130. LODGE INVESTMENTS.
Exclusive of a Lodge investment in an incorporated Masonic Hall Association or

equivalents, checking accounts, savings accounts and certificates of deposit) shall

B.

Resolution No. 10-08
Allows Early Presentation of the Diamond Jubilee Award
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow presentation of the Diamond
Jubilee Award at any time commencing twelve months preceding the anniversary
date.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, as our members age and their health diminishes, the Grand
Master or his designee are limited in their time of presentation, by presentation
only in the calendar year preceding the anniversary date; and
WHEREAS, the member whose anniversary date falls in January, the
presentation can only be made from the first of January, while the member whose
anniversary date is in December, the presentation can be made from the first of
January through December of that calendar year; and
WHEREAS, both members should be able to receive the Diamond
Jubilee Award under the same guidelines; and
WHEREAS, in the past, Grand Masters have often wrestled with the
problem to hold fast to the “Masonic rule of Law” by holding their breath in hopes
the Brother would remain healthy enough to receive this honor; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

179

WHEREAS, it is important to know exactly what makes one eligible
for just such an award. California Masonic Code Section 408.010, as well as
the Diamond Jubilee Award Ceremony, identified the key eligibility words as
“member”, “in good standing”, and the required number of “years”; and
WHEREAS, during the 2007 Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge, the members approved the early presentation of the Golden Veteran Award
with a definite time frame for early presentation; and
WHEREAS, if passed, each recipient will have the same opportunity to
receive their award as all other recipients.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 408.010 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§408.010. GOLDEN VETERAN AND DIAMOND JUBILEE AWARDS.
The Grand Lodge, upon request, shall provide a Golden Veteran’s Award to
members of this Jurisdiction who have been Master Masons in good standing for a
total of 50 years or more, presentation being made by the Grand Master, Inspector
or their representative with appropriate ceremony. The presentation of the Golden
Veteran Award may be made at any time commencing with the date six months
prior to the date on which the member shall otherwise become eligible.
The Grand Lodge, upon request, shall provide a Diamond Jubilee Award to
members of this Jurisdiction who have been Master Masons in good standing for
a total of 75 years or more, presentation being made by the Grand Master or his
designee with appropriate ceremony. The presentation of the Diamond Jubilee
Award may be made at any time commencing with the first day of the calendar
year in date twelve months prior to the date on which the member shall otherwise
become eligible.
In the case of a deceased Mason, if he was eligible for but had not received the
Award prior to his death, or in the case of an incompetent Mason, presentation on
request may be made to the family or heirs.
In computing the length of time requisite for issuance of either award, a period of
up to one year, during which the member held a Demit from any Lodge recognized
by this Grand Lodge, may be included; provided, however, periods during which
the member held a Demit for more than one year from the date of the Demit, or
was suspended for non‑payment of dues, must be added to the time when the
member would otherwise have been eligible to receive the award. The period
between the issuance of a Demit for the purpose of becoming a charter member
of a new Lodge and the institution of the new Lodge is not an interruption of the
required number of years of continuous membership.

Resolution No. 10-10
Eliminates the Short Form Oral Proficiency for
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts
The proponents of this Resolution seek to eliminate the option for Entered

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, a Lodge may advance an Entered Apprentice or Fellow
Craft to a higher degree whose oral proficiency consisted solely of reciting from
memory the obligation of his last degree, together with the signs and modes of
recognition of that degree;
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge has provided written material to assist
the candidate in becoming well qualified; and
WHEREAS, many valuable lessons given to the candidate during the
ceremonies of the degrees are not required to be recited during the proficiency to
show the candidate is well qualified; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

181

WHEREAS, the recitation requirements were reduced because some
candidates stated they did not have the time to learn the “long form” proficiency;
and
WHEREAS, in generations past, candidates who had jobs, families, and
other obligations were willing and able to recite the long form proficiency.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.620 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.620. ADVANCEMENT.
A Lodge may advance an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to a higher degree only
if:
A.

He has given satisfactory evidence, by examination in a tiled Lodge, that he
is proficient and well qualified in the degrees which he has already taken.
To demonstrate such proficiency, an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft
shall only be required to recite from memory the obligation of each degree,
together with the signs and modes of recognition of each degree. Any
number of applicants may be examined at a meeting, but not more than
five shall be examined at any one time with the questions being asked in
rotation. Such examination shall be held in front of the East between the
altar and the Master’s station.

B.

He has completed the Basic Masonic Education Course in the degrees
which he has already taken. He shall demonstrate such completion by
answering in writing and in open book fashion the questions appertaining
to each of the pamphlets of the Basic Masonic Education Course, as such
questions and pamphlets may be promulgated from time to time by the
Grand Master for this purpose. The candidate’s written answers shall be
approved by a committee of three elective officers of the Lodge or three
Past Masters of the Lodge or a combination thereof and shall be retained
as a part of the Lodge records for a period of not less than one year.

If for any reason there is an erroneous conferral of a degree or degrees, the candidate
retains the status reached but must wait one year, present an application for a higher
degree or degrees and comply with the provisions of this section.

182

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In this resolution, the proponents seek to require all Entered Apprentice
and Fellowcraft Masons to learn what has come to be known as the “long form”
proficiencies for those degrees.
The length of proficiencies has been a topic of proposed legislation since
at least 1991, when carryover Resolution 1990-16, proposing to limit proficiencies
to the obligations, signs, and modes of recognition failed after being carried over.
At that same communication, Resolution 1991-01, which sought to reduce the
number of questions in the proficiency, also failed. Several other similar proposals
also failed in the subsequent years, including a recommendation by Grand Master
R. Stephen Doan that pointed out that the true historical proficiencies were
much simpler. However, Resolution 1996-05, that also proposed limiting the
proficiencies for the Entered Apprentice and Fellowcraft degrees to the obligation,
signs, and modes of recognition, was carried over in 1996 and passed in 1997. At
that time, the major argument for most of these proposals was that many men
did not have time to learn the longer proficiencies and, as a result, were failing
to progress. In 1998 Grand Master Wordlow’s Decision 2 made the long form
optional and, in 1999, Grand Master Nahin’s Recommendation 5 added written
questions to the proficiency requirement.
It was the intent of all of the proposals to shorten the length of the
proficiencies in order to reduce the percentage of men who failed to progress.
The Grand Secretary provided this committee with the rates of non-completion
for the past 70 years; the rate in the decades of the 1940s, 1950’s, and 1960s were
5-7%. The rates increased in the 1970’s and 1980’s to 14% and 21% respectively.
It remained high, 23%, in the 1990’s, even though the proficiency length change
was in effect for the last three years of that decade. The rate in the first decade of
the 21st century rose to 31%.
Resolution 2010-10 will remove the option that the Entered Apprentice
or Fellow Craft has with regard to only memorizing the short-form, or more
abbreviated, material. However, should it pass, the proficiency requirement
would then be longer than it was in the past, since the candidates would still be
required to answer the written questions.
Since the “long-form” option is currently available, and since Masonic
Education is a value that we have, the resolution is consistent with the policy and
general purposes of this Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
In October of 1997 Carry-over Resolution 96-05 was adopted limiting
Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Proficiencies to the Obligations, Signs and
Modes of Recognition. The proponents believed that the full form proficiency

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

183

was too stringent and a shortened proficiency would benefit the candidates
by making it easier for them to advance through the degrees and become
Master Masons.
Resolution 96-05 has been in effect for approximately 13 years. Since
that time the promise of advancing stalled Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts
to Master Mason has fallen far short of these proponent’s expectations. One need
only go to our website, pick any lodge at random, and see the large numbers of
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts who have not advanced since the change in
our proficiency requirements. This sad revelation must indicate that other factors
must be in play which results in the non-advancement of our candidates. Some
may argue that uncaring or uninspired lodge leadership may have a role in new
candidates losing interest in progressing. Others may state that the candidate was
not given an honest and accurate explanation of the requirements for membership
and may have felt deceived. And, most important of all, the candidate himself may
have decided that, after experiencing the First or Second Degrees, our Fraternity
was not what he was seeking.
Contrary to what might be popular thinking, not every man who knocks
at Freemasonry’s door is a Mason in the making. Our fraternity is a special place
that should attract exceptional men who value and cherish our Masonic traditions
and its rituals. Our ceremonies and rituals are the cornerstone of our fraternity.
They are the essence of whom and what we are. We as Masons are justifiably
proud and zealously guard our ritual, and take great pride in the excellence of
its delivery. We maintain its purity and high standards of excellence by having
established a Grand Lecturer and a Committee on Ritual to oversee and protect
our ritual.
We must be ever mindful that when a man comes to us and asks that all
important question of, “How do I become a Mason,” we must understand that he is
asking for all the rights and privileges that come with his request. We must never
forget that when submitting his petition, the candidate clearly understands our
expectations and obligates himself to certain requirements that have been designed
to bring him into the light of Masonry. Many of the young men petitioning our
lodges today are expecting the full initiatic process. This includes excellence in
ritual conferral, meaningful mentoring and coaching as well as a comprehensive
Masonic Educational process. These men must be taught to trly understand
that becoming a Mason is a process that should not be rushed, but savored and
enjoyed. We must never forget that we are in the business of making Masons, not
just adding to our membership foles. The Full Form Proficiency for our Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts is an important part of our Masonic heritage and an
integral part of our educational process. Our full form proficiencies are necessary
tools in transforming a worthy candidate into a dedicated Master Mason.
The Committee on Ritual supports this resolution.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 10-11
Restores James R. Paden to Masonic Membership

The proponents of this Resolution seek to restore James R. Paden to membership
in Masonry.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code
provides that a Mason who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been
convicted of a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court shall be deemed
automatically expelled from membership in a Lodge in this Jurisdiction without
any further action of his Lodge or Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, James Paden was automatically expelled from membership
in this Jurisdiction because of the crime of driving under the influence (DUI); and
WHEREAS, James Paden may be restored to membership in Masonry
only by a resolution presented and adopted using the same procedure as an
amendment to the Ordinances of Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, a single DUI conviction, even with a penalty enhancement,
is not considered a case involving moral turpitude.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that, any provision of the
California Masonic Code to the contrary notwithstanding, James R. Paden be
restored to the rights and benefits of Masonry as of the date of his expulsion as an
unaffiliated Mason, with no lapse in membership, and that he no longer be subject
to expulsion from Masonry under the California Masonic Code because of the
death of his wife and injury to his daughter while he was driving an automobile
under the influence of an alcoholic beverage on or about October 22, 2000.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution No. 2010-11 seek to restore James R.
Paden to membership in to our Fraternity. Mr. Paden was expelled pursuant to the
automatic expulsion provision of the California Masonic Code Section 1404.820
Conviction of a Crime of Moral Turpitude. Mr. Paden had pled Nolo Contendere
to Vehicle Code 23153 (a) DUI with bodily injury and to the enhancement of
Vehicle Code 23558 for causing death or serious injury and injuring more than
one person while driving under the influence and was convicted of the offense.
California Masonic Code Section 1404.1050 details the technical steps
required for reinstatement of an expelled member. In order for the Grand Lodge
to properly assess whether an expelled member should be reinstated, it needs
to consider whether the individual has been rehabilitated from his criminal

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

185

offenses and is again worthy of being a member of our honorable Fraternity. The
Resolution, as presented, has not shown how the expelled member is rehabilitated
nor does it present anything in which the Grand Lodge might conclude that his
reinstatement be granted.
Moreover, it has come to our attention that the resolution does not address
the existence of a second episode. This episode was included in the original
notice of expulsion. A failure to resolve this issue may result in a continuation of
the expulsion.
This resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
In 2009, Grand Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3 set forth a detailed
set of criteria to be considered when determining whether an expelled Mason has
demonstrated rehabilitation from his past conduct so that his reinstatement would
not be contrary to our Masonic principles. These criteria include the stability
of his family life, the likelihood that he will repeat the conduct which gave rise
to expulsion, his acceptance of responsibility, remorse and atonement for his
conduct, and a change in attitude.
The proponents of this Resolution have offered no documentary or other
evidence that Mr. Paden has been rehabilitated from his criminal conduct.
According, the Committee on Trial Review recommends that Mr. Paden
not be reinstated.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

§810.050. LODGE ROSTERS.
A Lodge may publish a roster for Masonic purposes and for the benefit of its
members all Masons of that Lodge containing the names, mailing addresses,
and telephone numbers, electronic mail addresses, spouse’s names, birthdays,
anniversary dates, length of membership, Masonic history and status of all Masons
of that Lodge members, including Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Currently the California Masonic Code Section 810.050 permits a
Lodge to publish a roster for Masonic purposes and for the benefit of its members
containing the names, mailing addresses, and telephone numbers of all members,
including Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts. Resolution No. 2010-12 would
expand the list of permitted information to include email addresses, spouses
names, birthday, anniversary, length of membership, membership history, and
status of all members.
It has been the policy of this Grand Lodge to encourage timely and
informative communication between Lodges and their members, especially those
Brethren who may be unable to attend due to age, infirmity, or distance.
The aggregate of information contained in the proposed expanded roster
might pose a risk of enabling identity theft, particularly the coupling of name,
address, spouse’s name, phone number, and birth date. Although many Lodges
recognize birthdays in their Trestleboard this information is usually presented
without also specifying home address and phone number. Also, the publication of
email addresses in an easily-accessible form might result in a a deluge of spam.
Another issue is the publication of membership status. Section 804.840
stipulates the importance of confidentiality in matters regarding suspensions,
expulsions, and restorations. Section 1407.740 states that “Unless otherwise
authorized by Grand Lodge or the Grand Master, no suspension, expulsion or
restoration shall be published beyond the notifications provided in this Chapter”.
This resolution would permit public dissemination of such information.
This resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 10-13
Shortens Residency Period ror Veterans
The proponents of this Resolution seek to shorten the residency period for veterans
who have been recently discharged or separated from service.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, our nation is currently involved in armed conflicts; and
WHEREAS, many of our citizens are being assigned to serve in the
uniformed services of the United States in locations outside this Jurisdiction; and
WHEREAS, among these are men who find reason to seek our Fraternity
during that duty service; and
WHEREAS, these citizens defer exercising that decision until returning
to this, their home Jurisdiction.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.225 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.225. RESIDENCY.
A.

An applicant for the degrees must have been a resident within this
Jurisdiction during 12 months next preceding the date of his application;

B.

A member of any uniformed service of the United States, whose duty
station is at a facility or on a vessel having an officially designated home
port, shall be considered a resident of the Jurisdiction which includes
such facility or home port. If the member of any such uniformed service
has not resided at such facility or been attached to such vessel for at
least six months immediately preceding the date of his application, a
dispensation is required from the Inspector assigned to the Lodge
receiving the application;

C.

A man residing with his spouse who is a member of any uniformed
service of the United States, whose duty station is at a facility or on a
vessel having an officially designated home port, shall be considered a
resident of the Jurisdiction which includes such facility or home port. If
the spouse has not resided at such facility or been attached to such vessel
for at least six months immediately preceding the date of his application,
a dispensation is required from the Inspector assigned to the Lodge
receiving the application; and

D.

An application may be received from a man who has received an
honorable discharge or separation from any uniformed service of the

188

Proceedings of the
United States within the 6 month period next preceding the date of his
application, without regard to the 12 month residency requirement, if
both of the following additional requirements are met:

DE.

1.

He was a resident within this Jurisdiction during the 24 month
period next preceding the date of his most recent induction into
the uniform service of the United States; and

2.

He is a resident within this Jurisdiction on the date of his
application; and

Uniformed Service of the United States includes the U.S. Army,
the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, the U.S. Air Force, the U.S. Coast
Guard, the U.S. Public Health Service and the National Oceanic and
Atmospheric Administration.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents seek to expand the language in section 804.225 by
adding a new line. The new wording is reflected in line “D” and will include an
exception for uniformed servicemen and the other groups so noted in this section.
The proponents point out that, servicemen and the other named groups,
may have a unique problem with proof of residency in this jurisdiction as it applies
to the time requirement. Although a serviceman may have lived in California for
at least a year before his deployment outside California, he must wait another
twelve months upon his return in order for a lodge to receive his application. This
resolution would reduce that time to six months.
To overcome that challenge, the proponents are expanding section
804.225, line “D” to include language that would address these special
circumstances for servicemen seeking to make application in this jurisdiction.
It will add that if a serviceman can show that he has lived in this jurisdiction for
two years prior to leaving California and has lived in California within six months
of having been honorably discharged, the twelve month requirement in line “A”
is exempted.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.

The proponents seek to modify Section 814.000, paragraph L, of the

As such, the following Code sections apply to this Resolution: Section
804.710, states that “for an affiliation there is no requirement for investigation
unless an objection is made by any member of the Lodge to a ballot without an
investigation”. 1996 Grand Master Decision No. 1 in summary states that “If a

Resolution No. 10-15
Restores Roberto N. Valenton to Masonic Membership
The proponents of this Resolution seek to restore Roberto N. Valenton to
membership in Masonry.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code
provides that a Mason who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been
convicted of, a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court shall be deemed
automatically expelled from membership in any Lodge in this Jurisdiction without
any further action of his Lodge or Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, Roberto N. Valenton was automatically expelled from
membership in this Jurisdiction because he pled nolo contendere and was convicted
of one count of insurance fraud in 1993 and pled guilty and was convicted of three
counts of filing false federal tax returns in 1996, all crimes of moral turpitude (the
“Crimes”); and
WHEREAS, Roberto N. Valenton may be restored to membership in
Masonry only by a resolution presented and adopted using the same procedure as
an amendment to the Ordinances of Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, Roberto N. Valenton should now be restored to membership
in Masonry for the following reasons. While his license to practice medicine was
suspended because of his criminal activity, his medical license was restored in
2000 after the completion of his probation. His medical mission as well as his
humanitarian projects have never been interrupted by his criminal convictions.
Dr. Valenton has continuously demonstrated his upright conduct, exemplary
character, as well as good moral reputation in community and the fraternity,

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

193

making him a very worthy member of Artesia Sunrise Lodge No. 377 and to
the Masonic community as a whole. His expulsion from Masonry did not deter
him from assisting the needs of the Lodge and its members. He has always been
available to help and assist any public activities of Artesia Sunrise Lodge No. 377
resulting in very high regard and respect from its members as well as members of
other Lodges in southern California. Dr. Valenton became a Mason on February
15, 2007 in Artesia Sunrise Lodge No. 377 and disclosed his criminal convictions
on his application for membership.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that, any provision of the
California Masonic Code to the contrary notwithstanding, Roberto N. Valenton
be restored to the rights and benefits of Masonry as of the date of his expulsion
as an unaffiliated Mason, with no lapse in membership, and that he no longer be
subject to expulsion from Masonry under the California Masonic Code because
of the Crimes.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code states that any Mason
who has pled guilty or nolo contendere to a crime of moral turpitude shall be
automatically expelled without any other action by his Lodge or Grand Lodge.
Dr. Roberto Valenton pled nolo contendere to one count of insurance fraud
on April 15, 1993 and pled guilty to three counts of filing false tax returns on
December 2, 1996. He subsequently did serve the sentences given to him and
paid all of the required restitutions, fines, and penalties. His medical license was
suspended until he had completed his probation, and it was restored on July 7,
2000. He applied for the degrees in Masonry in 2006 and made a full disclosure
of these prior convictions at that time. After investigation by the Lodge, he was
elected to receive the degrees of Masonry and was raised on April 21, 2007, only
to be subsequently expelled because of the prior convictions. Dr. Valenton’s
former lodge informed this committee that there was a unanimous vote at a stated
meeting to request a restoration and the matter is now before Grand Lodge as
Resolution 2010-15.
Section 804.210 of our code expressly forbids membership in a Masonic
Lodge by a man who has been convicted of, or pled guilty or nolo contendere to, a
crime that is morally wrong. However, since this resolution is being presented as
a “private bill”, it overrides the general law for a specific person. In other words,
the law that the individual would not have otherwise been eligible for membership
is set aside in this particular case for this particular individual.
Section 1404.1050 describes the process for restoring an expelled Mason,
namely a two-thirds affirmative vote by the former brother’s lodge followed by
an application to Grand Lodge. Grand Lodge may then restore the man “if good

194

Proceedings of the

cause is shown”; the vote for restoration is comparable to what is required to
change our ordinances.
The determination as to whether or not good cause exists is ultimately
the job of Grand Lodge. In this case, it is the task of each member of Grand Lodge
to decide if the man in this case is no longer going to cheat on his billing practices
and tax returns. At least five years should have passed since the conclusion of his
sentence. He should have sincerely expressed remorse, and made amends, for his
actions and have an unblemished record with regard to the avoidance of any other
criminal activity. He should demonstrate a personal commitment to Masonic
values, have significant involvement in the community, and accept responsibility
for his actions. Any man who has been convicted of a crime can be viewed as one
who might violate his oath, so he has a substantial obligation to prove to us that
he has learned his lesson and that his word will subsequently be worthy of trust.
This resolution has been submitted in a manner that is consistent with the
policy of Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
In 2009, Grand Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3 set forth a detailed
set of criteria to be considered when determining whether an expelled Mason has
demonstrated rehabilitation from his past conduct so that his reinstatement would
not be contrary to our Masonic principles. These criteria include the stability
of his family life, the likelihood that he will repeat the conduct which gave rise
to expulsion, his acceptance of responsibility, remorse and atonement for his
conduct, and a change in attitude.
Dr. Valenton was convicted of insurance fraud and income tax evasion
arising from a scheme involving personal injury cases. The conduct giving rise
to the convictions occurred almost 20 years ago. The California Medical Board
placed his license on probation, which he successfully completed in 2000 and
he has been in good standing with the Board since that time. The proponents of
this Resolution have provided letters of support, court and other documents, and
interviews that show the following:
Dr. Valenton accepted full responsibility for his misconduct and sent a
letter to the Grand Master in which he expressed shame and remorse therefore.
He changed his manner of practice after his convictions and refused to accept any
personal injury cases. For the past eight years he has been a “house doctor” at a
psychiatric hospital. He has been married for 34 years and has three children; one
is the OB/GYN Chief Resident at Cedars-Sinai Hospital, one is an occupational
therapist with a Masters degree, and one is a junior at the University of Arizona.
He and his wife, an anesthesiologist, have paid and are still paying for their
children’s educations.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

195

For the past ten years, Dr. Valenton has participated in medical missions
lasting up to two weeks, rendering medical aid to indigents in the Philippines.
He is currently in the process of setting up a group to organize medical and
dental missions to serve the Aetas, an indigenous Philippine tribe that has no
medical services.
Based on a review of all of the eveidence provided by the proponents,
the Committee on Trial Review finds that Dr. Valenton has met Grand Master
Adamson’s criteria for rehabilitation, is a suitable candidate for reinstatement, and
this Committee recommends a yes vote on this resolution.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

1957; nor shall it be construed as prohibiting clubs organized for the purpose

Acacia Creek Board of Directors
By Michael D. Neben, President
On behalf of the Board of Directors of Acacia Creek, I am pleased to
present this report on the activities of Acacia Creek in the past year to the Masons
of California.
This has been an eventful year for this new venture. On Sunday, March
14, 2010, Most Worshipful Ken Nagel presided over the dedication ceremony for
Acacia Creek. It was an outstanding event, with approximately 450 in attendance,
at least 120 of whom took the formal tour afterwards. On Friday, June 25, yours
truly presided over the public grand opening, attended by community dignitaries,
including Mayor Mark Green of Union City. In late 2009, the Acacia Creek
Board of Directors, with the concurrence of its sole member, the Masonic Homes
of California, made the important decision to open admissions to Acacia Creek
to non-Masons. Because of the economic downturn and its associated issue, the
softness in the residential real estate market, sales of the units in Acacia Creek
had slowed considerably. The Acacia Creek Board of Directors took the action
based on its fiduciary responsibility to do what it could to make Acacia Creek a
viable entity.
The Board made this decision in full confidence that Acacia Creek
would remain Masonic in its values, and that serving non-Masons was compatible
with its mission. Preference in admissions and pricing continue to be offered to
Masons, and the Board instructed staff to ensure that compatibility with Masonic
values was a criterion in accepting non-Masons.
In January, 2010, the marketing campaign for the enhanced community
was kicked off, and the results have been positive thus far. We have had 735
leads, 53 of which became $1000 depositors, and 11 have advanced to 10%
depositors since January 1; nearly all of the leads and $1000 depositors have
come from non-Masons. While these numbers are good, conversions to 10% and
move-ins—the “acid test” of sales and marketing—have been much slower than
had been experienced by start-up retirement communities historically, a reflection
of the continuing economic woes of the nation.
The social mixing of Masons and non-Masons has been positive. In
fact, in a happy development, several of the non-Masons who have moved in

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

203

since January have expressed interest in becoming Masons! These men are being
referred to Siminoff Lodge and we hope to welcome them to our fraternity in the
near future.
Construction was substantially completed at the end of February, about
14 weeks behind original schedule, and our first residents moved in the first
week of March. As with any new facility, there were design and construction
related issues that needed to be corrected, and by the end of July, those have been
substantially completed. While final accounting was not fully complete at the
end of July, we anticipate that total hard & soft costs of construction will be just
under $92,000,000 or approximately $590,000 (0.64%) over original estimates,
pending resolution of some credits from outside funds. Marketing costs continue
to accrue as sales and marketing continue post opening. Of the 150 items on our
list of conditions of approval required by the City of Union City, only a handful
remain. Those should be completed shortly, though one item, the mandated
artwork at the entrance of Masonic Homes & Acacia Creek, may be delayed to
October because of logistics.
We are pleased that there is a piece of Franklin Lodge # 143 which will
live on at Acacia Creek. Nine beautiful stained glass windows have been placed
throughout Acacia Creek, courtesy of an amicable “swap” of windows with the
lodge. Backlit with lighting, they are a beautiful addition to the décor and provide
a constant reminder of our Masonic heritage.
There have been difficulties with the regulatory agency governing the
licensing category under which Acacia Creek operates; i.e., Residential Care
Facilities for the Aging (RCFE). It took an extremely long time and much
effort to finally receive our RCFE license from the State Department of Social
Services. We finally received the license in May. The second part of our license,
the provisional certificate of authority (PCOA) to operate as a continuing care
retirement community (CCRC), has not been received at the time of this report—
though in this case, the issue is not bureaucracy and staff cutbacks caused by
the State budget crisis, but rather our own sales pace (the PCOA is conditioned
upon our reaching a threshold sales level). This had cash flow effects on Acacia
Creek because the PCOA enables us to collect entrance fees. In the meantime, we
are operating on a month-to-month rental agreement with our residents and their
deposits and entry fees remain in escrow. This temporary difficulty was addressed
through bridge loans with Masonic Homes.
As of the end of July, 2010, 50 of Acacia Creek’s 152 units were occupied,
with a resident count of 72.
There has been an evolution within the Board of Directors itself. For
the past several years, it has served as a “founding board” with decision-making
roles that were more like management than a policy-making board. The Board
understood that with the opening of Acacia Creek, it needed to transition from

204

Proceedings of the

a working board to a strategic and policy-making board with clear delineations
between Board and management duties. That process was symbolized by the
move from monthly to quarterly meetings beginning in January, and the journey,
we expect, will continue throughout the year.
Certainly challenges remain for Acacia Creek. Our economy and the
real estate market are showing signs of bottoming out and perhaps the first signs
of recovery. But all reports indicate a slow and uneven recovery, so the pace
of sales will in all likelihood remain lower than expected. We have instituted a
number of incentives to counter this, but it remains a challenge.
Were it not for a dedicated and passionate Board of Directors and a very
capable staff, the challenge would be even more daunting. I take this occasion
to thank the Acacia Creek Board of Directors for their dedication to this new
retirement community and their commitment to our fraternity. I would also
be remiss if I did not acknowledge the support and assistance provided by the
Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, Grand Master Ken Nagel and Past Grand
Masters David Doan, Richard Hopper, and Larry Adamson, all of whom have
played a significant role in making Acacia Creek the finest new senior residential
community in the East Bay area.

Admissions Committee
By Timothy A. Wood, Chairman
The Admissions Review Program of the Board is a carefully developed
analysis and evaluation process that continues to be improved and refined to meet
the evolving needs to our applicants, as well as the Homes Staff and the Board.
The interview process and on site evaluation is done at the same time
the applicant visits one of the two facilities. A Staff report on this overnight visit,
together with the Medical Director’s comments on his/her review of the medical
information, is then added to the application. The staff then develops an executive
summary on the applicants and presents that to the Admissions Committee for
review and approval. Anytime the Staff recommends against admission the
full application is given to the Admissions Committee for detailed review and
discussion during the Admissions Committee meeting. Any recommendation
against admission requires the full Board confirmation.
Prior to the regular Admissions Committee meeting on the second
Tuesday of each month, the three Trustees, who form the Admissions Committee,

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

205

each receive and carefully study the complete applications not recommended
for Masonic assistance and the executive summaries for applications
recommended for Masonic assistance. Each Trustee reviews and evaluates
the applications and accompanying data and then discusses his viewpoint
during the Admissions Committee meeting. Home’s Staff and Administrators
attend the Admissions Committee meeting to answer committee member’s
questions and to provide additional information to the committee members. The
committee’s recommendations and comments are then presented to the full Board
for confirmation.
The number of applications handled by the Admissions Committee
varies from month to month. From July 1, 2009 to June 30, 2010, 33 applicants
have been admitted to the Union City Campus, while 9 have been admitted to the
Covina campus. Union City currently has 256 residents, including the 16 residents
in the Traditions Special Care Unit. Covina currently has 78 residents. For this
time period we had a total of 102 applications being completed by our brothers,
widows, and mothers.
The Masonic Outreach Service programs continue to grow, serving our
eligible Brethren and their families or widows within their local communities or
residence. Masonic Outreach provides case management to those in need of such
service and financial-case management to those who qualify. The Masonic Senior
Outreach program serves clients age 60 and older, and is currently serving 192
clients; three of whom are on outplacement by the Masonic Homes.
In August 2009, the Masonic Outreach Program developed a Family
Outreach program. This new program was developed in response to the growing
fraternal needs of our younger members, under the age of 60, and was designed
to provide a similar type of support to that of our Senior Outreach Program. The
Masonic Family Outreach program is currently serving 58 clients.
This year the committee has reviewed and approved a total of 51
applications for both of these programs. The care managers work closely with
the clients to ensure that their needs are being met, while fulfilling the programs’
guidelines. Through Masonic Senior and Family Outreach, we are able to serve
our “whole” fraternal family.
I would like to thank the other Trustees of the Admissions Committee,
John W. Herring and John F. Lowe, who labor long and hard over the applications.
I would also like to express my appreciation to the Executive Directors of Covina
and Union City Homes, their supporting staff, and the continued dedication of the
Masonic Outreach staff and the Board of Trustees.

Board Development Committee
By Michael D. Neben, Chairman
On behalf of the Board Development Committee, I am pleased to report
that during the second year of the committee’s existence, we have continued
to assist the Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes in refining its processes
and practices.
At the committee’s recommendation, the board adopted a consent
calendar to streamline meeting business and a meeting debrief – a quick review
during executive session to offer candid appraisals of the effectiveness of the just
concluded meeting.
With our assistance, the board has emphasized best practice protocols,
including, for example, speaking only upon recognition by the President, reducing
private and side discussions, and minimizing the number of repeat points made.
The committee developed a matrix of current trustee knowledge,
expertise and interests in order to provide a framework for considering potential
board members. The matrix suggested areas where specific new knowledge
or experience might prove beneficial to the board as a whole. The committee
developed a framework for a more formal mentorship program than had existed
in the past. The program will be refined in the coming year.
The committee shifted from an emphasis on education modules during
every quarter to emphasizing board attendance at educational conferences and
meetings, at which trustees could gain a deeper understanding of the field, often
with trustees from other organizations, Masonic & non-Masonic, and with staff.
In the past year, different board members attended the annual meeting of the
Masonic Communities and Services Association (the national association of
Masonic related communities and service providers), held in Elizabethtown, PA,
and a national conference convened by BoardSource, one of the most respected
sources for board education. At this writing, there are plans for one or more
trustees to attend the fall annual meeting of American Association of Homes &
Services for the Aging.
The Board Development Committee continued to refine the selfevaluation tool, though it did make a conscious decision to keep the framework
intact. It was felt that keeping the framework would enable better year-toyear comparisons and trending data that would enable the committee to look
strategically at board development.

Finance Committee
By Larry L. Adamson, Chairman
It has been an honor for the members of the Finance Committee to serve
your Masonic Homes of California this past year. This committee monitors and
manages the finances for the Masonic Homes of California and is charged with
the important responsibility of ensuring that we serve our residents today, while
protecting our legacy for future generations.
The Masonic Homes of California changed its fiscal year end from June
30th to October 31st in 2009. For the year ended June 30, 2009 the Masonic
Homes recorded a surplus of $3.893 million and for the four month stub year ended
October 31, 2009 recorded a surplus of $1.194 million. These results represent
favorable variances from budget of $1.174 million and $455,000, respectively.
In both years overall revenues met or exceeded the budget and along with strong
expense control contributed significantly toward the surpluses.
Operating expenditures of MHC have been guided by the Investment
Distribution Policy. This policy is set as a percentage of a five-year rolling average
of the General and Endowment Funds’ market value. This approach insures our
operating budget will be somewhat buffered from significant year to-year market
swings while protecting the integrity of the fund balances for future generations
of residents. The financial market turmoil in 2008 and 2009 caused the Investment
Committee to recommend that the Masonic Homes consider lowering its
Distribution Policy Payout from 5.0% to 4.5%. The Finance Committee took this
recommendation seriously and reduced the payout further, to 4.25% in 2010. This
committee is committed to constantly reevaluating the operations of the Homes to
ensure we are operating efficiently, all the while maintaining the highest level of
care and resident satisfaction. In addition, we continue to explore opportunities to
diversify the revenue sources of the Homes to better protect our assets for future
generations.
The Finance Committee reviewed regular reports from the Grand
Treasurer and Chief Financial Officer. These reports include quarterly investment
performance reports, monthly operating statements, quarterly capital project
reviews and various others. Moss Adams, LLP the auditors for Grand Lodge and
the Masonic Homes, have completed the annual external audits for the fiscal year
ended June 30, 2009 and the four month stub period ended October 31, 2009, with
both audit reports be unqualified. The Audit for the fiscal year ended October 31,
2010 will be completed in January and February of 2011.
