year 2011 budget using a zero-based approach. In the face of ever rising costs,
management proposed, the Finance Committee recommended and the Board
approved a budget which again used a 4.25% Investment Distribution payout.
The Finance Committee also worked with management to develop a
capital project budget to assure the Homes remain well-maintained and safe to
protect the comfort and safety of our residents. The Homes continues to fund
the Capital Reserve Fund from a percentage of the annual depreciation through

Medical Advisory Committee
By Gary Charland, Chairman
The Medical Advisory Committee oversees the quality of services
provided to the residents of the Masonic Homes of California at the Union City
and Covina communities. Quality of Life and a goal of culture change has resulted
in the renovation of the two occupied floors in the Lorber building (Skilled
Nursing unit) as well as program evolution at both campuses.
The Committee continues to monitor quality indicators for delivery of
care. The indicators are analyzed to identify trends or patterns. Comparisons
are made with National and State benchmarks, as they relate primarily to Skilled
Nursing data. Quality Measures are also evaluated in the Independent and Assisted
Living levels.
Union City’s Lorber renovation was completed in December with the
resident and staff moves occurring in early January. The renovations included
lighting, carpeted hallways, silent call light system, an enlarged beauty shop, a
large dining room and living room. The door to the 3rd floor parking lot was also
enlarged to allow greater efficiency with evacuation.
Cultural change is helping to transform the skilled nursing facility
from operating under a medical model of care philosophy to operating under a
wellness or more holistic philosophy with a resident-centered approach. This
process involves a multitude of efforts directed towards changing the habits
and assumptions of long-term care practice to support and maximize resident
strengths. In keeping with the culture change efforts, there is a hospitality area
that allows residents to entertain their family and guests in a home environment. A

210

Proceedings of the

Serenity Room provides residents and families a private and tranquil environment
to say farewell with peace and dignity at the end of life. The consistent staffing
model enhances quality of care and of life by encouraging greater knowledge of
each resident and their preferences by staff. This staffing model is currently being
piloted on the day shift in Lorber.
In the RCFE, there has been a change in the Health Clinic to improve
the quality of services to the residents, reduce costs to the Masonic Home and
prepare for additional clinic services for the Acacia Creek residents. A business
relationship was established with Washington Township Medical Group (WTMG)
to provide an in-house medical office effective October 5, 2009.
The Covina community introduced a Wellness Challenge of 2010.
Residents were challenged to focus on a healthy lifestyle to reduce their weight.
Education and coaching have been provided to all who have chosen to participate.
Metrics are an integral part allowing residents and staff to track their progress on
a regular basis. The Healthy Group is growing as residents reduce their weight.
In addition, Covina introduced ‘Free Style Dining’. The change from scheduled
meal times to an open dining room has been very well-received and has been a
success for residents and staff.
In response to the world-wide epidemic, there was a significant focus
on prevention of the flu and specifically the H1N1 virus. Flu shots and H1N1
vaccines were offered to residents and staff on both campuses. Vigil Monitoring
System was installed on both campuses to comply with the Department of Social
Service regulations for monitoring of residents. Staff were trained on proper use
of the equipment.
The Medical Advisory Committee is in transition as a result of the new
Philosophy of Care. With wellness as the primary focus, the name is being changed
to the Wellness Improvement Committee. To assure a fully comprehensive
perspective, Masonic Outreach Services (MOS) has been included as a committee
participant. MOS can assist those seniors who can be better served by remaining
in their own homes or closer to their families. We meet their needs by arranging
for help from experts in the community and provide the financial assistance to hire
those experts when warranted.
The Committee continues to provide guidance and advice with regard
to the development of the strategic direction of wellness services and related
programs. This includes quality of life and other initiatives at the Homes. One
of the responsibilities of the Board Liaison is to provide a quarterly report to the
Masonic Homes Board on the work of the Committee and all medical services,
initiatives, and programs, including any recommendations to improve service,
safety or compliance.

Strategic Planning Committee
By Mark N. Gibson, Chairman
One of the centerpieces of this year’s annual Board retreat was a full
explanation and adoption of a new philosophy of care that will help drive operations
and strategic thinking going forward. At its core, is a shift from a philosophy
embodied by the phrase “we will take care of you” to a new catchphrase, “we
will help you to achieve a high quality of life.” These are not mutually exclusive
concepts (one should have both) and at first glance, the change may appear to be
minor. However, it has already made a difference in our approach to operations
and strategic priorities by shifting the emphasis to improving residents’ and
clients capability and quality of life rather than caring for increasing frailties.
The Committee looks forward to updating the Craft on our progress and how this
new philosophy may enhance the guiding Mission and Vision Statements of the
Homes in next year’s report.
A task force convened under the auspices of the Committee to explore
alternative uses of the former Children’s Homes on the Covina campus. In
June, 2010, as a phase one decision, the Board approved the Committee’s
recommendation to use the Children’s Homes as a guest house and retreat center
for Masonic entities needing a place for planning or training retreats. The task
force continues to explore other alternative uses, including rental arrangements
(office space or some business compatible with the senior residences) or a
partnership with a local social service agency or school for a mutually beneficial
service.
During the year, the Strategic Planning Committee continued its research
into community-based aging-in-place models. These models are designed to have
services brought to seniors in their own homes as their needs and wishes change
(hence, “aging in place”). The Committee visited Avenidas Villages in Palo Alto,
which is a variation of the Beacon Hill Village model originated in Boston, and
the Eskaton Demonstration House near Sacramento, which is a prototype of how
architectural design and technology could enable a care and concierge service
model that might be brought to a senior’s own home. We learned more about
continuing care at home (the model that moves the entrance fee, continuing care/
future care concept from a “bricks and mortar” retirement community into the
senior’s own home). The committee will be discussing how these models might
merge with or enhance the valuable Masonic Outreach program.
Other Issues The Committee helped shepherd a review and update of
admissions policy regarding the “under 60” program to give it the flexibility
needed to address the needs of our brethren as a result of the current economy
and the challenges it has presented to many of our under 60 members (see Board
of Directors report). It also guided a review of the Masonic Homes Children’s
Program Alumni Scholarship policies to conform to today’s climate and enhance
its value as a true motivator to our former charges to continue their growth as
young adults.

212

Proceedings of the

The Committee recognized that the financial shortfall anticipated for
several years has not materialized as expected. That recognition, coupled with
the current economic climate has tempered several more aggressive and capital
intensive strategic initiatives. Efforts have been concentrating on enhancing
and improving current programs and initiatives. Subsequently, the Flatlands
development initiative has been placed on hold pending further analysis and
review.
The Committee has adopted and utilized a new management provided
tool to assist in identifying and prioritizing the several pending strategic initiatives.
I would like to express my extreme gratitude and respect for the members
of the Strategic Planning Committee, the Board of Trustees, Management and
staff for their tireless dedication of time and talent towards the improvement and
advancement of our services in a continuing effort to enhance the programs of the
Masonic Homes for our members.

President’s Report
By David R. Doan, PGM
My brothers, I have good news and bad news. The good news is that
in the last 12 months our Masonic Homes of California help over 583 masons,
widows or orphans. The bad news is that 583 is almost 90 more people than we
help in the previous 12 months and we are expecting to help 617 in the coming
year. Much of this increase is due to the difficult financial times that our nation
has endured for the last two years. During this year we began to help lodges deal
with their obligations to help our brothers under 60 who were facing difficult
times. This year, I am proud to say that we provided support to over 100 families
hard hit by job losses, health issues and other struggles. I am also proud to say that
the members we serve – no matter how difficult their lives and how overwhelming
their problems – are a credit to our fraternity and remind us all how fraternal
values sustain and ennoble us – even in the face of circumstances that bring us
low.
One of our members is 55 years old, married with a teenage daughter.
He has worked hard his whole life; done well and was proud of the work he did
and his ability to care for his family and his service to our fraternity. A few years
ago he found himself forgetting things; getting confused and uncharacteristically
making mistakes at work. This continued to the point where he lost his job and
was diagnosed with early onset Alzheimer’s. His wife went to work but the only
job she could find was part-time and the income was not enough to sustain them.
Their roof was leaking and their trash was no longer being picked up because they
hadn’t been able to pay the bill and they were at risk of losing their house. They
had no idea where to turn.
As members of our great fraternity, we turn to each other. His lodge
provided some immediate support and got in the touch with Masonic Family
Outreach Services. Our care managers got them enrolled in health insurance;
helped get the roof fixed and the trash picked up and are working on a plan to
ensure their long-term self-sufficiency.
The lives we saved are not numbers or a line item in a budget – they
are our brothers; our brothers’ wives and widows; our brothers’ children and
grandchildren.
In another case this year, an elderly man was found wandering, confused
and unable to tell police his name or where he lived. Luckily, he was carrying
an envelope with the return address of Grand Lodge. The police contacted Grand
Lodge who referred the call to MOS. MOS immediately contacted the local lodge
and together we moved him into the kind of safe and supportive environment that
he needed. He had lost his treasured Masonic ring, which his lodge replaced for
him while members visited regularly. He only lived for a few more months and
was then buried in his Masonic ring. Because of this partnership with Grand

214

Proceedings of the

Lodge, the local lodge and Masonic Outreach Services we made sure our brother
did not die alone or in need. He died surrounded by our care, our support and our
fraternal bond. This is the heart of Masonic Outreach Services.
In these difficult times, I am happy to report that the Masonic Homes
are doing well. Last year, I reported to you that we had implemented a five year
plan to deal with the downturn in our investment income. We have completed
the first year under the plan and we are meeting our spending and savings targets.
Because of our conservative fiscal management we have been able to do this
while helping more people and not reducing the quality of care we provide to our
residents. I am confident that we can weather these difficult times and continue to
maintain our high standards of care.
Last year I reported to you that the Masonic Homes was undertaking
a new effort to help children all across this great state. I pleased to report that
Masonic Center for Youth and Families will open before the end of this year. The
new Masonic Center for Youth and Families was conceived under the conviction
that children, teens, and their families deserved better than the fragmented,
confusing, and dispiriting system that now dominates services for kids with
behavioral and other issues. We are convinced that there is a better way. The
three foundations of the Center will be:
•

Comprehensive assessment at the outset to obtain a full picture of
the child or teen, including psychological testing and interviews with
important people in the youth’s life;

•

Experienced senior clinicians who develop strong individual relationship
with the child or teen and who also benefit from the best thinking that
emerges from thoughtful discussion with a multi-disciplinary team; and

•

Research on composite outcomes to help refine treatment planning and
add a unique perspective to the body of knowledge of the field.

While the Center will be based in San Francisco, its services will extend
beyond the Bay Area. Masonic families throughout the State will be able to access
the assessment phase of the Center’s services, and to the extent welcomed by the
family and therapist, we will provide follow-up monitoring and consultation.
Through this new Center, we will be able to serve more of our children
and make a profound difference in their lives. We will learn about our children
and adolescents in all their unique complexity –- their strengths and talents and
their wounds and vulnerabilities – and offer services that help them discover and
embrace their possibilities.
Through this new Center, we are going to serve a child or teen with
behavioral or learning problems in a way no one else in the country is doing. We
assembled a team of experts who are going to assess the complete child from all
angles. We are not looking to label kids – we are looking to understand them.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

215

We are going to do extensive testing, we are going to talk to their teachers, their
coaches and their ministers or rabbis and we are going to insist on the child’s right
to be known and understood. From this understanding, we are going to develop
a thoughtful treatment plan that addresses the needs of the child and the family.
And finally, we are committed to do research to improve our treatments
and share our knowledge with others. We will treat the complete child in a way
no one else is doing, and we hope our example will lead to improvement in
therapeutic services for others. We are working with experts from across the
country, and internationally, to ensure we do this right. Yale Child Study Center
and the Anna Freud Centre in London are supporting our efforts.
I only have time today to highlight a few of the important and exciting
programs going on at the Masonic Homes. Our strategic vision calls for us
to support member’s needs throughout life’s transitions and that is what these
programs are meant to do. Through these programs, we fulfill our fraternal
obligation to provide relief to members and their families in the name of every
California Mason. The status on all of the Masonic Homes Programs can be
found in the written report of the Board of Trustees in the Annual Proceedings.
Before I close I have a few words about the important partnership between
our lodges and the Masonic Homes. The Masonic Homes are here to serve our
members needs but we can’t serve them if we don’t know about them. You, the
lodge members, are in the best position to know when one of our brothers, their
widows or a brother’s child or grandchild is struggling. Please help us identify
these members in need and when you find them, call us and together we can ensure
that no member of our fraternal family is ever alone with those struggles. And of
course, please remember, that we depend on member contributions to advance our
charitable mission. Your annual donations go directly into our operating budget
and into the hands of our members in need. Together we can ensure that our
fraternal bonds are an active and alive force in the world. Together we can make
the world a better place.
Family Resource Center
During this past year, the action taken at the 2009 Board retreat to serve
under 60 Masons affected by the economic downturn was fully implemented. Six
resource fairs were held throughout the state offering information and referral,
resources for those struggling with mortgage payments and other financial
challenges, access to temporary assistance offered by various agencies, and other
assistance. In total 108 attended these resource fairs. Case management services
similar to Masonic Senior Outreach were provided through what came to be called
Family Outreach and temporary financial assistance was offered as needed. In
total over 100 families were served under Family Outreach. In March, 2010, the
Board approved staff recommendations regarding the case-management program
and authorized its continued funding for the coming year.

216

Proceedings of the
Flatlands Project

In February, 2010, the Board indefinitely suspended the flatlands project
in Union City. The project, which consisted of development of the flatlands along
Mission Boulevard with a combination of townhouses, senior residences and
community benefit facilities, was designed to support the charitable mission of
Masonic Homes, and the Board had, in 2007, approved a political campaign to
allow construction on the site. A previously passed voter initiative prohibited
construction on the hillside, which included our flatlands, thus necessitating
the political campaign. Unfortunately, the economic downturn, including
the downturn in the real estate market, made the project infeasible for the
foreseeable future.
Children’s Home Former Residents
When we transitioned out of the Children’s Residential Program in July,
2009, we made a commitment to the 18 children who were part of the program
to support them through case management and when needed, financial support.
Overall the kids have done well in academic & extracurricular activities, despite
some minor individual setbacks in grades. Four of 18 graduated from high school.
Three families required very little support, and the remainder needed assistance to
make the transition work. Five kids needed outplacement support because family
reunification was not possible. Overall, the kids continue to demonstrate the skills
they learned while residing in the Homes. We will continue to track our former
residents in the coming year.
Scholarship Policies
The Board approved the Scholarship Committee’s recommendation of
changes in policies that better reflect the changes we are experiencing in the State
while continuing to provide meaningful support to our former residents. Among
the more important changes: indexing scholarships to 50% of California State
University costs; requiring a minimum number of units per year; allowing up to
five years of scholarship support per individual; and setting a maximum award
per year.

Children’s Homes Alternative Use

Financial Performance
Masonic Homes continues to do well financially, building its operating
reserves in anticipation of a difficult stretch in the next three-to-four years. The
Board uses a prudent policy of basing its distribution from its endowment on a
rolling 20-quarter average asset balance to smooth out income. In the coming
3-4 years, high asset quarters will be replaced by the drastically lower quarters
caused by the economic downturn that started in the fall of 2008. The Board last
year adopted a five-year plan to deal with that issue, and it revisited the plan at
its annual planning retreat in March. More specific information about financial
performance is contained in the Board’s Finance Committee report.
Investment Policy
In March, the Board approved the recommendation of the Investment
Committee to add two new asset classes to its portfolio to increase its already sound
diversification and reduce overall risk. The Board also approved granting more
flexibility to its fund managers, commensurate with risk parameters, to prudently
invest on our behalf. I take this opportunity to thank the Grand Treasurer and the
Investment Committee for their oversight during these turbulent times.
Lorber Renovation
In January, 2010, the long awaited major refurbishment of Lorber, the
skilled nursing wing on the Union City campus, was completed, and residents
were treated to new dining facilities, updated bathing facilities, and other
improvements. For more information, please see the report from Dixie Reeve,
Executive Director of the Union City campus.

(1-888-466-3642) at the 2009 annual communications. A single number will now

or case-managed services through Masonic Outreach for both senior services and

I would like to thank the members of the Board of Trustees of Masonic

Report of the Executive Vice President
NEW PHILOSOPHY OF CARE
Woven into many of the reports that constitute the total report of
Masonic Homes of California is a new “Philosophy of Care” that is affecting
programming for resident and client services and the way we approach strategic
planning. In brief, it is a shift in emphasis from a philosophy of “we will take
care of you” to “we will help you achieve a high quality of life.” The former is a
laudable goal, particularly during a bygone time when there were few safety nets
for disadvantaged persons, and in truth there are times when it remains critical
today, such as when one of our residents or clients becomes very frail. But it is
also a philosophy based on illness or disability, emphasizing what a resident can
no longer do (the implied phrase after “we will take care of you” is “because you
can no longer do it yourself”). The new Philosophy of Care emphasizes quality
of life and its close cousin wellness; that is, it emphasizes maintaining both for as
long as possible and even improving them in all its components (mental, physical,
spiritual, social, etc.). It asks the question, what is important to your well-being
and how might we assist you to achieve this? Metrics (measurable indicators
of progress) will change with our new Philosophy of Care. We will continue to
track falls, use of psychotropics, unintended weight loss, and the like because
they remain very important. But they are illness- or disability-based metrics, and
we need to develop and track wellness metrics to complement the data. Why
shouldn’t we place as much emphasis on, for example, improvement in strength
and muscle tone as we do on number of falls? I expect that we will make good
progress in this journey in the coming year.
MANAGEMENT CHANGES
In June, 2010, the difficult decision was made to close down the
Development Department after the decision by the Board of Trustees to indefinitely
suspend the flatlands project (see below), and so we bade a sad farewell to Vice
President of Strategic Development John Howl, Project Manager Eric Sholty,
Executive Assistant Peggy Parker and Outreach Coordinator Sam Baum. John
and his team were responsible for shepherding the Acacia Creek project from
the very beginning—ably steering us through planning, entitlements, design,
financing, marketing and construction. Similarly, they were guiding us through
the flatlands project when it became clear that given the economic downturn and
the depressed real estate market, the project was not feasible right now and would
not be feasible in the foreseeable future. Previous to assuming his development
role, John was Executive Director of the Covina campus, ably guiding the campus
through its strategic growth and operational improvement, and Interim Executive
Vice President while the Board was conducting its search. We wish John and the
team well in their future endeavors.

220

Proceedings of the
ACACIA CREEK

Acacia Creek presented us with both moments of joy and its share of
challenges in the past year, as detailed under the Acacia Creek report authored
by Board President Mike Neben. We opened our doors in early March, and the
experience of serving members of the Masonic family in a new way has been
gratifying. In its five-plus months of operation, we see that we are already making
a difference in our residents’ lives.
Sales continue to be a challenge. We believe we are seeing signs of the
real estate marketing bottoming out, but we also believe the recovery will be long
and uneven, with a period of up-and-down movements that will add to uncertainty
in the short term. We have instituted a number of incentives that have helped us,
but we fully expect sales to continue to be slower than the historical pattern for
communities like Acacia Creek.
MASONIC CENTER FOR YOUTH & FAMILIES
Under Executive Director Steffani Kizziar’s leadership, the newly
renamed Masonic Center for Youth and Families is on schedule for opening in
late 2010. It will be a one-of-a-kind center of excellence featuring comprehensive
testing for and clinical treatment of behavioral and psychological conditions
among young people. MCYAF will be located in the Presidio in San Francisco
but will truly be a statewide program, able to positively affect the lives of children
throughout the State. Please refer to Steffani’s report in the Masonic Homes
proceedings.
CHILDREN’S SERVICES AND MASONIC OUTREACH
Please see the report of Sabrina Montes, Director of Masonic Outreach
Services, for details regarding the status of the children who were transitioned
out of the residential program last year (overall, they are doing well) and on the
status of the important Masonic Outreach program. As Sabrina’s report indicates,
Masonic Outreach has expanded its scope and grown its client base to better meet
the evolving needs of the Masonic family.
FLATLANDS PROJECT
In February, the Board of Trustees, upon the recommendation of
management, suspended the flatlands project in Union City. The project was
intended to develop the nearly mile long area adjacent to Mission Boulevard
for townhouses, senior living, local retail, and community benefit facilities. We
were in the mid-stage of our political campaign to get voter approval to develop

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

221

the property (our flatlands had been included in a hillside protection ordinance
previously approved by Union City voters), when it became clear the economic
downturn was going to continue for some time. A careful financial analysis,
including a series of possible scenarios, showed that the project would not be
feasible for the foreseeable future. Thus, the decision was made to suspend the
project. It was a difficult but prudent decision. The flatlands remains a possible
project in the future.
We look forward to the coming year. It is an exciting time, filled with
challenges to be sure, but also the opportunity to serve Masons of California
in new and better ways. On behalf of management staff, I thank you for the
opportunity.
Respectfully submitted,
Melvin Matsumoto

Report of the Executive Director/Administrator
Masonic Home at Union City
On behalf of the residents and staff of Masonic Homes of California,
Union City it is my pleasure to present the following 2010 annual report.
Washington Township Medical Group (WTMG) opened a satellite
medical office at Union City in October 2009. Bringing the professional medical
group on-site has improved the residents’ experience with health services and
addressed a resident satisfaction issue. Residents have the option to change
medical groups to have their physician visits here on MHC – Union City campus.
Operational efficiencies have improved and we are prepared to serve residents
from the new Acacia Creek Community.
Renovations have been made to The Masonic Homes area of the Chapel
of the Chimes Cemetery. The upgrades included replacing markers in addition to
revision of the landscaping. The additional trees and plants and revisions to the
walkways add to the peacefulness and beauty of the location.
Union City’s Lorber renovation was completed in December with the
residents and staff moves occurring in early January. The renovations included
lighting, carpeted hallways, silent call light system, a glamorous and enlarged
Beauty shop, a large dining room and living room. The door to the 3rd floor
parking lot was also enlarged to allow greater efficiency with evacuation.
A primary initiative this year has been on culture change. This process
involves a multitude of efforts directed toward changing the habits and assumptions
of long-term care practice to support and maximize resident strengths. In keeping
with the culture change efforts in Lorber, a hospitality area was created to allow
residents the ability to entertain their family and guests in a home environment. A
Serenity Room provides residents and families a private and tranquil environment
to say farewell with peace and dignity at the end of life. Currently, a consistent
staffing model is being piloted on the day shift in Lorber. Research has shown that
the consistent staffing model enhances quality of care and of life by encouraging
greater knowledge of each resident and their preferences by staff. Buffet dining is
scheduled to begin in the fall of 2010. The new Dining Service will be served as
buffet style with resident choosing their own food with the assistance of the staff.
In the RCFE, the change in the Health Clinic has resulted in mobile
services that will take the Assisted Living nurse to the resident when there is
a health care need. The residents are encouraged to remain as independent as
possible with support services available when required.
Dining and Facility Services are collaborating to develop a Recycling
and Compost Program. This will include composting food waste from the kitchen
and yard waste from the gardeners.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

223

The North Forty garden has been expanded to a full acre of land.
The additional space adds depth to the dining experience and provides greater
opportunity for residents to enjoy their gardening experience. Personal gardening
is provided for residents in the garden off Second Adams patio.
Residents are actively involved in committees that address improvement
to their living environment within the community. This year, a resident/staff
committee was formed to address the limited parking on-site. The committee was
successful in creating an overall increase in available parking spaces and resident
assigned parking. They then organized “The People Mover”. This is a volunteer
driven shuttle that assists staff, visitors and residents with transportation to and
from the outlying parking lots. The resulting “door to door” service has been
well-received.
A second resident committee developed this year is the Emergency
Disaster Team. Working with a staff liaison they have identified and trained
resident floor monitors are participating in fire and disaster drills. Training is
ongoing with staff and residents.
The resident scholarship committee selected Sarvesh Naranyan, to be the
2010 MHC Scholarship recipient this year. Sarvesh and his parents were lunch
guests with the Resident and Staff Scholarship Committee members. He worked
as a volunteer server in Dining Services last summer.

Proceedings of the

Report of the Executive Director

of Children’s Services and Masonic Outreach

I am pleased to present this report of our activities during the past year.
My report will focus on the soon to be opened Masonic Center for Youth and
Families. Please refer to the separate report regarding the status of the former
residents of the Children’s Homes in Covina and Masonic Outreach authored
by Sabrina Montes, who was promoted to Director of Masonic Outreach during
the year.
The new Masonic Center for Youth and Families was conceived under
the conviction that children, teens, and their families deserved better than the
fragmented, confusing, and dispiriting system (of lack thereof) that now dominates
services for kids with behavioral and other issues. We are convinced that there is
a better way. The three foundations of the Center will be:
•

Comprehensive assessment at the outset to obtain a full picture of
the child or teen, including psychological testing and interviews with
important people in the youth’s life;

•

Experienced senior clinicians who develop strong individual relationship
with the child or teen and who also benefit from the best thinking that
emerges from thoughtful discussion with a multi-disciplinary team; and

•

Research on composite outcomes to help refine treatment planning and
add a unique perspective to the body of knowledge of the field.

While the Center will be based in San Francisco, its services will extend
beyond the Bay Area. Masonic families throughout the State will be able to access
the assessment phase of the Center’s services, and to the extent welcomed by the
family and therapist, we will provide follow-up monitoring and consultation.
Since the Center was approved by the Board of Trustees in August, 2009,
we have worked on several fronts to implement the project plan. We have:
•

Refined the clinical model that is the heart of the program, utilizing the
best thinking of the internal team and renown experts in the field;

•

Recruited an outstanding team of senior clinicians and other professionals,
led by Terry Owens, PhD, our Clinical Director, and Phil Erdberg, PhD,
our Assessment and Research Director;

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

235

•

Developed or are developing the policies & procedures, organizational
structures, job descriptions, and other documents that will guide all
phases of our operations;

•

Created a marketing plan for both the Masonic and non-Masonic
audiences;

•

Pursued a license from the State of California to operate as a psychology
clinic; and

•

Developed the IT plan for the Center, including selection of specialty
software;

As of this writing, we are nearing completion of negotiations for rental
of a Civil War era house in the Presidio, San Francisco. The home-like look is in
keeping with the welcoming, non-institutional intent of the Center, and is ideally
located for access by our potential clients. Work to conform to ADA requirements
will start shortly thereafter. We anticipate an opening in late 2010.
Respectfully submitted,
Steffani Kizziar

236

Proceedings of the

Report of the Director

of Masonic Outreach Services

Children’s Services – Family Resources Center
Last fiscal year, the Children’s Residential program at Covina closed
its operations on July 31st, 2009. During this year of transition, we continued to
serve our former residents by way of case management and financial support. Of
the 21 children who were discharged last year, 3 graduated from high school and
were awarded a Masonic Homes Scholarship. The remaining 18 children were
provided financial and non-financial case management services. Financial support
was provided to ensure that the children would remain in stable and safe living
environments. Families were also assisted with accessing public benefits and
low-cost programs to help them better meet the needs of their children. Finally, of
the 18 children that were served this past year, 5 were provided with significant
financial support due to their need for outplacement services. These 5 children did
not have families, to whom they could transition to in July 2009.
As of June 2010, 4 children have graduated from high school and remain
eligible for the Masonic Homes Scholarship. Of the 5 children who needed
outplacement services, 1 graduated from high school; 1 reunified with family and
only 3 remain in out-of-home care. During this second year of transition, we plan
to continue serving the 13 remaining children by way of case management to
ensure their success. Of these 13, we know that 3-4 will need significant financial
support. The other children will be provided with nominal financial support to
help meet any educational, extracurricular or mental health needs. The families
have made good strides toward successful reunifications and overall the children
have continued to do well academically.
The Masonic Homes Scholarship Program has undergone significant
changes this past year to ensure the longevity of its financial endowments and to
further broaden the opportunities for the scholarship recipients. These changes
extended the time period for which alumni can make their initial application;
included graduate studies; and allowed for scholars to attend colleges/universities
outside of California. The other parameters of the program included up to 5 years
of scholarship eligibility toward undergraduate studies and 5 years of scholarship
eligibility toward graduate studies. Finally, due to the increasing number of
scholars and the extended reach of the scholarship program, annual caps have
been placed on the maximum award amount for a given year. Scholarship awards
will vary based on full time or part time status; the type of college or university
attended; and as to whether the scholar resides on campus or off campus. The
maximum cap is based on 50% of the cost of a Cal State program, for that specific
year. The scholars are also being provided with case management support to
ensure their academic success and to assist them with accessing needed resources.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

237

Masonic Family Outreach Services – Family Resource Center
As part of the strategic shift of our organization, we expanded the
services of the Masonic Family Resource Center, located on our Covina campus
in Southern California, to better meet the needs of our fraternal family. We have
offered case management services that are broad, flexible, and able to serve
families in their own communities. Our support includes identifying resources
for families struggling with today’s complex issues, such as the impact of divorce,
the stresses of a special needs child, and other significant life challenges.
In August of 2009, we began initiating a series of Resources Fairs that
would be held throughout the state of California to meet the growing needs of
our fraternal members, hard-hit by the recent economic down-turn. The six
Resource Fairs brought together local community vendors who offered supportive
services and low-cost programs. They included financial advisors; One Stop
Career Centers, low-cost insurance providers, mortgage brokers; adult education
programs, etc. Upon conclusion of the resource fairs, we began providing case
management support to the attendees and to fraternal members, who called our
Centralized Intake line seeking assistance and support.
This new scope of service, offered to fraternal members under the age of
60, has become known as the Masonic Families Outreach program. In October
2009, we formally began providing financial and non-financial case management
support. The parameters of this program were defined by eligibility requirements
for financial support as well as the time limits for such support. Financial support
is seen as short-term and intended to act as a bridge from economic hardship
toward self-sufficiency. All clients agree to partner with their Care Manager
toward this goal and must also apply and access any public benefits for which they
qualify. Case management has been extended to our entire Masonic family and
information-referrals are provided to all callers in need of information regarding
community resources. On average, we are now serving between 35-45 clients
per month with case management and 16 clients per month with financial case
management.
Through the generous efforts and guiding vision of Mrs. Judy Hopper,
promoting children’s literacy is also a key component of our Masonic Family
Resource Center. We are collaborating with the Masonic Foundation toward a
literacy outreach program and the development of an online Masonic readers club.

Masonic Senior Outreach Services

Many of our elderly brethren and their wives and widows have
been hard hit by recent economic events and as a result, we are serving more
members through our MSOS program than ever before in our history. This year,

MSOS program; another 250 received information and referral or ongoing case

Intake line has been identified as the single and direct point of inquiry for all
Masonic Assistance Programs, making is easier for our callers. The intake line
telephone number is now being printed on the new dues cards of our members, so
that it is readily available. Additionally, we have bolstered our outreach efforts by
conducting lodge presentations through out the state on a routine basis to ensure
that all of our members know about our services and how to access them.
All in all, it has been an extremely busy and productive year for our
Masonic Outreach and Children’s departments focused on long-term planning to
improve our services to our fraternal family and meet the needs of our members.
We have created a new service infrastructure model so that our programs are
regionally based and that better reflects the needs of our membership across the
generational spectrum. We look forward to the work ahead.

Report of the Administration
and Campus Health Services
On behalf of the residents and staff of the Masonic Homes at Covina,
we are pleased to present the following Annual Report highlighting the successes
and challenges of the past year. As you read our report we hope you will sense our
continued commitment to excellence as we serve our residents and families. We
would like to also express our sincere appreciation to the Board of Trustees and
our Masonic Lodges for their dedication and faithful support of our community.
During the past year we served a senior population which averaged 77
residents and represented a resident mix of 64% Independent Living, 29% Assisted
Living and 7% Skilled Nursing. Over the same period, we had 9 admissions, 6
deaths with one transfer to our Union City Campus.
Our Waiting List included 26 prospective residents representing 21
households. The average waiting period for admission was approximately
12 months. Our staff is committed to call each prospective applicant monthly
to inquire how they are doing both physically and financially. Referrals to our
Masonic Outreach Program are made if services and support are needed.
Our Senior Community offers a “Continuing Care” model of care that
provides a full spectrum of care and services. Each resident is treated with respect
and dignity as they “age in place” in a safe and caring environment. Our campus
does not have a skilled nursing facility or memory care site. To support the skilled
nursing needs of our residents, we have established special transfer arrangements
with our Union City campus and with four high quality skilled nursing facilities in
our surrounding community for those residents who would like to remain near the
Covina campus. Although our residents reside off campus, we remain involved
in the oversight of their care. Our staff and residents visit the skilled nursing
facilities regularly. We conduct routine quality reviews to assure high quality of
care for our residents.
As a resident centered, mission driven community, we are dedicated and
committed to carry out our mission to provide quality care to California Master
Masons, their wives, widows and mothers with dignity and compassion within an
atmosphere based on Masonic tenants, which fulfill the physical, social, spiritual
and nurturing needs of our extended community.
This year our focus has been on “Wellness” and “Successful Aging.”
In February 2010 we started a new program called “Wellness Challenge 2010.”
Residents were invited to participate; the focus was on the obese and overweight
group of residents. A monthly education session on exercise programs and
nutritional advice has produced an overall total weight loss among our residents
of 210 pounds.

Report of the Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
This marks a year of transition for your Masonic Foundation. Continuing
the strategic realignment begun by Right Worshipful John Lowe in 2009, your
Board of Trustees has worked diligently to efficiently execute the programs
currently in place, to assess the impact these programs have achieved, and to put
in place a strategic plan that transforms how your Foundation operates, meets the
desires of the brethren, and satisfies public education needs of our communities as
we aim for our 50th anniversary in 2019.
Culture of Philanthropy
A second strategic planning retreat was held this year with focus on
creating a culture of philanthropy which will guide the Foundation as it moves
forward. We adopted a board development model by which we can better enunciate
the vision and mission of the Foundation, how to communicate our successes to
the membership and the community, and how to establish an environment where
our members can have a direct impact on our ability to make a profound difference
through their charitable gifts. Your Trustees have committed to promoting
your good works through engagement with our members, our Lodges, and the
leadership in our communities.
Current Programs
This was a successful year for the current portfolio of programs
underwritten by your Foundation. The cornerstone of our support to public
education is our scholarship program. Over 2,000 applications were processed this
year using an improved evaluation process and utilizing volunteers from several
local San Francisco area Lodges to help complete the screening. Sixty-four new
scholarship commitments of $962,000 were awarded to deserving high school
seniors this year. In addition, our Claire V. Cunningham Fund for Leadership
in Nursing provided three $100,000 scholarship grants to three California State
University campuses for advanced degrees in nursing education and leadership
to help meet this critical need in our jurisdiction. We also continued our support
to children at risk by training faculty through the Masonic Student Assistance
Program (MSAP) by completing one regional workshop.
Your Foundation continued to underwrite Lodge growth and Masonic
education by funding the Masonic Formation series, the Institute for Masonic
Studies and the annual Masonic Symposium. We also supported our leadership

242

Proceedings of the

development efforts by funding the Wardens’ Leadership Retreats and the Lodge
Certification Program.
This year, the entire program portfolio was reassessed for continued
relevancy and impact versus the dollars being expended. Two programs were
found to no longer be the cutting edge, impactful programs they had been when
initiated by your Foundation.
The MSAP program was the first of its kind when brought to California
in 1994 by Most Worshipful Stovall and a fund established by Most Worshipful
Holsinger’s Grand Master project in 2003. Since then, we have trained over 5,000
teachers and school personnel free of charge, identified over 50,000 kids at risk,
and intervened in the lives of over 25,000. This program brought our fraternity
to the forefront of student assistance and direct participation in helping the
California Department of Education establish student assistance as a permanent
requirement in every county, and establishing several models, including MSAP,
to choose from. Brethren, we have accomplished what we set out to do, and as a
result, our program is no longer the only game in town. We must now recognize
that we can no longer afford to fund the entire effort and that Student Assistance
Programs are now the norm, rather than the exception. As such, your Board has
decided to continue offering the program, but by request and through a regional
model, where the majority of the cost is born by local Lodges and community
entities. In addition, Most Worshipful Holsinger has concurred to expand the use
of the MSAP fund to support future public education projects of the Foundation
that are in line with the strategic plan.
The Child ID program was begun to offer a needed service to our
communities and became an effective way for our Lodges to be involved
and visible in the community. To date, over 800,000 children have had their
photograph and thumb print provided to their parents free of charge using
software provided by the Foundation. Since its inception, numerous community
and law enforcement organizations have taken up the cause and this service has
now become widespread and not uniquely identified to the fraternity. Thus, your
Board has chosen to continue to offer the software capability in the future, which
will allow local Lodges to continue this service, but discontinue further funding
of the overall program.
Aligning to the Strategic Plan
In conjunction with the revision to the jurisdiction Strategic Plan
undertaken by the Executive Committee, your Foundation has moved to align our
strategic plan with that revision. After reviewing the town hall meeting inputs from
all over the jurisdiction, as well as inputs from school district officials, the Board
determined that the current program portfolio, although in line with the revised
Strategic Plan, does not adequately meet the needs identified by the brethren and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

243

the community school districts. As such, the Board began this year to revise our
strategies for addressing Public Education, a process that will continue in 2011.
These new strategies will aim at having a profound impact in three critical areas;
improving literacy in the K – 2nd grade level, middle school math education, and
establishing pathways to success for graduating high school seniors.
The cornerstone for our literacy thrust is the Take Home Book program
initiated this year. During Public Schools Month in April, Grand Master Nagel
presented a check for $25,000 to start the program in 34 kindergarten classes in
the seven lowest performing schools in the San Jose Unified School District. As
with MSAP, we hope to take the program state wide in the coming years and have
as profound an impact on literacy as MSAP has had on student assistance. I look
forward to reporting to you next year that these three strategic initiatives are in
place and beginning to make a profound difference in the educational career of
children in this jurisdiction.
Board Governance
The Board undertook an in-depth self examination this year to evaluate
the effectiveness of the Board in accomplishing its mission. To reduce costs, two
of our quarterly Board meetings were replaced with teleconferences and the third
was held in Covina. To increase communication and drive progress, the Trustees
held monthly telecons where Foundation activity, financials and results were
statused. Trustee roles and responsibilities were clarified as well as an updated
definition of the effort expected from a Trustee. The Trustees were surveyed to
understand their prospective of Foundation operation, the strategic path forward,
and their commitment to seeing our initiatives achieved. As a result, I am pleased
to report your Foundation is being well managed by a strong, committed Board
working together to achieve your strategic objectives.
Two long standing members of the Board will be stepping down at the
end of this Annual Communication and deserve recognition. Brother Tom Albers
has been key to helping transition our MSAP program from its original model to
our new regional model. Brother David Johnson has been a creative driving force
on both the Foundation Board and also the CMMT Board, where he has served
as President. We thank both of these brothers for their years of dedicated service.
Looking Forward to 2011
As the Foundation moves forward into a new year, the Board is excited
about the revised strategic plan and the initiatives we are undertaking to make
the plan a reality. We are poised to expand our portfolio and to meet the needs
of our public education system head on. We are ready to bring new, cutting edge
programs to the table and demonstrate our fraternity’s commitment to making

public education a success. We are ready to lead our Lodges and brethren in
making a profound impact on the lives of students throughout this jurisdiction.
But a truly effective difference cannot be made without your financial support,
my brothers. One brother who has consistently answered the call and has helped
this Foundation raise much of its funding is Brother Raymond Levy. A longtime
chair of the Public Schools Committee in the 1960’s, Brother Ray’s contributions,

profound difference in students’ lives.

Report of the Board of Trustees

of the California Masonic Memorial Temple

Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
This afternoon I am pleased to make the 56th annual report of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple since its incorporation in 1954.
The CMMT owns this great edifice in which we meet today and derives
tax-exempt revenue by leasing its space to the Grand Lodge of California whose
offices are on the third floor; to the Nob Hill Masonic Center that operates the
garage; the telecommunications facility on the roof and to other third parties
who lease space in the building. We also receive tax-exempt contributions from
candidates who are initiated into our California lodges. We are very happy that
this number continues to grow each year. In spite of a lower than expected
return on investments this year due to continued economic volatility, the CMMT
experienced a very healthy cash flow. This Board was most prudent in the expenses
for operating and maintaining this building and we look to an increase in building
use in order to fund necessary improvements in the future.
Upgrade of the Auditorium, California Room and Exhibit Hall
This year, our efforts continue to be devoted to implementing our vision
to keep your facility viable for the future and competitive in the ever changing
market in which we operate. Working with several business partners, we have
implemented plans to optimize the utilization of this building, enabling us to meet
our current and future operating needs, and provide the means for the increasing
costs of maintenance, repair, and restoration. The result will be to create this
auditorium into the premiere performance venue in San Francisco, make the
California Room a viable and welcome respite and transform the Exhibit Hall
and kitchen into a world class restaurant, all while maintaining our beautiful War
Memorial for all time; still serving the needs for our Annual Communication and
Grand Lodge while maintaining a positive relationship with our neighbors on
Nob Hill.
Upgrade of the Parking Garage
The entrance to the parking garage has been redesigned to improve traffic
flow on California Street and accommodate the increased usage of this building.
At the same time we have implemented policies to decrease noise pollution from
the various vendors who rent our facility.

Report of the Board of Directors

of the Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc. is the for-profit, income tax-paying entity
which leases and operates the parking garage at the Nob Hill Masonic. Profits
from the operation of the garage are paid to the Grand Lodge in the form of a
dividend. There are three primary sources of revenue for the parking garage: (1)
monthly parking, (2) transient parking, and (3) event parking.
Monthly parking has declined sharply since the economic downturn in
September 2008. At that time we had 275 monthly parkers. Each month the
number has declined, and it now stands at 178. This loss of 97 monthly parkers
has resulted in the loss of approximately $350,000 in revenue. The losses for
this current year have been greater than expected. In our operating budget we
estimated $641,000 of revenue in monthly parking, but now project that we will
end the fiscal year with $525,000. We continue to aggressively market our garage
for monthly parkers, but remain in a climate where residents and workers in the
area are choosing not to drive or to utilize street parking.
Transient parking revenue is also down from this year’s operating budget.
We budgeted for $512,000 in transient parking revenue and are now projecting
$465,000 for year end. As was the case with monthly parking, the economy has
affected transient parking as well. More and more commuters are looking for
more economical ways to commute in and out of the city.
Event revenue is lower than expected as CMMT and Live Nation
continue to work to get the necessary permits and licenses for the renovation of the
Auditorium. In this fiscal year we anticipated $262,000 in event parking revenue,
and we now project our total income for event revenue will be $251,000. Once
the renovation of the auditorium is undertaken and completed, it is anticipated
that revenue from event parking will increase significantly.
One of the greatest expenses in operating the garage is labor. Until late
this year, our garage was staffed 24 hours seven days a week. This year Nob
Hill undertook a garage automation project to reduce these costs. As a part of
this project the long planned improvements to the garage entrance were also
completed. The entrance, exiting and payment operations were also automated.
Initially this will enable Nob Hill to reduce its labor costs by 50% with possible
additional reductions as we become more comfortable with the new automated
operation. This represents an approximate annual savings of $80,000, after
factoring in financing costs and the depreciation of the new automated system.
The cost of the project was approximately $250,000. This amount is being
financed over a period of 10 years at an interest rate of 5.5%.

On Finance

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Code requires the Committee on Finance to
review all of the proposed Recommendations and Resolutions to be considered at
the Annual Communication and to report on the financial impact these items may
have on the Grand Lodge budget.
Earlier this year, the committee reviewed the Grand Master’s
Recommendations and the Carry-Over and new Resolutions as provided by the
Grand Secretary. On July 20, we finalized our report on the cost impact of each
item and it was mailed to the lodges by the Grand Secretary on July 26 with the
legislation.
Only three items have any financial impact on the Grand Lodge, and in
as much as our written report has been distributed, I will report on them now and
not later during the session.
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 1:
Increases the
Representation on the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee: The
Grand Lodge reimburses the committee members for their necessary expenses
to attend the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee meeting. The
average reimbursement for the most recent meeting was approximately $200
per person. There are currently nine divisions so there would be six additional
committee members. Using these figures, the impact to the Grand Lodge budget
would be approximately $1,200.
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 3: Modifies Masonic Trial
Procedures: According to the Grand Secretary, the Grand Lodge currently spends
approximately $15,500 in administrative support of Masonic trials. It is expected
that the administrative responsibilities of the Grand Lodge will increase with
this new procedure by approximately one-third which could result in additional
expenses of approximately $5,100. This expense has been considered in the
preparation of the 2010/2011 Grand Lodge budget.
Carry-Over Resolution No. 09-01: Creates the Hiram’s Pillar Award:
The certificates will cost the Grand Lodge approximately %500. The resolution
stipulates that the medallion and pin will be made available by Grand Lodge for
purchase, but the potentical cost to Grand Lodge is the expense of any unsold,
returned, or damaged medallions and pins.
Again, in the view of the Committee on Finance, none of the other
legislation will have an impact on the Grand Lodge budget.

Report of the Committee

on Institute for Masonic Studies

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
This report provides information as to the activities of the Institute
for Masonic Studies for the year 2009–2010. The Institute is an agency of the
Grand Lodge of California that seeks to educate the Freemasons and the general
community about the philosophy, values and tenets of Freemasonry and enrich our
understanding of its symbolism and rituals. Regular meetings are held quarterly
during the fiscal year.
The Institute is charged with providing resources to encourage the study
of Freemasonry and oversees programs of the Grand Lodge created to accomplish
these activities.
These responsibilities include the development and implementation of
Masonic Formation programs including Masonic symposiums, membership and
candidate education materials and lodge Masonic education training programs;
the promotion and development of Masonic Formation Committees within
individual lodges in this jurisdiction; and stewardship over the Henry Wilson Coil
Library and Museum.
During this year the following actions were accomplished:
•

At the request of the George Washington National Memorial a
truncated version of the special exhibit (Builders of Dreams)
was provided which included a video presentation of California
Masonry for exhibition at the Memorial.

•

A list of artifacts held by the Henry Wilson Coil Library and
Museum that do not have significant historic or Masonic value
has been developed for de-accession. The disposition of these
items may be by return to original Lodges or individuals related
to the item.

•

The 2010 California Symposium, “Masonry, Military and the
Emergence of American Democracy” was held on June 5, 2010
at the San Francisco Scottish Rite Center. There were 183
registered persons in attendance. The first presenter was the 2010

254

Proceedings of the
Henry Wilson Coil Lecturer, Dr. Steven C. Bullock, Professor of
United States History in the Department of Humanities & Arts
at Worcester Polytechnic Institute in Worcester, Massachusetts
whose paper was: “How Did Military Lodges Unite America’s
Elites?”. The second speaker was Mathew Crow, a fourth year
graduate student in American history at UCLA. Mr. Crow’s
paper was: “Why did Jefferson argue that Masonry was
incompatible with a healthy democracy?”. The third speaker
was Dr. Jessica L. Harland-Jacobs, an Associate Professor of
Modern British and Imperial History in the Department of
History at the University of Florida in Gainesville, Florida.
Her paper was: “How did Military Lodges change after the
American Revolution?”. The symposium concluded with a
panel discussion on Masonry, Military and the Emergence of
American Democracy. The panel included the three symposium
speakers and Dr. John L. Cooper, our Past Grand Secretary, as
the moderator.
•

Masonic Formation workshops were conducted in Newport
Beach, San Diego, Sacramento, and Pleasanton. Work on
revision of the Masonic Formation Mentorship Manuel
is progressing.

•

After some technical delays completion of the Fellow Craft
DVD and Master Mason DVD is expected for release following
the 2010 communication.

•

The Institute has continued administration and oversight
support of the UCLA project to provide off campus classes in
Masonic topics.

The Institute acknowledges with gratitude the support it has received from
the Grand Master, Grand Secretary and Grand Lodge office staff during this year.

Report of the Committee
on Insurance
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Overview
The Insurance Committee is tasked with the responsibility of reviewing
the Grand Lodge property and casualty insurance program, working with the
broker selected by Grand Lodge and making recommendations regarding the
coverages. The Insurance Committee reports directly to the Grand Secretary on
all insurance matters (except Life and Medical Coverage and other benefits for
employees) who makes the final decision regarding the different coverages and
limits to purchase or renew. The Committee also works closely with the Chief
Financial Officer on an ongoing basis.
Currently there are three meetings a Masonic year of the full Committee
and, if needed, an additional meeting late in the calendar year of just the Chairman,
Vice-Chairman and CFO with the Grand Lodge’s insurance broker. The purpose
of this meeting is to update the broker on the current status of the different Grand
Lodge programs and any changes that will be taking place and to receive any
information back from the broker on changes in the insurance market place
regarding costs and coverages. The date for the renewal quotes for the following
policy year is also set at this meeting.
Review of Committee Meetings
The three full Committee meetings are as follows:
1.

The first meeting of the full Committee takes place in January. At this
meeting the broker reviews all of the current coverages presently in
effect and advises the Committee and Grand Lodge personnel on the
status of the insurance markets as to the availability of coverages and
current pricing. The broker also presents recommendations for changes
that could be made with the current coverages or the limits of coverage.
The Grand Lodge staff updates the broker and the Committee on any
changes in operations being made or that will be made that would affect
the coverages that are needed for the upcoming policy year.

2.

The Second meeting of the full Committee takes place on the date set for
the renewal proposals (normally in mid-March) from the broker to be
presented. In addition to presenting the premium quotes for each policy
to be renewed the broker also presents alternative proposals for changes
in limits of coverage or specific coverages themselves. The Committee
then makes recommendations to the Grand Secretary as to how each
policy should be renewed and at what limits of coverage. Once the Grand

256

Proceedings of the
Secretary has these recommendations from the Insurance Committee he
makes the final decision on the recommendations of the Committee. The
renewal policies are then ordered.
3.

The third and final regular meeting of the Committee takes place in
June. By this date all of the renewal policies should have been received
from the broker. The Committee reviews all of the policies to be certain
that they contain the coverages and limits of coverages as ordered and
that there are no new or unusual restrictions or limitations added to the
policies. The Committee works with Grand Lodge staff to be certain
that each policy names as an insured each of the Grand Lodge entities to
which the coverage is to apply.
Key Initiatives

During the past year the Insurance Committee, working with the broker,
put in place a short-term liability insurance program known as Tulip. This program
makes available to Hall Associations short term insurance coverage that can be
purchased by lessees of the Hall Association premises. This coverage guarantees
the Association that liability coverage is available insuring them against liability
claims arising out of actions of the lessee. In the first nine months of the programs
forty-seven Associations availed themselves of the program.
In connection with the leasing of Hall Association properties a sample
premises lease for use between the Association and a lessee is being finalized.
This sample lease will be reviewed by the Grand Lodge legal council and the
Insurance Committee and then make available to the Hall Association.
The Acacia Creek project at Union City was completed during this past
year and is now occupied. The Insurance Committee, working with the broker
and Grand Lodge staff, reviewed needed new insurance coverages and made
recommendations to the Grand Secretary regarding these new coverages, which
were then ordered from the broker.
The Committee is continuing to monitor a new Grand Lodge program
called Masonic Center for Youth and Families. This program will provide
comprehensive services for children and families. Physical facilities for this
program are now being secured in the Presidio in San Francisco. The necessary
new insurance coverages will be reviewed and recommended as the project moves
toward completion.
The Insurance Committee has continued with its function of reviewing
the different insurance coverages of Grand Lodge and working with the broker
to minimize costs but providing the coverages and limits of insurance desired by
Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee
on Investments
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Overview
The Investment Committee is charged with the prudent handling of
Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist primarily of the General
and Endowment funds for the Masonic Homes of California, but also include the
investment portfolios of the California Masonic Foundation, California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the Grand Lodge Retirement plan and the Grand Lodge
itself. We take this charge very seriously. In its simplest terms, we manage the
investment funds with an eye both for growth and preservation of capital. We
strive to maintain a diversified portfolio that is designed to generate the necessary
funds for the continuing operation of the Masonic functions as well as allow for
growth for future needs. In doing so, we constantly scan the horizon in an attempt
to manage the funds to take advantage of long-term trends and opportunities.
The Grand Lodge Investment Committee utilizes the services of professional
investment management firms to gain access to the capital markets. Funds are
primarily invested in U.S. and international equity and fixed income markets,
although we have recently embarked on investing in less traditional vehicles
which are not as correlated to the stock and bond markets.
The capital markets in which the Grand Lodge invests had negative
performance over the past fiscal year (now ending October 31), however, the 4th
quarter of last year showed significant improvement which continued into the 1st
and 2nd quarters of this calendar year.
Grand Lodge Investment Performance
For the year ended 6-30-10
Our U.S. equity portfolio was down 28.3% compared to -26.6% for the
Russell 3000 Index. The Non-U.S. equity portfolio was down 30.9% compared to
-31.4% for the MSCI EAFE Index. Global Equities were down 23.7% compared
to -29.3% for the MSCI All-Country World Index. The fixed income portfolio was
up 6.3% compared to a gain in the Barclays bond Index of 6.0%. Our Alternative
Investments were down 15.8% compared to -15.1% for the HFR Fund of Funds

258

Proceedings of the

Index. Finally the Global Tactical Assets Investments were down 7.0% compared
to its benchmark of a positive 3.5%. Following a very strong rebound in the
equity markets in 2009, markets have been very mixed in the first half of 2010.
Detailed manager performance can be found in the tables following this report.
The U.S. and world economies have just endured the longest and most
severe downturn since the Great Depression. The recession was initiated by an
extended period of excessive credit across the globe and a collapse in U.S. housing
prices. While it is too soon to pronounce the worst is behind us, it is probably
fair to say that a world-wide meltdown in the financial system was averted. The
Federal Reserve has kept interest rates near zero in an effort to stimulate the
economy, while keeping an eye to preventing a resurgence of inflation.
The Investment Committee does not attempt to take advantage of
perceived short-term anomalies in the markets by chasing the most recent top
performing asset class. Rather, it arrives at its recommended allocation to stocks
and bonds and other asset classes only after very careful due diligence and
consideration. The purpose of the funds, their spending requirements, investment
time horizon and ability to assume risk are all factored into the recommendations.
The possibility and duration of potential losses are carefully weighed against the
long-term potential for appreciation of assets after withdrawals are taken into
account. The Investment Committee recommends asset allocations that will
provide the highest probability that the funds will be able to meet their respective
objectives over the long-term.
Grand Lodge & Related Entity Investment Performance
For the year ended 6-30-10
The market value of the Masonic Home’s portfolio as of June 30, 2010,
was $600.9 million compared to $783.7 million a year earlier. This, combined with
the investment portfolios of the other entities which the Investment Committee
advises, resulted in combined assets totaling slightly more than $642.5 million
compared to $837.5 a year ago.
As of June 30, 2010, the combined funds of Grand Lodge and the related
Masonic entities were down 19.8% for the twelve-month period. This compares
to -21.0% for the custom benchmark index.
For the three-year period ending June 30th, the combined Grand Lodge
and related entities funds were down 4.2% versus -4.1% for the benchmark.
Since inception, however, our funds have returned 7.0% annually versus the 6.8%
return of the benchmark. Detailed Entity performance can be found in the tables
following this report.

Grand Lodge Investment Management
For the year ended 6-30-10
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand Lodge
Investment Policy and Philosophy, the Investment Committee meets quarterly
with our Investment Consultant, Hewitt EnnisKnupp and our individual portfolio
managers. We review their respective performance compared to various indices
representing their objective. This process provides the Investment Committee
with the necessary data to adequately evaluate each investment manager on a
timely basis, and to observe whether they continue to achieve the objectives of
their mandate.
Our Investment Consultant, EnnisKnupp was recently purchased by
Hewitt and Associates. This combination of firms was closely followed by
the announced acquisition of Hewitt EnnisKnupp by Aon Corporation. The
Investment Committee is evaluating the ramifications of these changes to ensure
that the quality and independence of the advice we receive from our consultant is
not diminished in any way.
Not only is the Investment Committee responsible for managing the
portfolios of our various organizations, but it also oversees the management of our
planned gift investments. The current portfolio of planned gifts includes nearly
$10 million, including $7.5 million in charitable trusts and just over $2 million
in charitable gift annuities. Despite the obvious difficulties in our economy, the
Grand Lodge fundraising staff had another successful year in the solicitation of
planned gifts. Particular recognition should go to Bro. Richard “Dick” Kellogg,
our Planned Giving Officer, who has raised many charitable planned gifts from
brethren and their families interested in leaving a charitable legacy this year. The
Investment Committee is grateful to the entire staff at the offices of Philanthropy
and Finance for their support and hard work this past year, and look forward to
another successful philanthropic campaign in 2010-2011.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee is also available to assist
individual lodges in determining appropriate investment strategy. One available
vehicle to aid in this effort is the “Lodge Investment Options Program” which
is intended to assist Lodges in determining an appropriate investment strategy
and asset allocation. This program has recently been completely revised and
updated. Whether you currently have Lodge investments or are considering
implementing such a program, we direct your Lodge trustees’ or investment
committeemen’s attention to the Grand Lodge website for more information on
this turnkey program. We are also here to help Lodges establish a set of policies
and procedures that are designed to ensure assets are invested according to the
needs of the Lodge and to safeguard against the misuse of funds. Investment
Committee members continue to make themselves available to the Lodges for
assistance with this program and other questions regarding Lodge investments.

Report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The
Committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered
at the next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the Committee’s view, those of Grand Master Nagel’s decisions and
dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion. In the
Committee’s view, the legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 26th of
this year is sufficient to carry out the intent of the proponents, and the legislation
contained in Grand Master Nagel’s recommendations which he will present in his
message is sufficient to carry out his intent. We believe that each piece of this
legislation has the legal effect set forth in it.
The legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 26th of this
year and the legislation contained in Grand Master Nagel’s recommendations
require no separate motion because they are automatically before this Annual
Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote required for the
passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation which does not
amend the California Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple majority only
for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or the Ritual must
be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a simple
majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries over to the next
Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote is required for
adoption.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.
Respectfully submitted,
R. Stephen Doan, PGM, Chairman
